true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate def self.downsize redefines the public API and silently breaks 5-argument callers

The file now contains two def self.downsize definitions. In Ruby the second definition (line 149) completely replaces the first (line 145), so the 5-argument form downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={}) is now dead and unreachable. Any caller that still uses the 5-argument signature (plugins, jobs, or other internal code) will instead hit the 4-argument version downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={}), which interprets the third positional argument as a dimensions string (e.g. "100") rather than a width, and the fourth as opts (so a hash expected for opts will receive an integer and crash on opts[:allow_animation]). Either remove the unused first definition, or keep the 5-argument form as the canonical signature and remove the new 4-argument overload.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 10MB client-side limit breaks max_attachment_size_kb for non-image uploads

validateUploadedFile is called for both images and attachments (type is 'image' or 'attachment'). The previous code used Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'] so attachment uploads respected SiteSetting.max_attachment_size_kb. The change to a hardcoded 10MB means any admin who has set max_attachment_size_kb to anything larger than 10MB will see those legitimate attachment uploads rejected client-side, even though the server side still allows them. The intended behavior of letting oversized images through for downsizing should only apply to images, not attachments, since attachments are not downsized in this PR.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

false_positives.candidate:
Downsize loop silently proceeds if file cannot be reduced under max_image_size_kb

After up to 5 iterations of OptimizedImage.downsize at 80%, the loop only checks tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes. The return value of OptimizedImage.downsize (which can be false if convert/gifsicle fails) is ignored, so an unsupported/corrupt image produces no error. More importantly, if the loop exhausts attempts and the file is still above max_image_size_kb, the code falls through and calls Upload.create_for anyway, so an oversized file is stored with no feedback to the user. The user has spent bandwidth uploading a file that should have been rejected. Either surface an error if the loop ends without success, or break out and skip the upload.

FileHelper.download limit raised to 10.megabytes, allowing oversized URL fetches

The download cap was changed from SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes (e.g. 4MB) to a hardcoded 10.megabytes. The only motivation is to fetch a larger image so it can be downsized locally. As a side effect, the server will now happily fetch up to 10MB from any URL the API caller supplies (and then potentially store a 10MB file even if the configured max_image_size_kb is, say, 500KB, if the downsize loop fails to bring it down). For sites that intentionally keep max_image_size_kb small to limit storage, this widens both bandwidth and disk exposure. The cap should stay tied to (or be a multiple of) SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb, not unconditionally 10MB.

OptimizedImage.downsize is invoked with source and destination pointing at the same tempfile path

OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, '80%', ...) reads from and writes to the same file. ImageMagick's convert typically needs to fully open the input before writing the output, and on many filesystems this fails or corrupts the source. Use a separate Tempfile for the destination and move it back over the original on success.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation crashes with NoMethodError when host is nil

`before_validation do; self.host.sub!(/^https?:\/\//, ''); self.host.sub!(/\/.*$/, ''); end` invokes `String#sub!` on `self.host` with no nil check. If a record is built without a `host` (e.g. via `EmbeddableHost.new`, the controller's `save_host(EmbeddableHost.new)` flow with no host supplied, or anything that ever constructs a record with `host` unset), Rails calls this `before_validation` callback first and raises `NoMethodError: undefined method `sub!` for nil:NilClass` before the format validation ever runs. Either guard with `self.host = (self.host || '').sub(...)` or move the stripping into a setter / `after_initialize` that tolerates nil.

true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
update and destroy actions crash with NoMethodError when the host id is invalid

`update` does `host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first; save_host(host)` and `destroy` does `host = EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first; host.destroy`. If `params[:id]` does not match any record (typo, stale client, manual request), `host` is `nil` and `save_host(nil)` raises `NoMethodError` from `nil.host = ...` / `nil.category_id = ...`, and `nil.destroy` raises `NoMethodError: undefined method 'destroy' for nil`. Both branches should respond with `not_found` (or render_json_error) before calling `save_host`/`destroy`, since the staff user otherwise gets a 500 for what should be a 404.

true_positives.golden_comment: The contents of `category_fabricator.rb` and `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` have been swapped, resulting in the loss of original category fabricators and potentially causing errors in fabricator usage.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fabricator file contents appear to be swapped between category_fabricator.rb and embeddable_host_fabricator.rb

`spec/fabricators/category_fabricator.rb` after the PR contains only `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)`, while the newly-added `spec/fabricators/embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` contains all of the `Fabricator(:category)` / `:diff_category` / `:happy_category` / `:private_category)` definitions that used to live in `category_fabricator.rb`. The fabricator gem registers by symbol so specs will still execute, but the contents are clearly the wrong way round — the file named for categories defines the embeddable_host fabricator and vice versa — which makes future maintenance (and any code that auto-loads fabricators via filename) confusing and fragile. Move `Fabricator(:embeddable_host)` into `embeddable_host_fabricator.rb` and restore the category fabricators to `category_fabricator.rb`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The SQL query in the `app/controllers/admin/embeddable_hosts_controller.rb` file uses string interpolation (`'#{h}'`) to insert values, which is vulnerable to SQL injection. It should use parameter binding or proper quoting to prevent this security vulnerability.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
SQL injection via interpolation in migration INSERT

The migration interpolates the per-line `h` value from `site_settings.embeddable_hosts` directly into a raw SQL INSERT string: `INSERT INTO embeddable_hosts (host, category_id, created_at, updated_at) VALUES ('#{h}', #{category_id}, ...)`. Any value containing a single quote in the site setting breaks the SQL and any crafted value can inject arbitrary SQL (CREATE FUNCTION, UPDATE site_settings, exfiltration, etc.). The migration must use parameterized queries (e.g. `conn.exec_params(...)` via a PG-specific helper, or sanitize/quote the value) instead of string interpolation. The same applies when `category_id` is 0 and the uncategorized fallback is used as `#{category_id}` — the assumption that this is a safe integer is asserted, not validated, and any non-integer returned by the SQL fallback would also break the query.

true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration will fail (or insert garbage) when uncategorized_category_id is the default -1

The fallback `category_id = execute(... WHERE name='uncategorized_category_id')[0]['value'].to_i` reads the raw `site_settings.value` for `uncategorized_category_id`. On a fresh install this setting is its YAML default of `-1`, so `category_id` becomes `-1` and the subsequent INSERTs write `category_id = -1`, which either violates the FK to `categories.id` (migration fails partway, leaving a half-applied state) or silently inserts invalid rows that no other code path can legitimately surface. The migration must guard against `category_id <= 0` (no valid category to assign) and either skip inserts or refuse to run with a clear error rather than blindly use whatever integer was read. Additionally, on databases where the `embed_category` lookup returns no rows, `[0]['id']` is `nil` and `[0]['value']` further on can also be `nil`, causing `nil['id']`/`nil['value']` NoMethodErrors that crash the migration.

false_negatives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.

Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.

false_positives.candidate:
Embedding PUT /admin/customize/embedding is a no-op that silently accepts writes

`update` only re-renders `@embedding`; it never persists anything. Combined with the front-end `saveChanges` action in `admin-embedding.js.es6` which calls `this.get('embedding').update({})`, a staff user clicking any future 'save embedding settings' button would appear to succeed (200 + refreshed JSON) while nothing was actually written. If this controller is genuinely a placeholder, it should at minimum 405 / log so it's obvious; if saving per-host records is the intended workflow (which is what the rest of the page does) then the unused `saveChanges` action and PUT route should be removed so future readers don't waste time tracing a dead path.

Imported embed posts will fall back to uncategorized when no EmbeddableHost record exists

`TopicEmbed.import` now uses `category: eh.try(:category_id)` where `eh = EmbeddableHost.record_for_host(url)`. When the referring host has no matching `embeddable_hosts` row (the previously-existing `SiteSetting.embed_category` was a simple string default), `category_id` will be `nil`, so the post is filed in the uncategorized bucket rather than the admin-configured embed category. Historically a setting ensured there was always a category; with the setting removed, the only path to a real category is registering the host. This is a behaviour change worth flagging for operators who relied on `SiteSetting.embed_category` to retroactively file old imports — it now silently does nothing for unconfigured hosts and any future import race-condition (host not yet saved) goes to uncategorized. Either restore a default-category fallback at the call site or document the new requirement explicitly in `config/locales/server.en.yml`.

Migration performs destructive, non-reversible work inside `change`

The migration uses `def change` but it does irreversible things inside: it deletes `site_settings` rows for `embeddable_hosts` and `embed_category` and only inserts new `embeddable_hosts` rows. Running `rake db:rollback` will drop the `embeddable_hosts` table (the only part Rails knows how to reverse) but cannot restore the deleted site settings or the host data, so a rollback silently loses configuration. Migrations that move data should be split into explicit `up`/`down` methods, or at minimum copy the affected `site_settings` rows into a backing table before deleting so the data can be restored on rollback. There are also no tests covering the migration's data-move behavior, only the host-validation and host-allow logic.

No behavioural specs for EmbeddableHostsController create/update/destroy or save_host

The only assertion is that the class inherits from `Admin::AdminController`. The actual behaviour — assignment of `host` and `category_id` from `params[:embeddable_host]`, the fallback to `SiteSetting.uncategorized_category_id` when category_id is blank, the JSON error render when the model is invalid, and the success response shape — has no spec. Given the SQL-injection-adjacent migration and the controller-level nil-handling bug reported elsewhere, this controller deserves at least a happy-path create spec and a 404 / not-found spec.

No presence validation on category despite NOT NULL DB constraint

The migration declares `category_id` as `null: false` and the controller/admin UI relies on every embeddable host having a category, but `EmbeddableHost` only `validates_format_of :host`. The model has `belongs_to :category` but no corresponding `validates :category, presence: true`. As a result, an admin can save a host via direct API or through any future code path with `category_id: nil` and the failure surfaces only as a generic ActiveRecord `NOT NULL` DB error from the SQL adapter instead of a friendly validation error. Add `validates :category_id, presence: true` (or `validates_presence_of :category`) so the failure mode is consistent with the other validations.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TopicUser.find_by result used without a nil check, raising NoMethodError

`tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` at line 105 may return nil — for example when the recipient has never visited the topic, when a `TopicUser` row was removed independently, or when the notification email was sent by a path that didn't go through `TopicUser.change` and so never created the row. The next two lines (`tu.notification_level > …`, `tu.notification_level = …`) and the subsequent `tu.save!` all dereference `tu` and will raise NoMethodError, surfacing a 500 instead of performing the unsubscribe. Use `TopicUser.change(current_user.id, params[:topic_id], notification_level: …)` (which creates a row when missing), or guard `tu` against nil and respond with a redirect or 404.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

false_positives.candidate:
MessageBuilder spec does not assert that the per-topic unsubscribe URL reaches the email body

The test was updated to pass `unsubscribe_url: "/t/1234/unsubscribe"` to MessageBuilder, but the only body assertion in the `add_unsubscribe_link true` context still only checks for the global `user_preferences_url`. There is no expectation that the supplied `unsubscribe_url` is interpolated into the rendered `body` (or `html_part`). A regression where the new `%{unsubscribe_url}` placeholder is silently dropped (e.g. a missing I18n interpolation variable, or a typo in the gsub) would not be caught. Add an assertion such as `expect(message_with_unsubscribe.body).to match("/t/1234/unsubscribe")` and one for `html_part` too.

New TopicsController#unsubscribe action has no controller spec

The `unsubscribe` action at lines 98-116 introduces nontrivial behaviour — slug-aware 301 redirect to `topic.unsubscribe_url`, conditional demotion of `TopicUser.notification_level` between `:regular` and `:muted`, mutation via direct `find_by` + `save!` rather than `TopicUser.change` (so it bypasses the `MessageBus` publish and `notifications_changed_at`/`notifications_reason_id` updates other code paths rely on), and rendering `show` via `perform_show_response` — yet the PR adds no controller request spec. The two bugs above (`ensure_logged_in` and the nil `tu` dereference) would both be caught by even a basic logged-in request spec.

Per-topic unsubscribe is a GET with side effects, no CSRF token, and no per-user signature Both unsubscribe routes are defined as `get` and the controller action mutates `TopicUser#notification_level`. There is no signed token in `topic.unsubscribe_url` (it is just `#{Discourse.base_url}/t/#{slug}/#{id}/unsubscribe`, which is guessable from the topic id alone) and Rails' request forgery protection only applies to non-GET verbs. Consequence is twofold: (1) any third-party page can CSRF a logged-in Discourse user into being silently demoted from a topic via `` or a similar tag; (2) combined with the `ensure_logged_in` issue above, the action also doesn't authorise the email recipient — once the recipient logs in, whoever's session that is has their preference for that topic changed, which is the wrong user. This should be either a POST endpoint protected by CSRF token, or a GET that requires a server-signed token tied to (user, topic) — the same pattern already used by `EmailUnsubscribeKey` in Discourse.

ensure_logged_in before_filter breaks the email one-click unsubscribe flow

`:unsubscribe` is added to the `ensure_logged_in` before_filter list (line 28), so a recipient clicking the unsubscribe link delivered in an email — who by definition is not authenticated — is bounced to the login page before reaching the action. The entire purpose of the per-topic unsubscribe link is to give the user a single, friction-free way out from their mail client; forcing a login defeats that. The action either needs to be excluded from `ensure_logged_in` and instead authorised via a signed, expiring token (the RFC 8058 one-click unsubscribe pattern), or the link should not be sent to anyone who isn't already signed in. As shipped, the new email copy added in server.en.yml (`unsubscribe_link`) and the `unsubscribe_url` interpolation in user_notifications.rb route users into a flow that will not work.

unsubscribe_link translation silently requires unsubscribe_url with no contract enforcement

The `unsubscribe_link` translation was rewritten to interpolate `%{unsubscribe_url}` (line 1855), but `Email::MessageBuilder` (lib/email/message_builder.rb) does not enforce that the key is present in `template_args` — it just calls `I18n.t('unsubscribe_link', template_args)` and `gsub`s the result. Any caller that sets `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without also passing `unsubscribe_url` will produce an email whose "click here" link has an empty `href` or a literal `%{unsubscribe_url}` placeholder. Today only `UserNotifications#send_notification_email` passes the new option, but there is nothing to stop the next mailer that copies the pattern from forgetting it. Either provide a default in the translation, document the requirement next to the `add_unsubscribe_link` keyword, or have MessageBuilder raise when the key is missing.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
EmailValidator triggers DB writes on every validation via BlockedEmail.should_block?

validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which writes to the blocked_emails table (match_count and last_match_at) on every match. ActiveRecord typically runs validators multiple times during a single save: the controller calls `user.valid?` before save, ActiveRecord re-runs validations inside save, and re-runs them again on retries after uniqueness/format errors. Each blocked-email signup therefore inflates match_count several times and adds several UPDATE queries to the request path. Worse, calling `record.valid?` (without saving) still updates persisted state, which is surprising for a validator. Statistics tracking should be moved out of the validator (e.g., to an after_validation hook on User, or a Redis counter incremented only on actual save) so validation remains side-effect free and counters are not inflated.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BlockedEmail lookup is case-sensitive, allowing blocklist bypass via email casing

`BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` is a case-sensitive comparison, so a blocklist row stored as `bad@spamclub.com` will not match `BAD@spamclub.com`, `Bad@spamclub.com`, or any other case variant. This is inconsistent with the rest of the user-facing email code: User.find_by_username_or_email calls Email.downcase before lookup, the regex built in EmailValidator#email_in_restriction_setting? matches regardless of case, and email comparisons elsewhere in the codebase are case-insensitive. An attacker registering with a case-variant email bypasses the block entirely. The lookup should normalize (e.g., `BlockedEmail.where(email: email.downcase).first`) or emails should be lowercased on insert (with a citext/case-insensitive column), and the matching test should explicitly assert case-variant behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

false_positives.candidate:
EmailValidator whitelist/blacklist logic is not covered by tests

The original User#email_validator implemented two branches (SiteSetting.email_domains_whitelist and SiteSetting.email_domains_blacklist) that were extracted into lib/validators/email_validator.rb. The new spec only stubs BlockedEmail.should_block? and never sets email_domains_whitelist or email_domains_blacklist, so the regex-based domain matching, the priority between the whitelist and the blacklist (if/elsif), and the email_in_restriction_setting? helper are completely untested. The .gsub('.', '\.') escaping, the @-anchored regex, and the if/elsif precedence are non-trivial and easy to silently regress, so each branch (whitelist match, whitelist mismatch, blacklist match, blacklist mismatch, both unset) needs at least one explicit test.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: Unescaped URL interpolation in the imported_from link enables stored XSS The string `"#{url}"` is interpolated into the stored raw HTML with no escaping. `url` comes from `i.link`/`i.id` in the RSS feed (or from `TopicEmbed.import_remote`). When it contains characters like `'` or `>`, the rendered `` breaks out of its attribute and any following text becomes new HTML, e.g. `https://x/?'>` produces `'>...`. Because the post is saved with `cook_method: :raw_html` and the embed view emits it via `<%= raw post.cooked %>`, the injected `

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError on nil feed content crashes the scheduled job

`content = CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)` calls `scrub` on `i.content` directly. `NilClass#scrub` does not exist, so whenever an RSS/Atom item is missing a `content` field (which is the common case for items that only carry a `<description>` or `<summary>`) the scheduled job raises `NoMethodError`. The job is `retry: false`, so the failure is permanent; the feed will never be importable. Guard with `i.content.to_s.scrub` (or check `i.content` first) before unescaping.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

false_positives.candidate:
Concurrent imports on the same embed_url race past the blank? check

`self.import` first does `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` to decide whether to insert, and only then calls `TopicEmbed.create!`. The migration creates a unique index on `embed_url`, but nothing in `import` rescues the duplicate-key exception that arises if a second concurrent job (e.g. two simultaneous loads of the same embeddable URL while retrieve_topic jobs run in parallel) reaches the insertion point. The losing transaction raises, and since the `Topic.transaction` block already ran a real `PostCreator.create`, an orphan topic and first post are left behind with no `TopicEmbed` row. Either guard the insert with the unique index in a single upsert, or rescue `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique` and re-read the existing record.

PollFeed is run synchronously on every embed retrieval

In `perform_retrieve`, when `SiteSetting.feed_polling_enabled?` is on, the retriever invokes `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` inline for every embed page load. PollFeed fetches and parses the full RSS/ATOM feed and calls `TopicEmbed.import` on every item. A busy embeddable page can therefore trigger many redundant full-feed imports. The scheduled job should be allowed to run on its own cadence and the retriever should not invoke it inline; only an explicit per-URL RSS lookup should be performed here.

X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL is not a valid directive, browsers ignore it

The controller sets `response.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = "ALLOWALL"`. `ALLOWALL` is not one of the standardized X-Frame-Options values (DENY / SAMEORIGIN / ALLOW-FROM uri) and browsers ignore unknown values, falling back to whatever default framing policy is in effect. If the host previously sent a stricter value, or modern browsers apply a stricter default, the embed iframe will be blocked cross-origin, defeating the purpose of the embed controller. Use a `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' https://<embeddable-host>` header (or `ALLOW-FROM` plus that host) to actually permit cross-origin framing.

cook_method column default is :raw_html, breaking all existing posts

The migration adds `cook_method` with `default: 1, null: false`, but in `app/models/post.rb` the Enum is declared as `Enum.new(:regular, :raw_html)`, which follows the standard 0-indexed convention (`:regular` = 0, `:raw_html` = 1). Backfilling every existing row to 1 makes every pre-existing post look like `:raw_html`, and `Post#before_save` then sets `cooked = cook(raw, ...)`; for any subsequently edited post, `cook` returns `raw` (Markdown text) instead of the rendered HTML. The default should be `0` (regular), so existing posts continue to use the cooking pipeline until they are explicitly imported with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Invalid -ms-align-items property in align-items mixin

The align-items mixin emits `-ms-align-items: $alignment;`, which is not a valid CSS property. The Microsoft/IE10 syntax for alignment is `-ms-flex-align`, which is already included on the preceding line. Browsers silently ignore unknown property names, so this line is harmless dead output, but it is misleading to future readers and clutters the compiled CSS. It should be removed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

false_positives.candidate:
order() applied to non-flex item has no effect

@include order(2) is added to .extra-info-wrapper at the top level of the selector, but the CSS in this file does not make .extra-info-wrapper (or any of its ancestors inside this PR) a flex container, and the property only takes effect on flex items. Consequence: the rule is dead code; the author appears to intend for this element to be reordered within a flex row, but the layout will not change at all, so the rendered topic header ordering is unchanged from before this PR. Either the parent (e.g. #topic-title) must be turned into a flex container, or the rule should be removed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.

false_positives.candidate:
Subdomain-vs-subdomain branch of website_name is not tested

The new `website_name` method in app/serializers/user_serializer.rb has three branches: exact host match, subdomain equality (website_host.split('.').length == discourse_host.split('.').length && > 2), and the parent/child fallback. The added specs cover the exact-match branch ('example.com' == 'example.com') and the parent/child branch ('example.com' vs 'forums.example.com'), but the middle `elsif` branch — for example `forum.example.com` vs `blog.example.com` (both have 3+ segments with a shared suffix like 'example.com') — has no test. This is a meaningful logic path that should be covered; without it, regressions in subdomain matching could ship unnoticed.

URI(website.to_s) is parsed three times in website_name

The `website_name` method calls `URI(website.to_s)` three times (once for `host`, then twice more for `.path` in each reachable branch). The serializer runs per user and is invoked for user lists (e.g. user cards, directory), so this is per-request overhead on every user serialization. Parse once into a local variable and reuse `parsed_uri.host` / `parsed_uri.path`.

website_name silently drops URL port, query, and fragment

`website_name` returns only `URI(...).host + URI(...).path`. For a user-supplied website such as `http://example.com:8080/users/123?ref=foo#bar`, the displayed link text becomes `example.com/users/123`, losing the port, query string, and fragment. The PR title says 'show complete URL path' but the implementation never defines what 'path' includes (path-only vs full-URL). At minimum this behavior should be documented in a comment on `website_name`, and ideally the intent (e.g., always show full URL via `URI#to_s` minus scheme, or only host+path) should be made explicit and tested.

The lightness for the light theme changed from 30% to 70%, which is a dramatic inversion

Lightness value changed for .group-member-info .name in light theme

true_positives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Race condition: members load after the template has already rendered

`setupController` calls `model.findMembers()` but does not return its promise, so Ember does not wait for the AJAX request to finish before the template renders. The `{{#each m in members}}` block in `group/members.hbs` will therefore render with `members` undefined for a brief flash of empty content, then re-render when the promise resolves. The previous implementation used `afterModel` whose returned promise was awaited by the router before `setupController` ran, guaranteeing the data was ready. This is a UX regression and should be fixed either by returning the promise from `setupController` or by reverting to `afterModel` (or by toggling a loading flag in the controller until `findMembers` resolves).

true_positives.golden_comment: The remove_member test uses xhr :put to call the remove_member action, but the route defines delete 'members' => 'groups#remove_member' requiring DELETE method.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test invokes remove_member with xhr :put but route is DELETE

At line 115, `it "cannot remove members from automatic groups"` does `xhr :put, :remove_member, group_id: 1, user_id: 42`. The route for `remove_member` is defined as `delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"` (HTTP method DELETE). No PUT route exists for this action, so Rails cannot match the request and the test will fail with `ActionController::UrlGenerationError`. The HTTP verb in the spec must match the route verb.

true_positives.golden_comment: Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined
true_positives.matched_candidate:
findMembers returns undefined instead of a resolved promise when name is empty

When `this.get('name')` is empty, the function executes `return ;` which yields `undefined`. The previous version returned `Ember.RSVP.resolve([])`. This violates the implicit promise-returning contract of a `find*` method: any caller that chains `.then(...)` will throw `TypeError: Cannot read property 'then' of undefined`. While the immediate callers in this PR (`admin_group_route.js`, `group-members.js.es6`, `admin-group.js.es6`) happen not to chain, future callers will. The function should return `Ember.RSVP.resolve()` (or at minimum `[]` so callers awaiting `.length` don't break) when name is blank.

true_positives.golden_comment: The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Controller requires params[:group_id] but routes are member routes requiring :id

The `add_members` action (line 66) and `remove_member` action (line 85) both call `params.require(:group_id).to_i`. However, the routes `delete "members" => "groups#remove_member"` and `put "members" => "groups#add_members"` are written directly inside `resources :groups do ... end` in `config/routes.rb`, not inside a `collection do ... end` block. In Rails, direct routes at this nesting level are treated as member routes, producing URLs like `DELETE /admin/groups/:id/members` (where `:id` is the group ID). The JS client sends `DELETE /admin/groups/{id}/members.json` which matches the member-route pattern, but then `params[:group_id]` is never populated, so every call raises `ActionController::ParameterMissing: param is missing or the value is empty: group_id`. The admin group-member add/remove feature is therefore entirely broken. To fix, either move the routes into a `collection do ... end` block and have the client pass `group_id` as a query/body parameter, or change the controller to read `params[:id]`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.

The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.

false_positives.candidate:
Redundant group.save after users.delete and swallowed errors

In `remove_member`, `group.users.delete(user_id)` calls `ActiveRecord::Associations::CollectionAssociation#delete`, which directly issues a SQL DELETE on the join record and is already persisted. The subsequent `group.save` therefore has no unsaved changes to commit and cannot fail because of the deletion. The `if group.save / else render_json_error(group)` branching is misleading. Additionally, any DB-level error raised by `delete` (FK violations, lock timeouts, etc.) is not rescued, so the controller would 500 instead of returning a clean JSON error.

Silent failure on non-existent usernames in add_members

In `add_members`, when `User.find_by_username(username)` returns nil, the `if user = ...` branch silently skips that entry. The action still returns `success_json` as long as `group.save` succeeds, even if zero users were actually added. Admins therefore have no signal that a typo or non-existent account caused some (or all) intended members to be dropped. The action should accumulate the missing usernames and return them in the response, or return a non-success status when any username is unknown. The same applies to usernames that contain stray whitespace after splitting on commas (`"a, b"` produces `" b"`).

Stray closing with no matching opening tag Line 19 contains a `` inside the `{{#each m in members}}` block but there is no corresponding opening `
` anywhere in the template. This is invalid HTML and will produce browser parser warnings and an unexpected DOM tree (the browser will silently ignore the orphaned closer, or restructure siblings). Either remove the stray tag or wrap the rows in a matching element.

Tests pass group_id but the member routes require :id in the URL

The `add_members` test (line 103) and `remove_member` tests (lines 115, 125) pass `group_id: group.id` as a request parameter. Because the routes are member routes that require `:id` in the URL path, Rails' URL generator cannot find `:id` in the parameters and will either raise `ActionController::UrlGenerationError` or substitute `group_id` for `:id` and produce an unintended URL. The tests must pass `id: group.id` (with the controller updated to read `params[:id]`), or the routes must be rewritten as collection routes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
@loaded_locales ||= [] in ensure_loaded! is racy

`ensure_loaded!` does `@loaded_locales ||= []` outside of `LOAD_MUTEX`. Under MRI this is benign because of the GIL, but the assignment is not atomic and the subsequent `@loaded_locales.include?(locale)` is also unsynchronized. The actual file loading is protected by `load_locale`'s mutex, so correctness is preserved, but the pre-check is misleading: two threads can both fall through to `load_locale` and serialize on the mutex for no reason, and a `reload!` interleaved between the `||=` and the include? check could change the meaning of the check. Move the include? and load inside the mutex, or accept the duplication explicitly with a comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mixed string/symbol in fallback list causes duplicate locale file loads

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` builds `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact`. `SiteSetting.default_locale` is a String (from the model) and `:en` is a Symbol, so the array mixes types. `Array#uniq` compares with `eql?`/`hash`, and `:en.eql?("en")` is `false`, so `["en", :en, :en].uniq` returns `["en", :en]` instead of one element. The result is then iterated by `ensure_loaded!`, calling `I18n.ensure_loaded!` for both `"en"` and `:en`. Each call ends up in `translate_accelerator.rb#load_locale`, where `Regexp.new("\\.#{locale}\\.yml$")` matches the same `*.en.yml` file for both the String and the Symbol, so the file is loaded and parsed twice on the first request from an English (or default-English) user. Fix by coercing consistently, e.g. `[locale.to_sym, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact`, and storing/comparing `@loaded_locales` as Symbols in `translate_accelerator.rb`.

false_positives.candidate:
FallbackLocaleList subclasses Hash but never uses Hash storage

`class FallbackLocaleList < Hash` only overrides `[]` and `ensure_loaded!`; no value is ever written to the underlying hash. This will silently drop any assignments made by `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` or callers that expect a real map (for example, an `I18n.fallbacks[locale] = [...]` override in a plugin or future Rails internal). Either drop the `Hash` superclass and just respond to `[]`, or actually populate the hash so callers can read the configured chain (e.g. for diagnostics or plugin overrides).

No test covers the new ensure_loaded! call in set_locale

The added `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` introduces a custom fallback chain (user locale → site default → English) and triggers translation loading on every request, but no controller or initializer test is included. In particular there is no coverage for: (a) anonymous users falling back to `SiteSetting.default_locale`, (b) a logged-in user whose `effective_locale` differs from the site default, (c) the dedup behaviour between `SiteSetting.default_locale` and `:en`. The PR description ("Test 9") does not point at any spec either.

PR description "Test 9" does not describe the change

The PR body is just "Test 9" and there are no specs in the diff, so reviewers and future archeology cannot tell what behaviour was intended to be exercised. At minimum the description should enumerate which fallback chains and which anonymous/logged-in locale combinations are being validated, and link to the relevant spec files.

true_positives.golden_comment: In UsernameForm.authenticate(), isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() is called without passing the required UserModel parameter.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Compile error: isConditionalPasskeysEnabled() called without required argument

In `UsernameForm.authenticate()` the expression `!isConditionalPasskeysEnabled()` invokes a zero-argument method, but the only declaration of that name in the inheritance hierarchy is `protected boolean isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user)` (added in this PR in UsernamePasswordForm.java at line 160). There is no no-arg overload and no static import of one, so the project will not compile and the build will fail. The intended call is almost certainly `!isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser())`, mirroring how the helper is used in UsernamePasswordForm.java.

true_positives.golden_comment: With isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(UserModel user) requiring user != null, authenticate(...) will not call webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context) on the initial login page where context.getUser() is still null, so conditional passkey UI will not be set up for first-time passkey login. Consider whether this should also be enabled when no user has been selected yet so ID-less passkey authentication on the initial login form continues to work.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
WebAuthn form data not populated for initial login (user not yet identified)

In `UsernamePasswordForm.authenticate()` the new guard `if (isConditionalPasskeysEnabled(context.getUser()))` requires `user != null`, because the helper at line 160 is `webauthnAuth != null && webauthnAuth.isPasskeysEnabled() && user != null`. The previous code path called `webauthnAuth.fillContextForm(context)` whenever passkeys were enabled, regardless of whether a user was already in the context. The new check therefore skips `fillContextForm` for the user-null branch (initial login, no user yet identified), so the login page no longer receives the WebAuthn challenge (`AUTH_CHALLENGE_NOTE`), `CHALLENGE`, `RP_ID`, `ENABLE_WEBAUTHN_CONDITIONAL_UI` and friends. The new tests `webauthnLoginWithDiscoverableKey_reauthentication` in PasskeysUsernameFormTest and `webauthnLoginWithExternalKey_reauthentication` in PasskeysUsernamePasswordFormTest both call `oauth.openLoginForm()` with no user yet identified and immediately expect a successful passkey login (`appPage.assertCurrent()`); without the server-side challenge the WebAuthn response cannot be verified and those tests will fail. The accompanying comment "setup webauthn data when passkeys enabled" also no longer matches the implemented condition, which additionally requires the user to be identified.

false_positives.candidate:
Unreachable assertion: driver.findElement throws before the matcher can run

In `reauthenticationOfUserWithoutPasskey()` the pattern `try { MatcherAssert.assertThat(driver.findElement(By.xpath("//form[@id='webauth']")), nullValue()); fail("Not expected to have webauthn button"); } catch (Exception nsee) { /* expected */ }` does not actually assert absence. Selenium's `driver.findElement` throws `NoSuchElementException` as soon as the element is missing, so the `assertThat(..., nullValue())` and `fail(...)` lines are unreachable and the catch block silently swallows the exception. The same try/catch is duplicated around line 311. The tests therefore pass regardless of whether the webauthn form is really absent. Use `driver.findElements(...)` and assert the resulting list is empty.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset branch is unreachable / raises AssertionError in Django

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0, the code does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with start_offset < 0. Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ asserts that a slice start must be non-negative (`assert (k.start is None or k.start >= 0), 'Negative indexing is not supported.'`), so this branch raises AssertionError in normal Python and produces undefined SQL offsets under python -O. Cursor.from_string happily parses a negative offset via `int(bits[1])`, so an admin who sends ?optimized_pagination=true with a crafted cursor (e.g. '0:-5:0') will crash the endpoint. The claim in the comment that 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong; Django never supported negative slicing on querysets.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When requests are authenticated with API keys or org auth tokens (which have user_id=None), organization_context.member is None. Line 71 attempts to access organization_context.member.has_global_access without checking if member is None, causing an AttributeError crash when optimized_pagination=true is used, even though the request passed all permission checks with valid org:write scope.
get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.
Importing non-existent OptimizedCursorPaginator

false_positives.candidate:
'Performance optimization' comments are misleading

The block comment at lines 179-181 and the docstring of OptimizedCursorPaginator (lines 822-832) claim this is a 'performance optimization', provides 'efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning', 'streamlined boundary condition handling', and 'optimized query path for large datasets'. None of these are real. Compared to BasePaginator, OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result only changes behavior when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0, and even that change is broken (see the negative-offset finding). The change to BasePaginator itself (line 182-184) only clamps a negative offset to 0 in the non-prev case; that is a defensive fix, not an optimization. The repeated blank lines at lines 819-820 also suggest the class was tacked on without review.

New paginator branch has no tests

No tests were added for the new optimized_pagination code path. A maintainer should at minimum cover: (1) optimized_pagination=true with a superuser hits OptimizedCursorPaginator; (2) optimized_pagination=true with a regular member falls through to DateTimePaginator; (3) OptimizedCursorPaginator with enable_advanced_features=True and a negative-offset cursor does not raise (today it will). The whole feature is unverified.

OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result (lines 845-911) is an almost line-for-line copy of BasePaginator.get_result (lines 136-215); the only meaningful difference is the negative-offset branch. Subclassing only to flip one branch in one method duplicates ~70 lines of cursor/offset/extra/hits/post_query_filter logic. Any future fix to BasePaginator (including the pre-existing `order_b` typo on line 105) must be made in two places. A maintainer would prefer a single `enable_advanced_features` flag on BasePaginator, or an override of just the slicing step.

Pre-existing typo 'order_b' silently breaks ASC re-ordering

Pre-existing but in the file being changed and directly relevant to pagination correctness. Line 105 reads `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` instead of `queryset.query.order_by = tuple(new_order_by)`. This means when the cursor's key is currently ordered DESC (`-%s` % self.key in order_by) and `asc` is True, the queryset's order_by is never actually flipped to ascending, so the descending-order rows are then compared with an ascending comparison operator, producing wrong results. Worth fixing while this file is being touched.

has_global_access on RpcOrganizationMember is not a known attribute

`organization_context.member.has_global_access` accesses a Python attribute on the RpcOrganizationMember RPC type. RpcOrganizationMember typically exposes role/flags (e.g. `flags.global_access` bit) rather than a `has_global_access` property. If the attribute does not exist, this expression raises AttributeError on every request from a non-superuser, which would 500 the entire audit log endpoint for ordinary members. The reviewer needs to confirm the actual attribute name and that it represents the intended privilege (vs. e.g. `role` or a flags bit). Also, since the entire `use_optimized and enable_advanced` branch is gated to superusers or admins, exposing it via a user-controlled `?optimized_pagination=true` query parameter does not actually grant any new capability and should be questioned.

true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`organization_context.member.has_global_access` may AttributeError if member is None

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` (line 71) unconditionally accesses `.member.has_global_access` whenever the requester is not a superuser. If `organization_context.member` is None for any path that reaches this endpoint (e.g., a service user or a context shape returned for non-members of the org being queried), the request will raise `AttributeError` and return a 500. The original code never touched `organization_context.member`, so this PR introduces the regression. Guard with `organization_context.member is not None and organization_context.member.has_global_access` (or equivalent), or move the check inside the `optimized_pagination` branch where it is actually consumed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator silently clamps negative offsets for non-prev cursors

The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` (line 182) introduces a behavior change from the original `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` for cursors with `is_prev=False` and a negative `offset`. Django's queryset slicing natively supports negative offsets; the new code silently clamps them to 0. The comment ('Performance optimization: For high-traffic scenarios, allow negative offsets…') is misleading — the change actually restricts offset semantics in the base paginator. Consequence: any caller (in this repo or downstream) that previously relied on Django's negative slicing for forward cursors will silently get the first page of results instead of the tail, with no error. There is no test that exercises the negative-offset path, and the change is rolled out to all paginator subclasses (DateTimePaginator, Paginator, etc.) via inheritance.

Comment claims int(offset) enables negative offsets but it doesn't

Lines 26–27 add `# Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios / # This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets`, but the actual code is the unchanged `self.offset = int(offset)`. `int()` is just a numeric coercion — it does not 'allow' negatives (Python ints already accept them) and does not change pagination behavior. The comment misleads readers into believing the Cursor constructor is doing something that it is not; the actual negative-offset semantics were (re)moved in `paginator.py`. Either delete the comment or move the explanatory text to the place that actually implements the feature.

Eviction silently drops spans from oversized segments without logging

Lines 62–64 add `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`, which silently removes the oldest (lowest `end_timestamp_precise`) spans from any set exceeding 1000 entries. The previous Python-side check at `_load_segment_data` would `metrics.incr('spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded')` and log an error before discarding the entire segment; this is now gone (see `src/sentry/spans/buffer.py`). The new behavior silently loses individual spans with no metric, no log, no error — only `zpopmin` happens. Consequence: for any segment with more than 1000 spans, downstream flushing will emit truncated segments, and operators will have no signal that data was dropped. Also note that `zpopmin` breaks ties by lexicographic member order when `end_timestamp_precise` is identical (common for sibling spans in the same transaction), making the lost-span set effectively non-deterministic.

No tests cover the new eviction-on-insert behavior

The PR adds Lua-side eviction at >1000 spans (`zpopmin`), but no test in `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py`, `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_buffer.py`, or `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_flusher.py` constructs a segment with more than 1000 spans to assert (a) the cap is enforced, (b) which spans are kept vs dropped, or (c) that a metric/log is emitted. The existing parametrized tests use 4–5 spans per case. Without a test, a future change to the score semantics (e.g., switching from `end_timestamp_precise` to something else) or to the threshold could regress silently and drop arbitrary spans in production with no detection. At minimum, add a test that pushes >1000 spans into one segment and asserts the flushed result contains exactly 1000 and that the kept spans are the latest by `end_timestamp_precise`.

No tests cover the redirect-loop limit change (10000 -> 1000) or the new OptimizedCursorPaginator path

Two important behavioral changes ship without test coverage: (1) the add-buffer.lua redirect-resolution loop limit is reduced from 10000 to 1000, and (2) the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True` (used by `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` for superusers/global-access members) is exercised in no test in this PR. The audit-logs endpoint change should at least have a test that constructs a request as a superuser with `?optimized_pagination=true` and asserts it returns a successful paginated response, and the redirect limit should be covered by a test feeding a synthetic deep tree.

OptimizedCursorPaginator is a near-verbatim copy of Paginator/BasePaginator with misleading docstring

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` (lines 821–911) duplicates `get_item_key` and `value_from_cursor` byte-for-byte from `Paginator` (lines 222–227) and reimplements `get_result` almost identically to `BasePaginator.get_result`, differing only in whether a negative offset passes through when `enable_advanced_features` is set. The docstring claims 'Negative offset support for efficient reverse pagination', 'Streamlined boundary condition handling', and 'Optimized query path for large datasets', but only the first is implemented (and Django natively), and the others describe no actual behavior. Consequence: dead code, false documentation, and a privileged code path ('control optimizations') that is exposed via a query parameter (see `organization_auditlogs.py`) for superusers, with no test coverage in the diff. A senior reviewer would want this consolidated into a flag on `BasePaginator` rather than a duplicate class.

Privileged pagination feature is gated by a client-controlled query parameter

`use_optimized = request.GET.get('optimized_pagination') == 'true'` (line 70) lets any requester who is also a superuser (or has global access) flip on `enable_advanced_features=True` for that single request. Privileged behavior is typically gated by server-side configuration or user attributes, not a query parameter, because query-parameter gating leaves no audit trail and is trivially selectable. The 'feature' itself just re-enables Django's native negative-offset slicing that the BasePaginator change (line 182 in paginator.py) just removed. Either move the toggle behind a server-side feature flag/setting, or drop it — the parameter offers no functional benefit beyond Django's existing behavior.

Redirect resolution loop limit silently reduced 10000 -> 1000

The redirect resolution loop iterates from `for i = 0, 1000 do` (line 30) but the original code used `for i = 0, 10000 do` and explicitly noted in the comment that this limit governs whether deep segment trees are joined correctly: 'theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' Reducing the limit to 1000 silently breaks any trace whose redirect chain has depth between 1000 and 10000 — those spans will not be merged into the same set. No tests exercise deep trees, so this regression is not caught. Consequence: traces with deep span trees (1000+) end up split across multiple buffer sets and get flushed as incomplete segments, losing parent/child relationships downstream.

`cast(SpanEvent, …)` provides no runtime validation; missing `end_timestamp_precise` will KeyError

Line 134 does `val = cast(SpanEvent, rapidjson.loads(payload.value))`, which is purely a type-hint operation at runtime — it does not validate the payload. The very next reference, `end_timestamp_precise=val['end_timestamp_precise']` (line 141), will raise `KeyError` if any incoming payload (older producers, schema drift, malformed Kafka message) omits the field, and `TypeError` if it is `None`. Consequence: a single bad message kills the batch processing and the consumer may stall. Either validate against the schema (e.g., `sentry_kafka_schemas.codecs.decode`) before constructing the `Span`, or guard with `val.get('end_timestamp_precise', default)` and skip/log the malformed message.

`max_segment_spans` constructor parameter is now orphaned

`SpansBuffer.__init__` (around line 150) still defines and stores `self.max_segment_spans = max_segment_spans` with default 1001, but the consumer-side enforcement in `_load_segment_data` that read `self.max_segment_spans` was deleted in this PR. The parameter is still accepted in `__reduce__` callers and tests, but never used. Consequence: configuration knob is misleading and dead; anyone increasing `max_segment_spans` expects larger segments to be allowed, but the Lua-side eviction now silently caps segments at 1000 regardless. The Python constant and constructor argument should either be removed or actually consulted (e.g., passed to the Lua script as a configurable limit).

true_positives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache key built from non-deterministic hash()

The cache key uses `hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))`. CPython randomizes the tuple hash seed per process via PYTHONHASHSEED, so each gunicorn/celery worker computes a different integer for the same project list, producing different cache keys. The 60-second cache claimed as a 'performance optimization' therefore never hits across workers in production and the shared Redis cache slot will be silently bypassed. Replace `hash(...)` with a stable digest such as `hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted_ids).encode()).hexdigest()` (or any non-secret, deterministic hash) before generating the key.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.

false_positives.candidate:
Empty submodule pinned to base commit with no justification

The PR adds a `sentry-repo` submodule entry pointing to exactly the same commit as the base (`a5d29095...`). Nothing in the diff or description references this submodule, no path within it is consumed by any of the changed Python files, and pinning a submodule to the parent commit typically only matters if downstream tooling relies on it. Remove the submodule entry, or document in the PR description what depends on it and why it must move in lock-step with the parent.

Stale cached True keeps upsampling projects that just left the allowlist

The allowlist check is cached for 60s, but `invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined yet never wired into any option-set/management signal. If a project is removed from `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist`, the cached `True` continues to be served for up to a minute, and `_get_event_stats` will then transform `count()` into `upsampled_count()` for a project whose events no longer satisfy the upsampling contract. That makes reported error counts incorrect (over-counted by the sample_weight factor). Either shorten TTL dramatically, call `invalidate_upsampling_cache` whenever the allowlist option is written, or include the allowlist version in the cache key.

Substring match for event.type:error causes false positives

`_is_error_focused_query` does `if "event.type:error" in query`, which matches any query where that substring appears anywhere. Real queries like `event.type:errorBoundary`, `tags.event.type:error`, or note-style payloads containing `event.type:error` text will all be classified as error-focused and have their counts upsampled even though they are not error events. The docstring says 'err on the side of caution', but the current implementation is the opposite — it over-applies the transform. Use proper token-based matching (split on whitespace/punctuation and check for an exact `event.type:error` token).

Unrelated error-message change for topEvents validation

The diff rewrites `{"detail": "If topEvents needs to be at least 1"}` to `{"detail": "topEvents needs to be at least 1"}`. This is a user-visible API response change bundled into a feature PR for error upsampling, with no description in the PR body. Anyone parsing this message string (CI checks, docs, downstream tests) will see a silent change. Either revert the message and keep the PR scope tight, or call it out explicitly so consumers can update.

Upsampled-count assertion depends on unverified sample_weight semantics

`test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` asserts `count == 10` after storing events with `client_sample_rate: 0.1`. This only holds if Snuba's `sample_weight` is exactly `1 / client_sample_rate` AND the factory's new `sample_rate` hook propagates through event ingest into that column — none of which is asserted in this PR. If either assumption is wrong, the test will be a false positive that masks the most important data-integrity claim of the feature. Add an explicit assertion (or a smaller unit test) that demonstrates the sample_weight value produced for a known input, e.g. assert `sample_weight == 10.0` for a stored event with sample_rate 0.1.

_are_all_projects_error_upsampled takes organization but ignores it

`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled(project_ids, organization)` accepts an `Organization` argument but only reads `options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist", [])`, which is a global option. This is misleading — callers and reviewers reasonably expect the allowlist to be per-organization — and if per-org allowlists are ever introduced, this signature will silently do the wrong thing. Either drop the parameter, or actually consult an organization-scoped option.

invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code; allowlist edits have no effect for 60s

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined and exported, but a repo-wide search shows no caller. Combined with the 60-second TTL this means any operator change to `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` (or any future project-level toggle) cannot be observed promptly, and there is no signal that this is intentional. Either wire it into the option-set path (and any UI/admin endpoint that edits the allowlist), or delete it so callers do not assume it works.

setUp reassigns self.user after login_as, leaving auth against stale user

In `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.setUp`, `self.login_as(user=self.user)` is called, then `self.authed_user = self.user` saves a reference, then `self.user = self.create_user()` reassigns `self.user` to a brand-new user. Subsequent `store_event` calls use `tags={"sentry:user": self.user.email}` referring to the new (non-authenticated) user, while the request still runs as the original user. This makes the test setup brittle: any future test that depends on the authenticated user's identity vs the tagged user's identity will silently break. Move all `create_user`/`store_event` setup before `login_as`, or use distinct attribute names.

upsampled_count drops NULL sample_weight rows and truncates to Int64

The new `upsampled_count` aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. Two correctness issues: (1) `sum(sample_weight)` silently excludes rows where `sample_weight` is NULL (pre-upsampling or legacy events ingested before sampling rolled out on that project), so the upsampled count will be lower than the real event count and inflate/de-inflate arbitrarily as the rollout progresses; and (2) `toInt64(...)` truncates fractional sums — e.g. 10.7 becomes 10 — so reported counts can be off-by-one for any bucket whose weighted total is not integral. Wrap with `COALESCE(sample_weight, 1)` (or similar) and either keep the result as a float or round explicitly before casting.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using zip(error_ids, events.values()) assumes the get_multi result preserves the input order; dict value order is not guaranteed to match error_ids, so event data can be paired with the wrong ID (missing nodes also shift alignment).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
fetch_error_details pairs nodestore results assuming order preservation

`fetch_error_details` calls `nodestore.backend.get_multi(node_ids)` and then does `for event_id, data in zip(error_ids, events.values()):`, which only produces the correct (event_id, event_data) pairs if `get_multi` returns values in the same order as the requested keys. Some nodestore backends (e.g. concurrent/Nydus-style backends) do not guarantee that, so when more than one error is fetched the AI summary can receive mismatched titles/messages/timestamps for different events. The code should key the lookup by node_id (`events[node_id]`) rather than relying on the order of `events.values()`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoded empty data passed to TableWidgetVisualization causes it to always render an empty table instead of displaying actual results when the feature flag is enabled.

TableWidgetVisualization rendered with hardcoded empty data

false_positives.candidate:
Replays AI summary no longer honors ?project= URL override

The component previously obtained the project via `useLocationQuery({fields: {project: decodeScalar}})`, allowing the `?project=<id>` query parameter to choose a different project than the one stored on the replay (commonly used for cross-project replays or admin-impersonated views).
