dcg_to_slow_conditions built from dcg_ids instead of dcg_to_groups.keys()

Previously `get_condition_query_groups` computed `dcg_to_slow_conditions = get_slow_conditions_for_groups(list(event_data.dcg_to_groups.keys()))` while `fetch_data_condition_groups` was fed `event_data.dcg_ids`. After the refactor both consume `event_data.dcg_ids`. If `EventRedisData.dcg_to_groups` and `dcg_ids` ever contain different sets (e.g. one includes a DCG that the other omits), `dcg_to_slow_conditions` will look up a stale or missing entry and the `KeyError` path or `slow_conditions` could be wrong. Either confirm the two sets are always equal (and add a guard) or pass the key set that actually drives `data_condition_groups`.

get_environment_info hits nodestore for every issue

`get_environment_info` calls `issue.get_recommended_event()` for every issue included in the PR/MR comment. That helper performs a nodestore lookup (`Event.objects.get(id=...)`) per call. For a comment that lists N issues this produces N sequential nodestore round-trips on the hot path of PR comment generation, and each call is wrapped in a broad `except Exception` that swallows programming errors and only logs at info level. Consider caching the recommended event per group, batching lookups, or limiting the lookup to cases where an environment field is actually useful.

true_positives.golden_comment: Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Backup code comparison is case-sensitive though generated codes are lowercase hex

`crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")` always emits lowercase, but the lookup uses `credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` with no `.toLowerCase()` and no `.trim()`. A user who pastes or types a code with caps, surrounding whitespace, or different separators (space, period) will get `IncorrectBackupCode` even though they have a valid code, which is especially painful here because the input is a long hex string with no character-class hint. Normalize the input (`replaceAll("-", "").replace(/\s+/g, "").toLowerCase()`) on both the login and the `disable` handler so users don't silently burn codes for a casing/whitespace mismatch.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TOCTOU race allows a single backup code to be used to log in more than once

The backup-code branch decrypts `user.backupCodes`, calls `indexOf`, sets `backupCodes[index] = null`, then re-encrypts and `prisma.user.update`s — but this is done as separate read/transform/write with no `WHERE backupCodes = ...` predicate or transaction. Two concurrent login attempts using the same code both find it at the same index before either write lands, both set the slot to null, and both succeed. Backup codes are explicitly documented as single-use, so reuse defeats the feature. Either wrap the read+write in a transaction with a predicate that matches the current `backupCodes` value (optimistic concurrency) or, better, persist codes as rows so consumption can be a single atomic UPDATE/DELETE on the matching row.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blob URL for backup-codes download is never revoked on close or unmount

When the setup step succeeds, a Blob URL is created from the backup codes and stored in `backupCodesUrl`. `URL.revokeObjectURL` is only called when a fresh URL is generated, so when the user closes the modal (which calls `resetState`, which doesn't touch `backupCodesUrl`) or the component unmounts, the previous Blob and its URL remain pinned in memory until the page reloads. This is a slow leak that accumulates each time a user opens the enable flow, and it also leaves a stale `blob:` URL reachable from the previous render. Add a useEffect cleanup (or revoke in `resetState` and on `onOpenChange(false)`) so the URL is released whenever the modal closes or the component unmounts.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The exported function TwoFactor handles backup codes and is in BackupCode.tsx. Inconsistent naming.
Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

false_positives.candidate:
No end-to-end coverage for backup code login or backup-code disable flow

The PR adds the new backup-code login branch in `next-auth-options.ts`, the new `backupCode` field in the login form, and a new disable-via-backup-code branch in `disable.ts` and `DisableTwoFactorModal.tsx`. The e2e file only exercises the post-enable display dialog (download/copy/close buttons) and does not cover the security-critical paths: logging in with a backup code, exercising the 'Lost access' toggle on the login page, or disabling 2FA via a backup code (the exact flow the feature was built for, and which is gated by `twoFactorLostAccess` and `backupCode` in `DisableTwoFactorModal`). The author explicitly flagged this as a TODO at line 12. Given that backup-code handling involves the TOCTOU race and decrypt-and-parse logic reviewed in the other findings, an e2e that signs in with a valid code and a second time with the same code (expecting rejection) is necessary before merging.

Uncaught JSON.parse on decrypted backupCodes can break 2FA disable

Same issue as in `next-auth-options.ts`: `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY))` is not wrapped in try/catch. If the encrypted payload is unreadable (corruption, schema drift after key rotation, partial DB write), the handler throws an uncaught error and the user is unable to disable 2FA via a backup code — which is the very path designed for 'lost access'. The handler should catch the failure, log it, and return a clear error (e.g. `ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes` or `InternalServerError`) rather than letting it bubble to a 500.

Uncaught JSON.parse on decrypted backupCodes can crash every login for affected user

`const backupCodes = JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY))` will throw if the stored ciphertext is ever tampered with, truncated, or encrypted under a different `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY` (e.g. a key rotation on a self-hosted deployment). The throw is not caught, so the NextAuth `authorize` call aborts with a generic exception and the user — including admins — is locked out of their own account with no actionable error. Wrap the decrypt+parse in try/catch and return `ErrorCode.InternalServerError` (or a clearer code) so the response is well-formed and the failure is logged with the user id, instead of an unhandled exception surfacing through NextAuth.

true_positives.golden_comment: A null reference occurs in GoogleCalendarService.createEvent() and updateEvent() when mainHostDestinationCalendar is destructured from evt.destinationCalendar but evt.destinationCalendar is null or an empty array, causing mainHostDestinationCalendar to be undefined.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Read of `integration` on potentially-undefined destination calendar can throw

Line 119 reads `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` without first checking if `mainHostDestinationCalendar` is defined: `if (evt.location === MeetLocationType && mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar")`. The destructure `const [mainHostDestinationCalendar] = evt.destinationCalendar ?? [];` yields `undefined` whenever `evt.destinationCalendar` is null/empty (which is exactly the case the Google Meet fallback is meant to handle, since non-team or no-destination flows now produce `null`). Accessing `.integration` on undefined throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'integration')` and the request fails before the location is rewritten to Cal Video. The check should be `!mainHostDestinationCalendar || mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration !== "google_calendar"`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateEvent fallback uses a self-referential find that can never match

Line 256 reads `const selectedCalendar = externalCalendarId ? externalCalendarId : event.destinationCalendar?.find((cal) => cal.externalId === externalCalendarId)?.externalId;`. When `externalCalendarId` is null/undefined (truthy is false), the predicate compares `cal.externalId === externalCalendarId`, i.e. `cal.externalId === undefined`. That condition is false for any real calendar (externalIds are real strings), so the find returns undefined and `selectedCalendar` becomes undefined. The previous code used a plain `event.destinationCalendar?.externalId` fallback. Net effect: updateEvent currently passes `calendarId: undefined` to `calendar.events.update` (and the subsequent `events.patch` at line 168/277) instead of either `primary` or the booking's actual destination calendar externalId. That's a regression from the single-destinationCalendar behavior and is likely to produce 400/404 errors or update the wrong calendar. The same tautological pattern is duplicated at line 317 in `deleteEvent`, where `selectedCalendar` falls back to the local `defaultCalendarId = "primary"` — meaning cancellations without a propagated externalCalendarId will try to delete from "primary" and may delete the wrong event.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Calendar interface now requires createEvent(event, credentialId), but some implementations (e.g., Lark/Office365) still declare createEvent(event) only—this breaks the interface contract (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BaseCalendarService.createEvent signature breaks the Calendar interface contract

The Calendar interface in packages/types/Calendar.d.ts was changed to require `createEvent(event: CalendarEvent, credentialId: number): Promise<NewCalendarEventType>`. The BaseCalendarService (this file) is declared as `abstract class BaseCalendarService implements Calendar`, but its createEvent still has signature `createEvent(event: CalendarEvent): Promise<NewCalendarEventType>` and is not marked abstract. TypeScript will error out at build time because the implementation is not assignable to the interface (the missing required `credentialId` parameter). Additionally, concrete CalDAV-derived integrations (Apple Calendar, etc.) inherit this method, so EventManager.createAllCalendarEvents's third argument `destination.externalId` is silently dropped. The base signature must be updated to accept and forward `credentialId` (and likely ignore it where appropriate) for the project to compile and behave correctly.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. This change, combined with requestedSlug still being set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, results in both properties being set when billing is enabled, and neither when disabled

The `credential` may be undefined when passed to `updateEvent` if `reference.credentialId` is set but the credential is not found. This can lead to a runtime error when `updateEvent` is called with an undefined credential, which should be handled to prevent crashes.

false_positives.candidate:
Behavior-preserving spread refactor buried in a destinationCalendar PR

Two spread ternaries are rewritten (`...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED && { slug })` → `...(IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED ? { slug } : {})` and the matching `requestedSlug`). The results are equivalent because `false` is ignored when spreading. This isn't a bug, but the change is unrelated to the destinationCalendar refactor and should be moved to its own commit to keep the diff focused on the PR's stated purpose.

Booking record only stores the first host's destinationCalendar for collective events

When writing the new Booking row, only `evt.destinationCalendar[0].id` is used (`destinationCalendar: { connect: { id: evt.destinationCalendar[0].id } }`). For collective events the PR explicitly pushes every team member's `destinationCalendar` into the array (lines around 1074-1078), so multiple hosts each get their own calendar event via EventManager.create — but the Booking row ends up linked to only the organizer/first host's destination calendar. Later operations that read `booking.destinationCalendar` (handleCancelBooking.ts:251-255, paypal-webhook.ts:152-156, payments webhook.ts:101-119, the booking reminder cron at bookingReminder.ts:107-130, etc.) will only see one of several destinations and may therefore miss cancellations, reminders, or webhooks for other hosts. The BookingReferences table mitigates the calendar delete path, but anything keyed on `booking.destinationCalendar` (emails, webhooks, cron reminders, refund flows) silently drops the rest.

Comment-only change: typo fix is unrelated to the PR

The commit changes `orginalBookingDuration` → `originalBookingDuration` in `ensureAvailableUsers`. That's a fine cleanup, but it isn't mentioned in the PR description and isn't related to the destinationCalendar-array refactor. Mixing unrelated typo fixes into a feature/bugfix PR makes bisecting and reverting harder; either split it into its own commit or document it explicitly.

Empty firstName/lastName fields added to team member objects

The team-member promise at lines 986-1000 now sets `firstName: ""` and `lastName: ""` in the returned object. The TeamMember/CalendarEvent.team.members TypeScript type (in packages/types/Calendar.d.ts) does not declare these keys, so they are extra/missing properties on every team attendee. They will be ignored by CalendarService implementations today, but they leak into the persisted meeting attendee list on every external calendar (e.g. ICS attendee fields, Google Meet attendee payloads generated by translateAttendees in larkcalendar/office365). The change is undocumented in the PR description and can interact with downstream consumers that expect only the documented TeamMember shape.

Legacy cancellation fallback runs once per reference, producing N×M extra delete calls

The new code at lines 422-484 wraps both the credentialId-keyed path and the legacy fallback (no `credentialId`) inside `for (const reference of bookingCalendarReference)`. For any booking with multiple calendar references that lack `credentialId` (i.e. bookings created before the reference→credentialId migration), the legacy branch executes for EACH reference: it fetches ALL user calendar credentials and pushes `deleteEvent(uid, evt, externalCalendarId)` for each. The original (pre-PR) code only invoked the legacy fallback once per cancellation. The author explicitly acknowledges in the checklist that tests were not added. Specific regression surfaces that are not covered: (a) collective COLLECTIVE bookings where multiple destinationCalendars are stored on the evt and propagated through handleNewBooking→EventManager.create→each CalendarService.createEvent with the correct credentialId; (b) cancellation when a booking has multiple bookingReferences with different credentials (the N×M legacy path bug); (c) the calendar-removal credentialId fallback in updateEvent/deleteEvent; (d) the BOOOKING_CREATED / BOOKING_REJECTED / BOOKING_REQUESTED webhook payload shape (only one of three test expectations was updated in webhook.e2e.ts). At minimum, a smoke test exercising collective new-booking/cancel/reschedule end-to-end on the dev stack is warranted before merge.

Organizer email may be overridden by undefined main destination calendar

Inside the attendees payload at line 122: `email: mainHostDestinationCalendar?.externalId ? mainHostDestinationCalendar.externalId : calEventRaw.organizer.email`. When the array is empty the optional chain resolves to undefined and the fallback correctly uses `organizer.email`, so this is fine for the empty-array path. There's no distinction between "no destination" and "destination missing externalId".

createAttendees only adds attendees to the first destination calendar

In `createEvent` at line 128 the first host's calendar is selected for the event, then `createAttendees` (line 164) re-selects the same first element. The catch path at line 158 (`await this.deleteEvent(eventId, event, calendarId)`) cleans up by deleting from `calendarId` (the first). For a collective event whose other hosts' calendars the EventManager separately creates via createAllCalendarEvents, those other events will not have attendees attached at all (organizer + invitees included) because Lark's createAttendees only runs inside this one createEvent call. The destinationCalendar → attendee invite propagation described in the PR for collective bookings is not actually implemented for Lark.

destinationCalendar built from booking.destinationCalendar falls back to user.destinationCalendar unsafely

The expression `booking?.destinationCalendar ? [booking.destinationCalendar] : user.destinationCalendar ? [user.destinationCalendar] : []` will wrap a single `DestinationCalendar` row in an array. Downstream `EventManager.create(evt)` will then process only that one destination, ignoring the user-level `user.destinationCalendar` even when the booking actually intended to be a team/collective booking with multiple destinations. For collective events that require confirmation, the hosts that are not represented in `booking.destinationCalendar` will not be invited when the organizer confirms. Confirm `booking.eventType.schedulingType === COLLECTIVE` and append the team members' destinations (mirroring handleNewBooking.ts ~line 1074) before passing to EventManager.

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Refresh token is overwritten with the literal string "refresh_token"

After a successful parse, the function unconditionally does `if (!refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token) { refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"; }`. Whenever the parsed payload lacks `refresh_token` (which is true for every credential-sharing response, since the broken schema above never retains one), the real refresh token is replaced in-memory with the placeholder literal `"refresh_token"`. The integrations then write this garbage value into the database (`prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`). Future refresh attempts will send the literal string `"refresh_token"` to the OAuth provider and fail with `invalid_grant`, permanently invalidating the credential. Even outside sharing mode, any integration whose schema makes `refresh_token` optional will silently corrupt its stored refresh token.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
`minimumTokenResponseSchema` is invalid zod; every sharing-mode response is rejected

The schema uses computed object keys `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()`. `z.string().toString()` returns the schema's typeName (e.g. `"ZodString"`), so the produced keys are the literal strings `"ZodString"` and `"ZodOptional"`, not catch-all matchers. The schema therefore requires the response object to contain numeric properties literally called `"ZodString"` and `"ZodOptional"`, which no real OAuth response ever has. `parseRefreshTokenResponse` then unconditionally throws `"Invalid refreshed tokens were returned"` whenever `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` is true. Consequence: every refresh-token call routed through credential sharing fails; the outer `try/catch` blocks in the integrations then return the stale, expiring auth and token refresh silently regresses. This is the central defect that breaks the new sync path.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sharing-mode return type incompatible with most callers

When `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT && userId` is true, the function returns whatever `fetch(...)` yields — a `Response` object — and never reads its body. The signature is typed as `() => any`, and each integration expects a specific post-shape immediately after the call:

- `packages/app-store/zoho-bigin/lib/CalendarService.ts:96` does `tokenInfo.data.error` — `Response.data` is `undefined`, so `.error` throws.
- `packages/app-store/zohocrm/lib/CalendarService.ts:217` does `zohoCrmTokenInfo.data.error` — same issue.
- `packages/app-store/larkcalendar/lib/CalendarService.ts:84` passes the `Response` straight into `handleLarkError`, which then attempts `data.data.refresh_expires_in`. Without a documented sync-endpoint shape, Lark silently breaks the moment the response format is not exactly what the local refresh returned.

The other integrations (office365calendar, office365video, webex, zoomvideo) happen to call `handleErrorsJson`/`handleWebexResponse`/`handleZoomResponse` which accept a `Response`, but they then rely on `parseRefreshTokenResponse` (which is itself broken — see other findings), so they are still non-functional in sharing mode. false_positives.candidate:
Credential sync endpoint contract is undefined and inconsistent across integrations

The function POSTs only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` (form-urlencoded) to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` and returns the raw response unmodified. But each integration expects the response to have a different exact shape: google expects `{access_token, expiry_date}`, office365 expects `{access_token, expires_in, refresh_token?}`, hubspot expects a full `HubspotToken`, lark expects `{data:{access_token, refresh_token, expires_in, refresh_expires_in}}`, etc. Self-hosters implementing the parent endpoint have no documentation describing these required shapes (or the URL/return value must instead be customized per app — which contradicts the function being shared). Without a clear spec, the feature is unusable in practice.

Missing `prisma` import causes runtime ReferenceError

The new code added in this PR calls `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key: ... } })` (line 96) but `prisma` is not imported in this file. The imports end at `getAppKeysFromSlug` and `parseRefreshTokenResponse`. Hitting the salesforce CalendarService code path (which happens on every salesforce CalendarService instantiation that goes through `getClient`) will throw `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined`, breaking salesforce bookings entirely for everyone — including self-hosters that never opt into credential sharing. This is an immediate runtime crash for a previously-working integration.

No tests cover the new credential-sharing sync path

The PR introduces three pieces of behavior with no test coverage: the new `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` webhook (including auth/secret checking, decryption, and the find/update/create branches), `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts` (sharing vs. non-sharing branches, including what the returned value looks like to callers), and `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts` (the broken minimum-token schema and the refresh-token overwrite). The PR description explicitly states no tests were added and existing tests were not run. Given the multiple integration-affecting bugs above, merging without tests risks regressing every OAuth integration.

Outbound call to sync endpoint has no authentication from Cal.com side

`fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)` is sent with no headers, no signature, and no client identity. The receiving service has no way to verify that the call came from this Cal.com instance or that `appSlug`/`calcomUserId` weren't tampered with by a network attacker or a mis-routed proxy. Combined with the fact that `userId` is trusted blindly to look up tokens server-side, anyone who can intercept traffic to the configured endpoint can impersonate any user. The endpoint should require a Cal.com-issued signature (e.g. an HMAC of the body using a shared key) so the parent service can reject forged refresh requests.

Webhook handler accepts any HTTP method and has no body-size, replay, or method check

The handler does not check `req.method`, so any method with the correct secret header (e.g. GET, PUT) reaches the database mutation path; only the secret comparison and `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` flag gate it. There is also no body-size limit, no timestamp/nonce, and no signature scheme beyond a static shared secret. Combined with the fact that anyone in possession of `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` can create or replace credentials for any userId in the system, an attacker who learns or leaks the secret (e.g. via logs, env backups) can rewrite every user's app tokens by replaying the request. At minimum, restrict to POST and verify a recent timestamp.

findFirst-then-create is not atomic; webhook can produce duplicate credentials

The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst(...)` followed by `prisma.credential.create(...)` if no row matches, with no transaction and no unique constraint to lean on. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same `(userId, appId)` will both observe no row and both insert a new credential, leaving the user with multiple rows for the same app — a state the rest of the codebase assumes does not happen (e.g. lark's callback, webex/zoom/office365 callbacks all explicitly delete pre-existing rows). The `findFirst` lookup also doesn't filter by `type`, so when the same `appId` exists with multiple legacy `type` values, an update may be applied to the wrong row. The docstring even acknowledges this with "Can't use prisma upsert as we don't know the id of the credential", but a race-free approach (e.g. `prisma.credential.deleteMany({ userId, appId })` inside a transaction, or an upsert on a composite key) would be safer.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.

Duplicate-email and blacklist checks ignore email case

`uniqueGuests` filters new guests with case-sensitive comparisons: `guest === attendee.email` and `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)`. The blacklist list is lowercased, but the attendees list is not, and RFC 5321 mailbox names are case-insensitive. As a result a user can submit `Foo@Example.com` against an existing attendee `foo@example.com` and bypass the dedupe, or against a lowercased blacklist entry and bypass the block. Both comparisons should be case-insensitive (e.g. `.toLowerCase()` on both sides).

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Permission check requires user to be both team admin AND owner

The variable `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed with `&&` instead of `||`: `(await isTeamAdmin(...)) && (await isTeamOwner(...))`. The naming and the rest of the check (`!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer && !isAttendee`) imply the intent is "admin OR owner", so that either role can add guests to a team booking. As written, only users who are both admin and owner (effectively owners only, assuming owner implies admin) are granted access, which is stricter than the variable name and likely the intended UX.

Wrong guest list passed to sendAddGuestsEmails

`sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` is called with the original input `guests`, but `guests` can contain addresses that were filtered out (already on the booking or blacklisted) and never made it into `uniqueGuests` or the database. Inside `sendAddGuestsEmails` the branch `if (newGuests.includes(attendee.email))` is used to decide whether an attendee is "new" (gets `AttendeeScheduledEmail`) versus an existing attendee (gets `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail`). Because the input list is used instead of `uniqueGuests`, existing attendees whose email happened to also be in the input will be re-classified as "new" and receive a fresh `AttendeeScheduledEmail` instead of an `AttendeeAddGuestsEmail`. true_positives.golden_comment: Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Empty/whitespace entries are not stripped before validation

`handleAdd` runs `ZAddGuestsInputSchema.safeParse(multiEmailValue)` directly. `multiEmailValue` can contain blank rows (initial state is `[""]`, and the X control only deletes the entry but does not trim). The schema rejects the whole array as soon as one empty entry is present, so a user with one valid email plus an extra empty row is forced to manually delete the empty row. The dialog would be more forgiving if it filtered `multiEmailValue.map(s => s.trim()).filter(Boolean)` before validating and submitting.

false_negatives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.

The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

false_positives.candidate:
Attendees can add additional guests to a booking

`isAttendee = !!booking.attendees.find(a => a.email === user.email)` grants any current attendee the right to add new guests to the booking. In most scheduling products only the organizer (or a team admin/owner) should be able to invite additional participants, because adding guests changes who has access to a meeting link, video room, or recording. The check should likely be `if (!isTeamAdminOrOwner && !isOrganizer)` (drop the `!isAttendee` branch) unless adding guests is explicitly part of the product design here.

Email-send errors are silently swallowed with console.log

The handler wraps `sendAddGuestsEmails` in a try/catch that does `console.log("Error sending AddGuestsEmails")`. The actual error is discarded (no `err` passed), the level is wrong (`console.error` would be appropriate), and the function returns success to the client even though the user was told guests were added but no notification emails were delivered. At minimum, log the error object via `console.error` and consider re-throwing or surfacing a partial-failure response so the UI can warn the user.

Hardcoded English message returned from handler

The handler returns `{ message: "Guests added" }` with a hardcoded English string. Every other booking mutation in this router uses translation keys (e.g. `booking_confirmation_success`). The frontend toast logic in `AddGuestsDialog.onSuccess` already calls `t("guests_added")` and never reads `data.message`, so the field is currently unused, but exposing a non-i18n string from the API creates a contract that downstream consumers will rely on. Either drop the field or return a translation key consistent with the rest of the codebase.

No size limit on guests array in schema

ZAddGuestsInputSchema accepts `z.array(z.string().email())` with no `.min()`/`.max()`. Combined with the `MultiEmail` component, which lets the user add arbitrary rows, a malicious or accidental request can submit an enormous array that is then inserted via `createMany`, triggering a large number of calendar/email side effects in `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees` and `sendAddGuestsEmails`. Add a reasonable bound (e.g. `.min(1).max(50)`).

No tests cover the new addGuests handler or dialog

This PR introduces a new public TRPC mutation, a new dialog component, two new email templates, and several new translation strings, but ships without any tests for the handler (permission rules, case-insensitive dedupe, blacklist handling, transaction/side-effect behavior), the AddGuestsDialog (validation reset, empty-row handling), or the email templates. At minimum add a handler test that covers: organizer happy path, team admin vs owner permission, attendee duplicate (case-insensitive), blacklisted email, empty guests array, and missing booking.

No transaction wraps DB update, calendar sync and email send

The handler commits `prisma.booking.update` first, then calls `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` and finally `sendAddGuestsEmails`. There is no surrounding transaction and no rollback if the calendar integration or email send fails partway through, the new attendees remain in the database but are missing from the underlying calendar/video meeting and from the participants' inboxes. This produces a data-integrity inconsistency between Cal.com state and the third-party calendar/video provider. Either wrap the side effects so the booking update can be rolled back, or at minimum document that a partial failure leaves the booking in this state and add a recovery path.

Subject crashes when booking has no attendees

`name: this.calEvent.attendees[0].name` will throw `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` if `attendees` is empty. While every normal booking has at least the original booker, edge cases (data backfill, attendees deleted manually, etc.) can produce a zero-attendee booking, in which case sending this email will crash inside `getNodeMailerPayload` and abort the whole `Promise.all` batch in `sendAddGuestsEmails`. Use a safe fallback such as `this.calEvent.attendees[0]?.name ?? this.calEvent.organizer.name` (or skip the name interpolation) before accessing `.name`.

isInvalidEmail state not cleared after successful submission

In the `addGuestsMutation.onSuccess` handler, `setIsInvalidEmail(false)` is missing. The flag is set to `true` when validation fails, but if the user fixes the input and the mutation succeeds, the dialog closes without resetting the flag. Because the dialog component lives inside `BookingListItem` and stays mounted, reopening the dialog later shows the "Emails must be unique and valid" error immediately, even though the input is empty. Add `setIsInvalidEmail(false)` in `onSuccess` (and ideally on cancel too, which is already done).

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount update is non-atomic; parallel runs double-count

The handler reads `reminder.retryCount` from the findMany result and writes `reminder.retryCount + 1` in a separate update. If two cron invocations (or this handler and any other process touching the same row) overlap, both will read the same `retryCount` value and both will write `value + 1`, undercounting retries by 1. This matters here because the deletion threshold (`gt: 1`) is tight — a single lost increment means a perpetually-failing reminder is retried indefinitely instead of being deleted after 2 attempts. The update should use a conditional increment (`{ retryCount: { increment: 1 } }`) or be guarded by a `where: { id, retryCount: reminder.retryCount }` clause so concurrent writers can't clobber each other.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount delete branch is not scoped to SMS method

In the new OR clause of the deleteMany, the `retryCount > 1` branch has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, while the sibling branch is filtered to SMS. The original deleteMany only ever deleted SMS reminders. retryCount is currently only ever incremented in this SMS handler, so today no non-SMS row can reach retryCount > 1, but the schema places `retryCount` on the shared `WorkflowReminder` model (used by EMAIL/SMS/WHATSAPP). If a future change (or manual DB edit) sets retryCount > 1 on an EMAIL or WHATSAPP reminder, this cron will silently delete it. The OR branch should be wrapped under the same `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` predicate as the other branch, e.g. `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, scheduledDate: { lte: now }` OR `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, retryCount: { gt: 1 }`, or expressed as `method: SMS AND (scheduledDate <= now OR retryCount > 1)`.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests cover the new retry/delete behavior

The PR introduces a meaningful behavior change in a cron-handler that mutates the database on every run (increment of retryCount on Twilio failure and on throw, plus deletion of reminders with retryCount > 1). There are no tests in the diff covering: (a) retryCount increments on a falsy return from twilio.scheduleSMS, (b) retryCount increments inside the catch block, (c) deleteMany removing reminders with retryCount > 1, (d) a reminder that fails twice being deleted on the subsequent run. Without tests, regressions in retry semantics (e.g. off-by-one in the threshold, double-increment under retry, or accidentally deleting scheduled rows) would go unnoticed.

Retries continue past scheduledDate once retryCount is < 2

The findMany filter is `scheduledDate: { lte: dayjs().add(7, 'day').toISOString() }`, which still includes reminders whose scheduledDate is in the past. Combined with the new retry logic, a reminder that fails twice will sit in the DB with retryCount=2 and scheduledDate in the past, then be deleted on the next cron run by the `retryCount > 1` branch. However, on the second cron run, after the first failure (retryCount=1) the reminder with a past-dated scheduledDate is not deleted by either branch (date <= now but method=SMS only matches the first OR branch, which it does — actually the date-past branch matches, so this is fine). The real concern is that between the first and second failure, the reminder whose date has passed continues to be passed to twilio.scheduleSMS in subsequent cron runs even though Twilio will obviously reject a send in the past, only to fail again and waste the second retry budget. The findMany should either skip past-dated unscheduled rows or the deleteMany should also delete past-dated + retryCount > 0 rows so a wasted retry isn't spent on an already-elapsed reminder.

Stale comment above deleteMany

The comment `//delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date` no longer describes the deleteMany. The query now also deletes reminders with `retryCount > 1`, and after the OR rewrite it deletes any reminder (regardless of method) that matches either branch. false_positives.candidate:
findMany method removed without documentation of caller migration

The findMany method previously exposed on InsightsBookingService was removed and replaced with getBaseConditions (now at line 68). External callers using service.findMany(...) will no longer compile. The PR description focuses on test updates and does not document this breaking change or describe how existing consumers should migrate to the new pattern of calling getBaseConditions() and passing the resulting Prisma.Sql into prisma.$queryRaw. Before merging, reviewers must confirm there are no remaining callers of service.findMany in the codebase, or that those callers are updated in the same change. Note also that callers using the previously removed type Prisma.BookingTimeStatusDenormalizedWhereInput will need to switch to consuming Prisma.Sql directly.

toEqual comparisons of Prisma.Sql will fail for SQL built via reduce

Three tests assert expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql`...`) against SQL returned by the service. The service builds SQL using a reduce over a Prisma.Sql[] array (insightsBooking.ts lines 119-122, 171-174, 204-207), wrapping each inner Sql with `(${acc}) OR (${condition})` or `(${acc}) AND (${condition})`. Each wrap adds new entries to the inner strings array (one per interpolation point introduced by the wrapper). The expected SQL in the tests is written as a single tagged template literal, producing a Sql whose strings array only has entries at the original placeholders. Prisma's Sql class does not override equality, so Vitest's toEqual does structural comparison of strings and values. For example, the team scope test (line 295) expects strings of length 3, while the service produces strings of length 7 after the OR-reduce wraps the two inner Sql fragments with parens. The same mismatch affects the org scope test at line 332 (3 vs 7) and the combined filter test at line 429 (4 vs 7). The simpler tests pass (NOTHING_CONDITION, user scope, single filter eventTypeId, single filter memberUserId) because they use a single template literal in the service that matches the test literal exactly. Suggested fix: compare conditions.toString() against the expected SQL string, build the expected Sql with the same nested reduce pattern, or assert against actual database query results rather than Sql structure. The PR description already flags that tests were not run due to runner configuration issues, but the structural mismatch will cause these specific tests to fail regardless.

updateManyByCredentialId called with empty data

true_positives.matched_candidate:

Line 68 runs `sed -i '' -E "..." "$ENV_FILE"`. true_positives.matched_candidate:
Hardcoded 'en-US' locale for cache timestamp formatting

Line 89 instantiates `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" })`, which forces en-US date formatting regardless of the user's actual locale. The component already has `useLocale()` in scope (line 37) and uses `t()` for surrounding strings, but the formatted timestamp bypasses the user's locale. Non-US users will see US-formatted dates/times for "Cache last updated". Format with the user's locale instead of hard-coding "en-US".

false_negatives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests for new deleteCache handler, repository methods, or component

The PR introduces the `deleteCache` tRPC mutation and `deleteCacheHandler` (this file), `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` on `CalendarCacheRepository`, `updateManyByCredentialId` on `SelectedCalendarRepository`, and the `CredentialActionsDropdown` UI component, plus an empty-data `updateMany` call in `CalendarService.fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache`. None of these additions ship with unit tests or component tests, so the empty-data `updateMany` bug and the missing-query-invalidation behavior are not regression-protected. Add at least a handler test (verifying the user/credential ownership check and the cache deletion), tests for the two new repository methods, and a component test covering the dropdown's invalidation flow.

deleteCacheMutation does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query

The `deleteCacheMutation` defined at lines 42-50 only fires `onSuccess` (toast + `onSuccess?.()` callback) but never invalidates the `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` query. After a successful deletion the dropdown still shows the old "Cache Status: Last updated: ..." line because `cacheUpdatedAt` is not refetched. The neighbouring `disconnectMutation` (lines 53-65) correctly invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` in `onSettled`; `deleteCacheMutation` should mirror that pattern so the UI updates immediately after deletion.

getCacheStatusByCredentialIds ignores expiresAt

`getCacheStatusByCredentialIds` (lines 173-188) groups all `CalendarCache` rows by `credentialId` and aggregates `_max.updatedAt` without filtering by `expiresAt >= now()`. The cache reader elsewhere (`getCachedAvailability`) only returns non-expired entries, so a credential whose only caches are expired (CACHING_TIME is 30 days) will still display a misleadingly recent "Last updated" timestamp even though the cache will never actually be served. Add a `where: { ..., expiresAt: { gte: new Date(Date.now()) } }` predicate so the status reflects cache that is actively being served.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Workflow deletion races with SendGrid cancellation

At lines 212-218, scheduledReminders.forEach calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true) without awaiting. These calls perform async SendGrid POST /v3/user/scheduled_sends cancellations. The next statement, `await ctx.prisma.workflow.deleteMany` at line 220, runs immediately and cascades through WorkflowStep.onDelete: Cascade to delete the workflowReminder rows. The SendGrid cancellation request may not have been sent, let alone processed by SendGrid, before SendGrid's scheduled send time, so the cancelled email is still delivered. Fix: await the cancellation calls (e.g., `await Promise.all(scheduledReminders.map(async (r) => { ... }))`) before issuing the workflow delete.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.

The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests for the new CRON cancellation flow

The PR introduces a new WorkflowReminder.cancelled field, a new branch in scheduleEmailReminders.ts that finds and cancels cancelled reminders in SendGrid, and significant new logic in deleteScheduledEmailReminder (new signature with reminderId and immediateDelete option, plus the soft-cancel path that only sets cancelled:true). None of these have automated test coverage. The original bug (#7225) was specifically about cancelled reminders still being sent; without tests, regressions in this code path would re-introduce the same user-visible problem and would not be caught.

Past cancelled reminders are deleted without being cancelled in SendGrid

The deleteMany at lines 34-41 runs BEFORE the new cancellation block at lines 44-77. It deletes ALL email reminders with scheduledDate <= now, including ones marked cancelled:true that have not yet been cancelled in SendGrid. The subsequent findMany at lines 44-51 cannot find them because they were already deleted, so the SendGrid cancellation is never sent. If a booking is cancelled while its reminder's scheduled time has already passed (e.g., when the CRON has been unavailable for an extended period), the email is still sent by SendGrid. The cancellation lookup is also written to include past reminders (lte: now+1h), so the design clearly intended them to be cancelled here. Fix: add `cancelled: { not: true }` to the deleteMany where clause, or reorder the steps so cancellation runs first.

Workflow step deletion races with SendGrid cancellation

Same race as the workflow-deletion finding. At lines 519-525, remindersFromStep.forEach fires SendGrid cancellations via deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId, true) without awaiting, then `await ctx.prisma.workflowStep.delete` at line 527 cascades to delete the workflowReminder rows before the SendGrid cancellation requests may complete. Cancelled-step reminders can still be sent.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getCalendar does not handle dynamic-import failures

Line 15 awaits the dynamic import directly: `const calendarApp = await appStore[calendarType.split("_").join("") as keyof typeof appStore];`. After the PR, `appStore` values are dynamic-import Promises that can reject if the underlying module fails to evaluate (bad syntax, missing dependency, server-side import error, etc.). There is no try/catch around the await, so any such failure propagates and aborts the whole calendar operation (booking creation, cancellation, reschedule, busy-time fetch). The existing post-await guard only handles the `undefined` / missing-`lib` case. The function should catch import errors, log them, and return `null` so that one broken app module doesn't take down operations for users who don't even use that app.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach(async ...) swallows errors from getCalendar in recurring cancellation path

Lines 457-470 use `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... })`. `Array.prototype.forEach` does not await async callbacks, and there is no try/catch around the dynamic import. If `await getCalendar(credential)` rejects (for example because one of the calendar app modules fails to load), the rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection rather than being routed to the existing `logger.error`/cancellation logic, and the corresponding calendar entries are never deleted. The booking is marked cancelled in the DB while the actual calendar event remains. The surrounding `try/catch` at lines 135-139 (in the reschedule files) gives the false impression that errors are caught — they are not, because async callback errors from forEach escape. The same pattern exists in other files modified by this PR.

false_positives.candidate:
No tests added for the async app-store refactor

This PR converts a large surface area of calendar/video/payment loaders from synchronous to dynamic-import-based, including `getCalendar`, `getVideoAdapters`, `getCalendarCredentials`, the reschedule handlers in `vital` and `wipemycalother`, the cancellation handlers in `handleCancelBooking`, the `requestReschedule` tRPC mutation, the `confirm` mutation's refund path, and both `handlePayment` and `deletePayment`. Despite touching every booking lifecycle path, no test files are added or modified in the diff. There is no coverage that the now-dynamic imports resolve and behave identically, that error paths (missing app, broken module) return null instead of throwing, or that the new `await` placements actually preserve execution ordering. Given the scale of the refactor, this is a significant test gap.

forEach(async ...) in requestReschedule swallows getCalendar failures

Lines 553-567 fire calendar/video deletions with `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); })` and there is no try/catch at all in this scope. Because forEach does not await the async callback, a rejection from `await getCalendar` (from the now-dynamic `appStore[...]` import) becomes an unhandled rejection. The mutation returns success while the prior calendar events on the attendee/organizer calendars may never have been deleted, leading to stale events being shown on those calendars after a reschedule.

forEach(async ...) in vital reschedule swallows getCalendar failures

Line 125 wraps the reference-cancellation loop in `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` inside a `try { ... } catch` block. forEach does not await async callbacks, so a rejection from the dynamic import (`getCalendar` → `appStore[calendarType]` → `import("./...")`) propagates as an unhandled promise rejection rather than being caught by the surrounding try/catch (which only sees sync throws and the resolved values of the inner promises). The reschedule returns success even when calendar delete calls never executed, leaving stale calendar events on the user's calendars.

forEach(async ...) in wipemycalother reschedule swallows getCalendar failures

Same pattern as in `packages/app-store/vital/lib/reschedule.ts`: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` inside a try/catch. forEach does not await async callbacks, so any rejection from `await getCalendar` (caused by a broken app module or a missing dependency) is not routed to the existing `logger.error` branch and becomes an unhandled rejection. Calendar/video deletions can silently fail.

getCachedResults awaits all getCalendar calls sequentially inside the map

In `getCachedResults`, the calendars are now loaded with `await Promise.all(calendarCredentials.map((credential) => getCalendar(credential)))`, which is correctly parallelized. However the subsequent `results = calendars.map(async (c, i) => { ... })` then immediately awaits via `Promise.all`, which is fine. The new `getCalendarCredentials` function on the other hand still loads calendars sequentially (one `flatMap` callback at a time), and the `getVideoAdapters` factory in `packages/core/videoClient.ts` was also rewritten as a serial `for` loop rather than a `Promise.all` over credentials. For tenants with several credentials the first booking/cancellation pays N×(module-fetch latency) serially; parallelizing the per-credential fetches would substantially reduce tail latency of the first request after a cold start.

getCalendarCredentials returns Promise values from a synchronous function

After the async refactor, `getCalendar(credential)` now returns `Promise<Calendar | null>`, but `getCalendarCredentials` is still declared as a synchronous function and pushes that Promise into the returned objects as `calendar`. This silently changes the public contract of the exported function: callers that previously received a `Calendar | null` now receive an unawaited Promise, and any new caller (and any existing caller that does not already do `await item.calendar`) will silently treat the Promise as truthy and call methods on it, causing runtime TypeErrors. `getCalendarCredentials` should be made `async` (or the calendar should be awaited inside the flatMap) so the returned `calendar` field is always `Calendar | null`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Identical start/end in working hours check

In the new `workingHours.find((workingHour) => { ... })` callback, both `start` and `end` are computed from the same expression `slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()`. This is a copy-paste error: the intent is clearly to compare the slot start time against `workingHour.startTime` and the slot end time against `workingHour.endTime` (i.e., `end` should be `slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()`). Because both sides compare the same point, a slot starting 5 minutes before the working-hour end but lasting well past it (e.g., 60-minute event ending at 6:05 PM with hours ending 6:00 PM) is wrongly considered available.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Identity comparison of two dayjs objects

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')` compares dayjs instances with `===`. Dayjs objects should be compared with `.isSame()`. The strict equality only works for the same instance reference; two separately constructed dayjs objects representing the same moment are not `===`. This branch is intended to detect zero-length (start == end) overrides, and will not trigger when it should.

false_positives.candidate:
Date override day comparison mixes timezones

The override day is computed via the server's local timezone (`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format(...)`) which is fragile and depends on the server's TZ. The slot's day is in UTC (`slotStartTime.format(...)`). For slots near midnight in either timezone, the comparison may disagree with what the organizer would consider "their" day, so slots can be mis-attributed to (or wrongly excluded from) a date override. The conversion should be done with the timezone plugin explicitly: e.g. `dayjs(date.start).tz(organizerTimeZone).format('YYYY MM DD')` compared to `slotStartTime.tz(organizerTimeZone).format('YYYY MM DD')`.

Date-override timezone offset formula is incorrect

The new formula is `offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset`, then `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + minute()`. Because `override.start` is a moment in time already represented in UTC, adding `organizerUtcOffset` (the organizer's offset) actively shifts the result away from the correct invitee-local minutes. The correct conversion is to add the invitee's offset only (`dayjs(override.start).utc().add(inviteeUtcOffset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + minute()`) or, cleaner, `dayjs(override.start).tz(timeZone).hour() * 60 + minute()`. With the current formula, an organizer with a non-UTC timezone paired with any invitee in a different timezone will produce override start/end values that are off by the organizer's UTC offset, causing slots to appear at the wrong hour for the invitee.

New test does not actually verify the timezone fix

The added test reuses the IST schedule for both the IST and the BDT invitee and only asserts the same UTC strings (`08:30:00.000Z` ... `11:30:00.000Z`). Since slots are always returned in UTC and the override's UTC moment does not change, both code paths (original buggy `getUTCHours()` and the new formula) happen to land on the same UTC times for this scenario. The test would not catch the offset-formula bug above (e.g., an organizer in IST with a 14:00 IST override, plus an invitee in `Asia/Dhaka`, would yield wrong slot hours). The PR claims a timezone regression; the test must use a cross-timezone schedule (e.g., organizer in `Asia/Kolkata`, override "14:00" local, invitee in `America/New_York`) and assert the resulting invitee-local slot times to actually prove the fix works.

Selected-slot availability check skips date overrides and working hours

In the selected-slots branch (lines 581-588), `checkIfIsAvailable` is called with only `time`, `busy`, `...availabilityCheckProps`, and `organizerTimeZone`. It does NOT spread `...userSchedule` (which contains `dateOverrides` and `workingHours`). Because `dateOverrides` and `workingHours` are defaulted to `[]` in the function signature, the date-override and working-hours checks are completely skipped for slots held by users with `selectedSlots`. A user that is on a date-override that closes their availability can still block / be blocked through `selectedSlots`, leading to bookings that violate the organizer's date override.

Unnecessary Date#toString and redundant dayjs calls

`dayjs(override.start.toString())` converts a Date to an ISO string and back to dayjs, which loses no information but is a code smell and risks platform-dependent string formatting. The same `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute')` is computed twice in the return expression; caching it into a local would halve the work and make the intent clearer. Not a correctness bug on its own but worth fixing alongside the offset formula.

Working hours day check uses UTC, not organizer timezone

`slotStartTime.day()` is computed from `time.utc()` and returns the UTC day-of-week, while `workingHour.days` are in the organizer's timezone (the schedule TZ). For a slot at e.g. 18:30 UTC on Tuesday, the organizer (IST, UTC+5:30) is already at 00:00 Wednesday; `workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())` will fail to match a Wednesday working-hour entry. Slots near the day boundary in the organizer's TZ will be incorrectly marked unavailable. Consequence: false double-bookings prevented, or more commonly, valid slots hidden.

Working hours time check uses UTC, not organizer timezone

`slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` is UTC minutes-since-midnight, but `workingHour.startTime` / `workingHour.endTime` are minutes-since-midnight in the organizer's timezone (per the WorkingHours type comment). Comparing UTC minutes against organizer minutes produces incorrect results for any organizer not in UTC. Even though `checkIfIsAvailable` receives `organizerTimeZone`, it never uses it for the day/time comparison, making the parameter useless for its main job.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError when reinstalling integrations without sender in metadata

In `GitHubInstallation.dispatch()`, the code accesses `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]` to compare with the authenticated GitHub user. However, integrations created before this change may not have a `"sender"` key in their metadata (it is only set in `build_integration` when `state.get("sender")` is truthy). When such an existing active integration is encountered (e.g., during a reinstall flow), this line will raise `KeyError`, producing a 500 error for the user instead of the intended graceful error page. The access should use `.get()` with a safe default, e.g. `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Null reference if github_authenticated_user state is missing
OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
No timeout on OAuth token exchange request

`safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)` is called without a timeout argument. If the GitHub OAuth endpoint hangs or is slow, this view will block indefinitely. Given the other `safe_urlopen` callers in the codebase typically pass an explicit `timeout=`, this call should do the same to avoid tying up worker threads on a hung OAuth handshake.

OAuth token exchange does not send redirect_uri or Accept header

The token exchange POST to GitHub sends `code`, `client_id`, and `client_secret` but omits the `redirect_uri` and an `Accept: application/json` header. While GitHub is usually lenient about `redirect_uri`, many OAuth client configurations require it to exactly match the value used at the authorize step, and on failure GitHub returns the error body as JSON (which `parse_qsl` will misparse, leading to the generic "access_token not in payload" path instead of logging the real `error_description`). Both `redirect_uri` and `Accept` should be included for correctness and debuggability.

Uncaught exceptions in get_user_info will produce 500 errors

After exchanging the OAuth code, the view calls `get_user_info(payload["access_token"])` without any exception handling. If this call fails due to a network error, timeout, invalid token, or any other error, the exception will propagate up and result in a 500 error instead of the intended graceful error page. The view already catches broad exceptions when parsing the token response, so a similar try/except around `get_user_info` (and around `safe_urlopen` itself) is needed to ensure all failure paths return the `error()` page like the other validation failures do.

test_github_user_mismatch uses hardcoded state and may pass for wrong reason

`test_github_user_mismatch` builds `setup_path_2` with the hardcoded state `"9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3"` (the same value asserted in `assert_setup_flow`). It then logs in as a different user (`user_2`) in a different org (`org_2`) before issuing the GETs. If `pipeline.signature` depends on the user or organization, this state will not match the pipeline started by `user_2/org_2`, and the test will pass due to state mismatch — not user mismatch. The assertion only checks for the generic `"Invalid installation request."` string, which is the same error returned for state mismatch, so the test does not actually verify the user-mismatch code path. The test should extract the actual `state` from the redirect URL returned by `init_path_2` (or otherwise obtain the correct signature) and use that in `setup_path_2`, and ideally assert a more specific error indicator.

test_installation_not_found no longer tests installation-not-found behavior

`test_installation_not_found` stubs a 404 for `/app/installations/{installation_id}` and then calls the setup path with `installation_id` and again with `code` + `state="ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05"` (which deliberately does not match any pipeline signature). The first GET just bounces through `OAuthLoginView` to GitHub authorize; the second GET fails at the state check before ever reaching `build_integration`, so the 404 stub is never exercised. The test now only verifies that the generic "Invalid installation request." error is shown — the same error shown for state mismatch. Either the test should be renamed to reflect what it actually verifies, or it should be rewritten to complete the OAuth step (with a correct state) so that `build_integration` is reached and the 404 path in `get_installation_info` is actually tested.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mutable default value: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`

In a dataclass, a default value of `timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class definition time and is then shared by every instance created without an explicit `queued` argument. Every `AssignmentSource(source_name=..., integration_id=...)` constructed in a worker will therefore have the same `queued` datetime (the import time of the module), not the time the source was actually queued. The correct pattern is `queued: datetime = field(default_factory=timezone.now)`. The field is not yet consulted in any comparison logic in this PR, so the cycle-breaking itself still works, but the field is serialized through Celery as `to_dict` / `from_dict` and any future use of `queued` for staleness, deduplication, or analytics will be incorrect. The test `test_to_dict` only asserts the key is present, so it does not catch this.

true_positives.golden_comment: The method name has a typo: test_from_dict_inalid_data should be test_from_dict_invalid_data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test name typo: `inalid_data`

The test method is named `test_from_dict_inalid_data`. The intended spelling is `test_from_dict_invalid_data`. Renaming fixes a misleading test identifier that hides intent and breaks search/grep for invalid-input tests.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Method name says 'empty_array' but tests empty dict - consider renaming to 'test_from_dict_empty_dict' for clarity.
to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.

false_positives.candidate:
Missing test for cross-integration propagation (cycle break must not over-block)

The new `test_assignee_sync_outbound_assign_with_matching_source_integration` proves the loop is broken when the source equals the only target. It does not prove the other direction the PR's docstring relies on: when multiple integrations are linked to the same group, an inbound change from integration A must still propagate to integration B. Without a test that links two `ExternalIssue`s from two different provider integrations and asserts that `sync_assignee_outbound` IS called for the non-source one, the `should_sync` short-circuit could regress to blocking all outbound sync (e.g., by checking integration_id more broadly) and the suite would still pass.

No test catches the mutable-default bug for `queued`

`test_to_dict` only asserts that `result.get("queued") is not None`. A test that constructs two `AssignmentSource` instances in sequence (e.g., with a short sleep between them) and asserts that `s1.queued != s2.queued` would have detected the shared-default bug in the dataclass. Add this assertion, plus a `from_dict` round-trip test, before relying on `queued` for any logic.

`assignment_source.to_dict()` recomputed on every loop iteration

In `sync_group_assignee_outbound`, the expression `assignment_source.to_dict() if assignment_source else None` is evaluated inside the `for external_issue_id in external_issue_ids` loop, so `to_dict()` (and therefore `asdict()` plus a full copy of the dataclass) is run once per linked external issue. The value does not depend on `external_issue_id`; compute it once before the loop and reuse the dict in the kwargs. The `AssignmentSource` is frozen, but the inner dict is rebuilt unnecessarily for each outbound task.

true_positives.golden_comment: MetricAlertDetectorHandler inherits from StatefulDetectorHandler but only contains pass, failing to implement its required abstract methods: counter_names (property), get_dedupe_value(), get_group_key_values(), and build_occurrence_and_event_data(). This will cause a TypeError at runtime when the class is instantiated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
MetricAlertDetectorHandler now extends StatefulDetectorHandler without implementing required abstract methods

The PR changes `MetricAlertDetectorHandler` from `DetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate]` to `StatefulDetectorHandler[QuerySubscriptionUpdate]`, but the body remains `pass`. `StatefulDetectorHandler` declares abstract members `counter_names`, `get_dedupe_value`, `get_group_key_values`, and now also the newly-added `build_occurrence_and_event_data`. Since `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler = MetricAlertDetectorHandler` is wired up in the same file, this will break the moment anyone references `MetricAlertFire.detector_handler`. true_positives.golden_comment: Wrong value `6` passed for `group_2` occurrence — the data packet specifies `"group_2": 10`. Should be `10` to accurately reflect the test scenario, which will ensure the test produces the correct occurrence data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent value passed to build_mock_occurrence_and_event in multiple tests

Several tests pass `value=6` to `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` even though the data packet being evaluated contains different values. For example: `test_state_results_multi_group` calls `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(detector.detector_handler, "group_2", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)` while the data packet has `group_vals: {"group_2": 10}`; `test_results_on_change` calls it with `value=6` while the packet has `val1: 100`; `test_dedupe` calls it with `value=6` while the packet has `val1: 8`; `TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe` calls it with `value=6` while `evaluate_group_key_value` is invoked with `value=10`. Currently the value isn't used inside `build_mock_occurrence_and_event` so the tests pass, but the inconsistency obscures intent and any future change that incorporates `value` into the occurrence or event_data will silently produce wrong assertions.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Docstring says this returns a list of DetectorEvaluationResult, but the method now returns a dict keyed by DetectorGroupKey. Consider updating the docstring to match the new return type.

false_positives.candidate:
Kafka produce exceptions prevent state commit, causing duplicate detections

`process_detectors` calls `create_issue_occurrence_from_result` (which calls `produce_occurrence_to_kafka`) BEFORE `handler.commit_state_updates()`. If Kafka is unavailable or `produce_occurrence_to_kafka` raises, the exception propagates out of the loop and `commit_state_updates()` is never executed for that detector. The Redis dedupe value is therefore not updated, so on the next processing of the same data packet the detector will re-emit the same occurrence (and re-trigger downstream workflows). This is also exposed more by the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data` path which can now raise from subclass code and have the same effect. Either wrap the produce in a try/except or commit dedupe state after successful produces.

dedupe_update is enqueued before condition_group is validated

At runtime this raises `TypeError: missing 1 required positional argument: 'force'`, which is swallowed by the broad `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop`. The result is that offsets are never committed, the offset tracker grows without bound, and on restart the consumer re-reads everything it has already processed (defeating the whole point of the commit loop and potentially causing data-integrity issues for non-idempotent result processors). get_queue_for_group uses Python's hash(), not consistent hashing

`get_queue_for_group` is implemented as `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` and its docstring says "consistent hashing". Python's built-in `hash()` for strings is randomized across processes (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the same `group_key` can be assigned to a different queue on every restart. Within a single process lifetime ordering is preserved (which is what the consumer relies on, since in-flight items are lost on restart anyway), but the function does not provide the cross-process stability the docstring advertises, and it isn't true consistent hashing (e.g. it doesn't survive changes in `num_queues`).
