Auth-flow behavior change for ErrDeviceLimitReached has no test

Anonymous.Authenticate now propagates anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached up so authentication fails when the limit is hit. The new integration test (TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit) only covers the store-level CreateOrUpdateDevice path; there is no test that exercises Anonymous.Authenticate to confirm (1) ErrDeviceLimitReached causes Authenticate to return an error rather than a successful identity, and (2) other errors from TagDevice are still swallowed with a warning. This is a behavior change that warrants a dedicated test, including asserting what HTTP status / message a real request would receive.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

false_positives.candidate:
Extra COUNT(*) on every anonymous auth when limit is set

CreateOrUpdateDevice now issues a SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ... AND ... on every call when deviceLimit > 0. There is no caching of the count and the check runs unconditionally on the auth hot path, adding a full table scan (or index scan) to every anonymous request even when the limit is nowhere near being reached.

New device_limit setting has no user-facing documentation

The PR adds cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit read from [auth.anonymous] device_limit with default 0 (treated as unlimited), but no documentation file (e.g. docs/sources/setup-grafana/configure-grafana/_index.md or similar) is updated. Operators have no way to learn about the new key, its semantics (0 = unlimited, what happens at the limit, interaction with the 30-day cleanup window), or its env-var override name (expected GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_DEVICE_LIMIT). The default sentinel of 0 and the rejection semantics (new devices rejected, existing devices continue to update) also need to be called out.

TagDevice moved to synchronous request context

The previous implementation called TagDevice in a goroutine with an independent 2-minute context (context.Background() + WithTimeout). The new code calls TagDevice synchronously using the request context. Consequences: (a) every anonymous auth now pays the full DB latency (count + insert/update) on the hot path; (b) if the client cancels the request, the request context is cancelled and the device is never tagged, which both skews the usage stat 'stats.anonymous.device.ui.count' and lets a device avoid being counted against the limit. The async design should be retained for non-limit errors and only the limit-exceeded path needs to surface synchronously.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine cleanup logs use Error level

The new cleanup paths emit r.log.Error for normal, expected operations: 'Annotations to clean by time', 'cleaned annotations by time', 'Annotations to clean by count', 'cleaned annotations by count', 'Tags to clean', 'cleaned tags' (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). These are routine successful operations that will fire on every cleanup cycle. With the cleanup ticker in cleanup.go now firing every minute (a separate change in this PR), this produces a steady stream of Error-level log entries masking real errors. Severity is amplified by the same PR also logging all IDs ('ids', ids), which can be up to AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries (up to 32767) per batch, potentially producing enormous log lines. These should be Debug/Info level, not Error.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker shortened 10x without justification

Ticker changed from `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)`. The PR description is solely about fixing a MySQL deadlock via query restructuring; nothing in the description or the referenced issue (grafana/grafana#64979) justifies a 10x increase in cleanup frequency. This multiplies the database load of every cleanup job by 10x, including annotation cleanup, dashboard version cleanup, short URL cleanup, query history cleanup, etc. Combined with the noisy Error logs added in xorm_store.go, this materially changes operational behavior and should either be split into its own change or justified explicitly. Note also that `cleanUpOldAnnotations` is called inside this 1-minute loop, and the new fetch+delete implementation uses two round-trips per batch instead of one, compounding the load.

false_positives.candidate:
Log fields include 'err' even when fetch succeeded

Each new cleanup log line passes `"err", err` as a structured field. The `err` here is the result of `fetchIDs`, which is nil on the success path. Every successful cleanup therefore emits `"err": <nil>` in its log payload, which is misleading to operators triaging errors (especially since these are emitted at Error level - see the other finding). The 'err' field should only be included when err is non-nil, or the message should be split so success and failure paths log different things.

O(N^2) string building in SQLite IN-list inlining

In deleteByIDs, when SQLite is used and the configured batch size exceeds the parameter limit, IDs are concatenated into a SQL literal:
    values := fmt.Sprint(ids[0])
    for _, v := range ids[1:] {
        values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)
    }
Each iteration rebuilds the whole string from scratch, giving O(N^2) time and memory growth proportional to len(ids)^2. With AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize configured as high as 32767, this produces a string of ~300k+ characters built through tens of thousands of allocations on every cleanup batch. Should use strings.Builder (or similar) to build the IN-list in a single pass. Also, for the typical case where len(ids) is much smaller than the configured batch size (because there are simply few rows to clean), the branch condition checks `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` instead of `len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit`, so the slower inlining path is taken even when the placeholder path would work fine.

SQLite parameter-limit branch checks config, not actual ID count

The branch `if r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` decides whether to inline IDs into the SQL based on the configured batch size, not on `len(ids)`. The actual number of parameters needed equals `len(ids)`, which is bounded by `LIMIT AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` but usually far smaller (cleanup often finds only a handful of rows). When the operator sets a large batch size (e.g., the new test exercises 32767), the inlining path is taken on every call even if only a few rows are being deleted, building a needless literal string and skipping the (correct) parameterized path. Use `len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete attaches d.Log to context instead of the enriched logger

Every other method in this file does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` using the local `log` variable that already carries name/kind/method. Delete builds that local log on line 96 but then sets `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`, so the legacy store (and any code reading the logger from the context) only sees the bare DualWriterMode3 logger with mode=3 and loses name, kind, and method. Inconsistent with Create/Get/List/Update/DeleteCollection and reduces observability of async legacy writes.

true_positives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded under storage metric

In the async goroutine for DeleteCollection the legacy result is timed and then d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy) is called. This is the legacy path, so it should be d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). As written, a legacy DeleteCollection failure silently inflates the storage metric, and the legacy duration histogram never receives any samples from DeleteCollection.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Kind metric label is set to the resource name

The success branch of Delete calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). Every other recorder in the file uses options.Kind as the kind label, but here `name` (the resource identifier) is passed instead. This (a) makes the metric inconsistent with the rest of mode 3 and (b) blows up the metric cardinality because each deleted resource name becomes a label value. Should be options.Kind.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the cancelled request context

All four async goroutines (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) derive their context with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...). `ctx` is the API server request context, which is cancelled as soon as the handler returns and the response is sent. In practice that means the legacy goroutines often start in an already-cancelled context and the 10-second safety net never has a chance to fire. Result: legacy writes are aborted shortly after the user sees a success response, and because the failure is only logged via metrics, the user has no visibility. For 'safe measure' dual writes this defeats the purpose. Detach from the request lifetime (e.g. context.WithoutCancel or context.Background preserving values) and rely solely on the timeout.

No test verifies that the async legacy write actually happens

TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection all set up the legacy mock with m.On(...) but never assert that it was called (no mock.AssertCalled for the legacy backend). The goroutine in dualwriter_mode3.go has no synchronization with the test, so on a fast machine the test function can return and t.Run can finish before the goroutine has dispatched, meaning a regression that simply removed the goroutine would still pass the tests. Add an explicit AssertCalled (and ideally a small synchronization point) to prove the async write really happened.

Storage Update failure recorded under the legacy duration metric

Mirrors the bug on line 45. When d.Storage.Update fails, d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) is called, attributing the storage failure to the legacy backend in the metrics. The success branch on line 132 correctly uses recordStorageDuration, so the failure branch should be d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

Storage failure recorded under the legacy duration metric

When d.Storage.Create returns an error the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...). The metric name (legacy vs storage) is used by dashboards/alerts to distinguish the two backends, so a storage failure ends up inflating the legacy error metric and the storage success metric is never recorded for this path. The success path on line 48 correctly uses recordStorageDuration, so the error branch should mirror it: d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). The same pattern is repeated in the Update method (line 129).

TestMode3_Create 'unified store fails' case does not set up the storage mock

The second test case sets up only the legacy mock and leaves setupStorageFn nil. Mode3 calls d.Storage.Create before d.Legacy.Create (see dualwriter_mode3.go line 42), so on the testify mock the Storage.Create invocation is unexpected and the test will panic/fail before reaching the legacy mock at all. The test does not exercise the intended path ('storage Create fails, no legacy call'). It needs a setupStorageFn returning an error and either no legacy expectation or an AssertNotCalled for legacy.

TestMode3_Get creates a local Prometheus registry instead of using the package-level `p`

All other tests in this file (and the matching Mode1 tests in dualwriter_mode1_test.go, which were just refactored away from this pattern in the same PR) use the shared `var p = prometheus.NewRegistry()` declared in dualwriter_mode1_test.go. TestMode3_Get introduces a local `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` on line 119. It works but is inconsistent and looks like a missed cleanup. Use the shared registry.

Update no longer wraps objInfo for the legacy call

The previous implementation precomputed `updated` from the storage copy, then passed an `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: ...}` to both Storage.Update and Legacy.Update so both backends received the exact same resolved object. The new code passes the raw objInfo to d.Legacy.Update. If Storage and Legacy disagree on the previous object (e.g. they have drifted) or if objInfo.UpdatedObject behaves differently in the two implementations, the two stores can now persist different versions of the same object, producing data drift between unified storage and legacy storage. This is a real behavioural regression, not just a refactor.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing double-check after acquiring write lock

GetWebAssets releases the RLock before checking whether the cache is populated, then unconditionally re-reads the manifest after taking the write lock. Two concurrent callers that both observe a nil cache will both serialize on the write lock and each perform the full file read and JSON parse, instead of the second caller reusing the value just populated by the first. Adding a re-check of `entryPointAssetsCache` after the Lock() (classic double-checked locking) would eliminate the redundant I/O on the cold-start path. Not a correctness bug—safe under the mutex—but wasteful for concurrent first callers in production.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test added for the data race fix

The PR's stated purpose is to fix a data race on the shared `entryPointAssetsCache` global, but no test exercising concurrent calls to GetWebAssets is included. For a race-condition fix, the maintainer should expect at least one test that invokes GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines (intended to be run with `go test -race`) to guard against the race being reintroduced. Without such a test, the fix is verified only by inspection and there is no automated guard against future regressions on this exact path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions has dead code and misleading semantics

The function enableSqlExpressions always returns false because both the `if enabled` branch and the fallthrough return false, regardless of the feature flag value. The local variable `enabled` is the negation of FlagSqlExpressions, so the name reads as a double negative (`enabled := !IsEnabled(...)`). The net effect is just `return false`. This is a maintainability trap: a future developer trying to 'fix' the function to honor the feature flag will be misled by the dead branch and the variable naming, and could easily reintroduce SQL execution in a way that re-introduces CVE-2024-9264. The function should be a single explicit `return false` with a comment explaining the security reason, or the name should be changed to make the always-disabled behavior obvious.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
Misleading 'not implemented' error message

The error returned when SQL expressions are rejected reads `sqlExpressions is not implemented`. SQL expressions were implemented previously; they are now intentionally disabled as the mitigation for CVE-2024-9264. The message will mislead users and operators (and make log/triage harder) into thinking the feature simply wasn't built, rather than that it was turned off for security. It should reference the security reason (e.g. 'sqlExpressions have been disabled due to CVE-2024-9264').

Security-fix change to SQL expressions has no test coverage

This PR is the public fix for CVE-2024-9264 and changes both the gating (reader.go now rejects QueryTypeSQL) and the SQL backend (db.go stub, parser.go, sql_command.go). No test file is added or updated to verify that: (1) a QueryTypeSQL request now returns the documented error from reader.go, (2) NewSQLCommand / UnmarshalSQLCommand cannot produce an executable SQLCommand, and (3) SQLCommand.Execute, if reached, returns an error instead of executing user-controlled SQL. Without regression tests it is very easy for a future change (e.g. 're-enable SQL via feature flag', or deleting the stub) to silently re-introduce the vulnerability. The PR description also leaves the feature-flag-related docs unchecked; a test asserting behavior under the flag would at least lock the mitigation down.

Stub DB has no comment explaining why it exists

The new file pkg/expr/sql/db.go replaces the vulnerable scottlepp/go-duck-backed implementation with a no-op stub. There is no package or type-level comment stating that this stub intentionally exists to neutralize CVE-2024-9264 and that the real SQL execution backend must not be re-introduced without addressing that vulnerability. Without such a comment, a future contributor is likely to delete the stub and reinstate DuckDB execution, silently re-exposing the RCE/LFI.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent searches for the same NamespacedResource can trigger duplicate full index builds

getOrCreateIndex reads s.search.GetIndex (which checks a non-locked-ish cache via RWMutex) and, if nil, calls s.build, which in turn invokes SearchBackend.BuildIndex. There is no per-key synchronization. Two concurrent callers for the same key therefore both see a cache miss, both run the full document builder (potentially listing and indexing millions of rows), both flush, and the second write to b.cache[key] wins. The first caller's *ResourceIndex is still valid, but the cost of building was paid twice and the second build can also starve the watcher of resources. The pre-existing TODO right above the function (`// TODO??? // We want to block while building the index and return the same index for the key`) acknowledges this. The PR's change in bleve.go (releasing cacheMu before building) is correct for different keys but does nothing for same-key races; with the move from lazy to eager init the probability of overlapping first-request races goes up. At minimum the PR should add per-key locking around the GetIndex + BuildIndex sequence (e.g., singleflight.Group, or a sync.Map of per-key *sync.Mutex).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

false_positives.candidate:
BuildIndex still shadows the trace context with its span

Unlike search.go and sql/backend.go's GetResourceStats, bleve.go's BuildIndex uses `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, tracingPrexfixBleve+"BuildIndex")` and discards the returned ctx. The same trace-propagation bug the PR is trying to fix elsewhere therefore remains in this hot path: the call to `builder(idx)` (which runs the entire list-iterator + builder loop) does not see the BuildIndex span as its parent, and traces of the index build will be missing the bleve-level span. The same one-character fix (`ctx, span := ...`) should be applied here for consistency with the other files in the PR.

Goroutine and resource leak when NewResourceServer init fails

After constructing the server struct (which creates a cancellable ctx/cancel pair stored on the struct), NewResourceServer now eagerly calls s.Init(ctx). If Init returns an error (e.g., search.init fails partway through, or s.initWatcher fails), the function logs the error and returns nil, err. Because s is nil and cancel was never invoked, any goroutines that Init started cannot be cleaned up: the s.initWatcher goroutine + SQL poller run on s.ctx and will keep polling the database; the search.init watch goroutine (see search.go) runs on context.Background() and is not tied to s.ctx at all, so it is orphaned regardless. There is no way for the caller of NewResourceServer to stop them. Before this PR Init was idempotently deferred to the first RPC, where they would only be retained on the returned server. The fix is to defer cancel() at the top of NewResourceServer (and ideally make search.init's watchctx derive from s.ctx), so a partial init always tears its goroutines down.

Init error is logged twice

Init already logs `s.log.Error("error initializing resource server", "error", s.initErr)` inside the s.once.Do block, and the new caller in NewResourceServer then logs the same error again with the same message right before returning nil, err. Pick one site and drop the other to avoid the duplicate entry and to keep the error format consistent with the other NewResourceServer error paths (which only return).

Trace propagation fix is inconsistent across the sql backend

The PR correctly changes GetResourceStats from `_, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` to `ctx, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` so the span context flows into the WithTx call below it. The same broken pattern is left in place in this same file for WriteEvent (line 158), create (174), update (236), delete (298), ReadResource (353), ListIterator (388), poller (580), listLatestRVs (619), poll (664) and resourceVersionAtomicInc (718). All of them discard the returned ctx, so the OpenTelemetry spans they start are not parents of the SQL calls made inside them. The fix in GetResourceStats was presumably driven by tracing the new eager index build; the same one-line fix should be applied to all the other methods that start a span and then perform work under that context, otherwise half the storage trace tree is broken.

search.init's watcher uses context.Background(), preventing server.Stop from stopping it

In searchSupport.init the watch is set up with `watchctx := context.Background() // new context?` and the resulting events channel is consumed by `go func() { for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) } }()`. The author even left a question mark in the comment. Because watchctx is background, calling server.Stop (which cancels s.ctx) does not stop this goroutine or its underlying storage backend poller; it will only exit if the storage backend itself is independently stopped. The symmetric watcher created by initWatcher in server.go uses s.ctx and so is cancelled correctly. This asymmetry is also what makes the Init failure leak above worse: even calling cancel after a failed Init cannot reach this watch. search.init should accept and use the long-lived s.ctx (or a child of it) for both WatchWriteEvents and the goroutine, so a single Stop cleans up everything.

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.
Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.

false_positives.candidate:
remove() always queries DB for the IDP, even when the alias is already cached

The new line `IdentityProviderModel storedIdp = idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias);` is executed unconditionally on every `remove()` call, but in the cache-hit branch (lines 105-108) the `CachedIdentityProvider cached` is already available from the alias cache. The cached IDP could be passed to `registerIDPLoginInvalidation(...)` on line 111 (mirroring how `registerIDPInvalidation(cached.getIdentityProvider())` is already done on line 107), avoiding the extra DB round-trip in the warm-cache case. Previously, `idpDelegate.getByAlias(alias)` was only invoked inside the `isInvalid(cacheKey)` branch; the hoisted fetch now runs on every remove, which is a regression for the common case where the alias cache is populated.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() does not return BouncyCastle

Despite its name, `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns the Provider that backs the JVM's default keystore type (typically SUN or SunJSSE), not BouncyCastle: `return KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider();`. This is a deliberate workaround because the authz-client module does not depend on BouncyCastle, but the method name promises a BC Provider. Any caller that selects algorithms specific to BouncyCastle (e.g. certain EC curves, RSA-PSS variants, JOSE algorithms only BC exposes) will silently get the JCA default provider and may behave unexpectedly. The misleading contract should at least be renamed (e.g. `getDefaultProvider()`), or the method should throw UnsupportedOperationException to be consistent with the rest of this class.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead ASN1Encoder invocations in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

Lines 114-115 create two ASN1Encoder instances and call `write()` on each, then discard the results without ever consuming the produced bytes:
```
ASN1Encoder.create().write(rBigInteger);
ASN1Encoder.create().write(sBigInteger);
```
The real DER encoding happens on lines 117-121 via `writeDerSeq(...)`. The two statements above are pure dead code that allocates four throwaway ByteArrayOutputStreams for no purpose. They should be removed.

true_positives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
readSequence silently mishandles indefinite-length and over-long TLVs

`readSequence()` does two unsafe things:
1. If `readLength()` returns -1 (BER indefinite-length encoding, which `readLength()` explicitly supports), the `while (length > 0)` test is false on entry and the method returns an empty list while leaving the end-of-contents marker and the entire sequence body unread. Callers will then see a zero-length list and either index out of bounds or silently accept an empty signature.
2. `readNext()` can in principle return more bytes than the declared remaining length (malformed input); in that case `length` underflows, the loop exits, and the leftover bytes are silently swallowed instead of being rejected as malformed.
The reader should either reject indefinite-length as not supported for DER or read until the 0x00 0x00 end-of-contents octets, and should validate that the consumed bytes never exceed the declared length.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations

false_positives.candidate:
Test uses a single P-256 key for ES256/ES384/ES512

The constructor calls `KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair()`, which on the standard SunEC provider returns a P-256 (secp256r1) key. That same key is then used to exercise ES256, ES384 and ES512, each of which expects a different curve and a different raw signature length (64, 96, 132 bytes respectively). With a P-256 key the SHA384withECDSA/SHA512withECDSA signatures still have only 32+32 byte components, so `getSignatureLength()` returns 96/132 while the real signature is 64 bytes; the test only round-trips the bytes through DER<->concatenatedRS and so happens to pass even though no ES384/ES512-shaped signature is ever produced. The test does not verify the conversion for genuinely larger curves and does not assert that a signature produced by `signature.sign()` round-trips to the original signature value for the expected length. Generate (or load) a key of the appropriate curve per algorithm and assert the round-tripped bytes actually equal the original `sign()` output.

logger.debugf called with a plain string and no format arguments

`logger.debugf(builder.toString());` passes a String with no `%` placeholders and no varargs to `debugf(String, Object...)`. This is misleading because the signature suggests a printf-style format string. If any discovered CryptoProvider class name ever contained a `%` (unlikely but not enforced), it would be interpreted as a format specifier and could throw. Use `logger.debug(builder.toString())` (or `logger.tracef` if formatting is desired) instead.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Listener gated on V1 feature flag will skip V2 cleanup

registerListener now wraps all event handlers in `if (Profile.isFeatureEnabled(Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ))`. ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is the V1 flag; V2 is gated on ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 elsewhere (in evaluator()/management()). If only the V2 flag is enabled, the listener body never runs, so RoleRemovedEvent/ClientRemovedEvent/GroupRemovedEvent will no longer trigger setPermissionsEnabled(...) cleanup on the corresponding permission resources. The original code ran unconditionally and let management() route to V1 or V2. Either the check should be `ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ || ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2` (or just the V2 flag), or the V2 implementations must actually be wired up so these events still get processed.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission leaks the 'Clients' aggregate name into the result

resourceStore.findByType(server, "Clients", ...) returns every resource whose type is "Clients" — that includes both per-client resources (named by client.getId()) and the schema's aggregate 'all-clients' resource (named "Clients"). The lambda then does `granted.add(resource.getName())`. true_positives.matched_candidate:
isAccessTokenId matcher has both an off-by-one and an inverted condition

Two bugs in the new matcher body:
```
if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;
```
1. Off-by-one: the grant type is the last 2 characters of the 6-char prefix, i.e. indices 4 and 5. The call must be `items[0].substring(4, 6)`. The current call returns a mix of the second char of token type and the first char of grant type, not the grant type alone.
2. Inverted condition: the matcher is supposed to SUCCESS only when the grant type matches the expected shortcut, but the code returns false (no match) when the substring equals the expected shortcut. A correct version would be: `if (!items[0].substring(4, 6).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`.
As written, the matcher effectively accepts any well-formed encoded token ID regardless of which grant produced it, so integration tests that rely on it (expectCodeToToken, expectRefresh, expectDeviceCodeToToken, expectAuthReqIdToToken) will not be able to detect regressions in grant type encoding.

false_positives.candidate:
Access token `jti` now encodes grant type, session type and lightweight flag visible to clients

`initToken` now sets `token.id(encoder.encodeTokenId(tokenCtx))`, which prepends a 6-character prefix (e.g. `onrtac:`) to the UUID used as the JWT `jti` and as `Details.TOKEN_ID`. The prefix reveals to any party that sees the access token (resource servers, browser-side apps, logs, error reports) the grant type that minted the token (including `pre-authorized_code`, `token-exchange`, etc.), whether the session is offline/online/transient, and whether the token is a lightweight access token. While not secret, this leaks behaviour (e.g. presence of offline sessions, use of token exchange) that is otherwise not conveyed to clients and that may not be desirable in all deployments (e.g. compliance, fingerprinting of Keycloak version/features, ability to distinguish realms/configurations). Consider making the SPI opt-in or at least allowing operators to disable it, and documenting the information disclosure in release notes.

`Constants.GRANT_TYPE` is defined as `OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE`, which is the literal string `"grant_type"` (the standard OAuth2 form parameter name). It is used both as the form-parameter key to populate `OAuth2GrantType.Context.grantType` and as the attribute key on `ClientSessionContext`. Because session context attributes and form parameters are different objects, this is not a runtime bug, but the shared string is a sharp edge: any code that reads or writes `Constants.GRANT_TYPE` on the wrong object (e.g. on the form params) would be confused. Use a distinct namespaced key such as `Constants.GRANT_TYPE + ".attribute"` or move it to a session-context-specific constant to make the distinction explicit.

The diff deletes the `public Context(Context context)` copy constructor that was part of the public static nested class `OAuth2GrantType.Context`. There is no per-key synchronization. Two concurrent callers for the same key therefore both see a cache miss, both run the full document builder (potentially listing and indexing millions of rows), both flush, and the second write to b.cache[key] wins. The first caller's *ResourceIndex is still valid, but the cost of building was paid twice and the second build can also starve the watcher of resources. The pre-existing TODO right above the function (`// TODO??? // We want to block while building the index and return the same index for the key`) acknowledges this. The PR's change in bleve.go (releasing cacheMu before building) is correct for different keys but does nothing for same-key races; with the move from lazy to eager init the probability of overlapping first-request races goes up. At minimum the PR should add per-key locking around the GetIndex + BuildIndex sequence (e.g., singleflight.Group, or a sync.Map of per-key *sync.Mutex).

Goroutine and resource leak when NewResourceServer init fails

After constructing the server struct (which creates a cancellable ctx/cancel pair stored on the struct), NewResourceServer now eagerly calls s.Init(ctx). If Init returns an error (e.g., search.init fails partway through, or s.initWatcher fails), the function logs the error and returns nil, err. Because s is nil and cancel was never invoked, any goroutines that Init started cannot be cleaned up: the s.initWatcher goroutine + SQL poller run on s.ctx and will keep polling the database; the search.init watch goroutine (see search.go) runs on context.Background() and is not tied to s.ctx at all, so it is orphaned regardless. There is no way for the caller of NewResourceServer to stop them. Before this PR Init was idempotently deferred to the first RPC, where they would only be retained on the returned server. The fix is to defer cancel() at the top of NewResourceServer (and ideally make search.init's watchctx derive from s.ctx), so a partial init always tears its goroutines down.

search.init's watcher uses context.Background(), preventing server.Stop from stopping it

In searchSupport.init the watch is set up with `watchctx := context.Background() // new context?` and the resulting events channel is consumed by `go func() { for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) } }()`. The author even left a question mark in the comment. Because watchctx is background, calling server.Stop (which cancels s.ctx) does not stop this goroutine or its underlying storage backend poller; it will only exit if the storage backend itself is independently stopped. The symmetric watcher created by initWatcher in server.go uses s.ctx and so is cancelled correctly. This asymmetry is also what makes the Init failure leak above worse: even calling cancel after a failed Init cannot reach this watch. search.init should accept and use the long-lived s.ctx (or a child of it) for both WatchWriteEvents and the goroutine, so a single Stop cleans up everything.

Trace propagation fix is inconsistent across the sql backend

The PR correctly changes GetResourceStats from `_, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` to `ctx, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` so the span context flows into the WithTx call below it. The same broken pattern is left in place in this same file for WriteEvent (line 158), create (174), update (236), delete (298), ReadResource (353), ListIterator (388), poller (580), listLatestRVs (619), poll (664) and resourceVersionAtomicInc (718). All of them discard the returned ctx, so the OpenTelemetry spans they start are not parents of the SQL calls made inside them. The fix in GetResourceStats was presumably driven by tracing the new eager index build; the same one-line fix should be applied to all the other methods that start a span and then perform work under that context, otherwise half the storage trace tree is broken.

Init error is logged twice

Init already logs `s.log.Error("error initializing resource server", "error", s.initErr)` inside the s.once.Do block, and the new caller in NewResourceServer then logs the same error again with the same message right before returning nil, err. Pick one site and drop the other to avoid the duplicate entry and to keep the error format consistent with the other NewResourceServer error paths (which only return).

BuildIndex still shadows the trace context with its span

Unlike search.go and sql/backend.go's GetResourceStats, bleve.go's BuildIndex uses `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, tracingPrexfixBleve+"BuildIndex")` and discards the returned ctx. The same trace-propagation bug the PR is trying to fix elsewhere therefore remains in this hot path: the call to `builder(idx)` (which runs the entire list-iterator + builder loop) does not see the BuildIndex span as its parent, and traces of the index build will be missing the bleve-level span. The redirect resolution loop iterates from `for i = 0, 1000 do` (line 30) but the original code used `for i = 0, 10000 do` and explicitly noted in the comment that this limit governs whether deep segment trees are joined correctly: 'theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' Reducing the limit to 1000 silently breaks any trace whose redirect chain has depth between 1000 and 10000 — those spans will not be merged into the same set. No tests exercise deep trees, so this regression is not caught. Consequence: traces with deep span trees (1000+) end up split across multiple buffer sets and get flushed as incomplete segments, losing parent/child relationships downstream.

Lines 62–64 add `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`, which silently removes the oldest (lowest `end_timestamp_precise`) spans from any set exceeding 1000 entries. The previous Python-side check at `_load_segment_data` would `metrics.incr('spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded')` and log an error before discarding the entire segment; this is now gone (see `src/sentry/spans/buffer.py`). The new behavior silently loses individual spans with no metric, no log, no error — only `zpopmin` happens. Consequence: for any segment with more than 1000 spans, downstream flushing will emit truncated segments, and operators will have no signal that data was dropped. Also note that `zpopmin` breaks ties by lexicographic member order when `end_timestamp_precise` is identical (common for sibling spans in the same transaction), making the lost-span set effectively non-deterministic.

`max_segment_spans` constructor parameter is now orphaned

`SpansBuffer.__init__` (around line 150) still defines and stores `self.max_segment_spans = max_segment_spans` with default 1001, but the consumer-side enforcement in `_load_segment_data` that read `self.max_segment_spans` was deleted in this PR. The parameter is still accepted in `__reduce__` callers and tests, but never used. Consequence: configuration knob is misleading and dead; anyone increasing `max_segment_spans` expects larger segments to be allowed, but the Lua-side eviction now silently caps segments at 1000 regardless. The Python constant and constructor argument should either be removed or actually consulted (e.g., passed to the Lua script as a configurable limit).

BasePaginator silently clamps negative offsets for non-prev cursors

The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` (line 182) introduces a behavior change from the original `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` for cursors with `is_prev=False` and a negative `offset`. Django's queryset slicing natively supports negative offsets; the new code silently clamps them to 0. The comment ('Performance optimization: For high-traffic scenarios, allow negative offsets…') is misleading — the change actually restricts offset semantics in the base paginator. Consequence: any caller (in this repo or downstream) that previously relied on Django's negative slicing for forward cursors will silently get the first page of results instead of the tail, with no error. There is no test that exercises the negative-offset path, and the change is rolled out to all paginator subclasses (DateTimePaginator, Paginator, etc.) via inheritance.

OptimizedCursorPaginator is a near-verbatim copy of Paginator/BasePaginator with misleading docstring

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` (lines 821–911) duplicates `get_item_key` and `value_from_cursor` byte-for-byte from `Paginator` (lines 222–227) and reimplements `get_result` almost identically to `BasePaginator.get_result`, differing only in whether a negative offset passes through when `enable_advanced_features` is set. The docstring claims 'Negative offset support for efficient reverse pagination', 'Streamlined boundary condition handling', and 'Optimized query path for large datasets', but only the first is implemented (and Django natively), and the others describe no actual behavior. Consequence: dead code, false documentation, and a privileged code path ('control optimizations') that is exposed via a query parameter (see `organization_auditlogs.py`) for superusers, with no test coverage in the diff. A senior reviewer would want this consolidated into a flag on `BasePaginator` rather than a duplicate class.

No tests cover the new eviction-on-insert behavior

The PR adds Lua-side eviction at >1000 spans (`zpopmin`), but no test in `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py`, `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_buffer.py`, or `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_flusher.py` constructs a segment with more than 1000 spans to assert (a) the cap is enforced, (b) which spans are kept vs dropped, or (c) that a metric/log is emitted. The existing parametrized tests use 4–5 spans per case. Without a test, a future change to the score semantics (e.g., switching from `end_timestamp_precise` to something else) or to the threshold could regress silently and drop arbitrary spans in production with no detection. At minimum, add a test that pushes >1000 spans into one segment and asserts the flushed result contains exactly 1000 and that the kept spans are the latest by `end_timestamp_precise`.

No tests cover the redirect-loop limit change (10000 -> 1000) or the new OptimizedCursorPaginator path

Two important behavioral changes ship without test coverage: (1) the add-buffer.lua redirect-resolution loop limit is reduced from 10000 to 1000, and (2) the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True` (used by `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` for superusers/global-access members) is exercised in no test in this PR. The audit-logs endpoint change should at least have a test that constructs a request as a superuser with `?optimized_pagination=true` and asserts it returns a successful paginated response, and the redirect limit should be covered by a test feeding a synthetic deep tree.

`cast(SpanEvent, …)` provides no runtime validation; missing `end_timestamp_precise` will KeyError

Line 134 does `val = cast(SpanEvent, rapidjson.loads(payload.value))`, which is purely a type-hint operation at runtime — it does not validate the payload. The very next reference, `end_timestamp_precise=val['end_timestamp_precise']` (line 141), will raise `KeyError` if any incoming payload (older producers, schema drift, malformed Kafka message) omits the field, and `TypeError` if it is `None`. Consequence: a single bad message kills the batch processing and the consumer may stall. Either validate against the schema (e.g., `sentry_kafka_schemas.codecs.decode`) before constructing the `Span`, or guard with `val.get('end_timestamp_precise', default)` and skip/log the malformed message.

Comment claims int(offset) enables negative offsets but it doesn't

Lines 26–27 add `# Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios / # This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets`, but the actual code is the unchanged `self.offset = int(offset)`. `int()` is just a numeric coercion — it does not 'allow' negatives (Python ints already accept them) and does not change pagination behavior. The comment misleads readers into believing the Cursor constructor is doing something that it is not; the actual negative-offset semantics were (re)moved in `paginator.py`. Either delete the comment or move the explanatory text to the place that actually implements the feature.

The docstring says 'err on the side of caution', but the current implementation is the opposite — it over-applies the transform. The new `upsampled_count` aggregate is `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))`. Two correctness issues: (1) `sum(sample_weight)` silently excludes rows where `sample_weight` is NULL (pre-upsampling or legacy events ingested before sampling rolled out on that project), so the upsampled count will be lower than the real event count and inflate/de-inflate arbitrarily as the rollout progresses; and (2) `toInt64(...)` truncates fractional sums — e.g. 10.7 becomes 10 — so reported counts can be off-by-one for any bucket whose weighted total is not integral. `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled(project_ids, organization)` accepts an `Organization` argument but only reads `options.get("issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist", [])`, which is a global option. In `OrganizationEventsStatsErrorUpsamplingTest.setUp`, `self.login_as(user=self.user)` is called, then `self.authed_user = self.user` saves a reference, then `self.user = self.create_user()` reassigns `self.user` to a brand-new user. `test_error_upsampling_with_allowlisted_projects` asserts `count == 10` after storing events with `client_sample_rate: 0.1`. This only holds if Snuba's `sample_weight` is exactly `1 / client_sample_rate` AND the factory's new `sample_rate` hook propagates through event ingest into that column — none of which is asserted in this PR. If either assumption is wrong, the test will be a false positive that masks the most important data-integrity claim of the feature. Add an explicit assertion (or a smaller unit test) that demonstrates the sample_weight value produced for a known input, e.g. assert `sample_weight == 10.0` for a stored event with sample_rate 0.1.

invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code; allowlist edits have no effect for 60s

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined and exported, but a repo-wide search shows no caller. Combined with the 60-second TTL this means any operator change to `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` (or any future project-level toggle) cannot be observed promptly, and there is no signal that this is intentional. Either wire it into the option-set path (and any UI/admin endpoint that edits the allowlist), or delete it so callers do not assume it works.

Unrelated error-message change for topEvents validation

The diff rewrites `{"detail": "If topEvents needs to be at least 1"}` to `{"detail": "topEvents needs to be at least 1"}`. This is a user-visible API response change bundled into a feature PR for error upsampling, with no description in the PR body. Anyone parsing this message string (CI checks, docs, downstream tests) will see a silent change. Either revert the message and keep the PR scope tight, or call it out explicitly so consumers can update.

The PR adds a `sentry-repo` submodule entry pointing to exactly the same commit as the base (`a5d29095...`). Nothing in the diff or description references this submodule, no path within it is consumed by any of the changed Python files, and pinning a submodule to the parent commit typically only matters if downstream tooling relies on it. Remove the submodule entry, or document in the PR description what depends on it and why it must move in lock-step with the parent.

Uncaught exceptions in get_user_info will produce 500 errors

Without such a comment, a future contributor is likely to delete the stub and reinstate DuckDB execution, silently re-exposing the RCE/LFI.

This PR is the public fix for CVE-2024-9264 and changes both the gating (reader.go now rejects QueryTypeSQL) and the SQL backend (db.go stub, parser.go, sql_command.go). No test file is added or updated to verify that: (1) a QueryTypeSQL request now returns the documented error from reader.go, (2) NewSQLCommand / UnmarshalSQLCommand cannot produce an executable SQLCommand, and (3) SQLCommand.Execute, if reached, returns an error instead of executing user-controlled SQL. Without regression tests it is very easy for a future change (e.g. 're-enable SQL via feature flag', or deleting the stub) to silently re-introduce the vulnerability. The PR description also leaves the feature-flag-related docs unchecked; a test asserting behavior under the flag would at least lock the mitigation down.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing double-check after acquiring write lock

GetWebAssets releases the RLock before checking whether the cache is populated, then unconditionally re-reads the manifest after taking the write lock. Two concurrent callers that both observe a nil cache will both serialize on the write lock and each perform the full file read and JSON parse, instead of the second caller reusing the value just populated by the first. Adding a re-check of `entryPointAssetsCache` after the Lock() (classic double-checked locking) would eliminate the redundant I/O on the cold-start path. Not a correctness bug—safe under the mutex—but wasteful for concurrent first callers in production.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same problem: the GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern by failing to re-check if the cache was populated after acquiring the write lock.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test added for the data race fix

The PR's stated purpose is to fix a data race on the shared `entryPointAssetsCache` global, but no test exercising concurrent calls to GetWebAssets is included. For a race-condition fix, the maintainer should expect at least one test that invokes GetWebAssets from multiple goroutines (intended to be run with `go test -race`) to guard against the race being reintroduced. Without such a test, the fix is verified only by inspection and there is no automated guard against future regressions on this exact path.

When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
O(N^2) string building in SQLite IN-list inlining

In deleteByIDs, when SQLite is used and the configured batch size exceeds the parameter limit, IDs are concatenated into a SQL literal:
    values := fmt.Sprint(ids[0])
    for _, v := range ids[1:] {
        values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)
    }
Each iteration rebuilds the whole string from scratch, giving O(N^2) time and memory growth proportional to len(ids)^2. With AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize configured as high as 32767, this produces a string of ~300k+ characters built through tens of thousands of allocations on every cleanup batch. Should use strings.Builder (or similar) to build the IN-list in a single pass. Also, for the typical case where len(ids) is much smaller than the configured batch size (because there are simply few rows to clean), the branch condition checks `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` instead of `len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit`, so the slower inlining path is taken even when the placeholder path would work fine.

SQLite parameter-limit branch checks config, not actual ID count

The branch `if r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` decides whether to inline IDs into the SQL based on the configured batch size, not on `len(ids)`. The actual number of parameters needed equals `len(ids)`, which is bounded by `LIMIT AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` but usually far smaller (cleanup often finds only a handful of rows). When the operator sets a large batch size (e.g., the new test exercises 32767), the inlining path is taken on every call even if only a few rows are being deleted, building a needless literal string and skipping the (correct) parameterized path. Use `len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit`.

Each new cleanup log line passes `"err", err` as a structured field. The `err` here is the result of `fetchIDs`, which is nil on the success path. Every successful cleanup therefore emits `"err": <nil>` in its log payload, which is misleading to operators triaging errors (especially since these are emitted at Error level - see the other finding). The 'err' field should only be included when err is non-nil, or the message should be split so success and failure paths log different things.

Mixed string/symbol in fallback list causes duplicate locale file loads

The result is then iterated by `ensure_loaded!`, calling `I18n.ensure_loaded!` for both `"en"` and `:en`. Each call ends up in `translate_accelerator.rb#load_locale`, where `Regexp.new("\\.#{locale}\\.yml$")` matches the same `*.en.yml` file for both the String and the Symbol, so the file is loaded and parsed twice on the first request from an English (or default-English) user. Fix by coercing consistently, e.g. `[locale.to_sym, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact`, and storing/comparing `@loaded_locales` as Symbols in `translate_accelerator.rb`.

For slots near midnight in either timezone, the comparison may disagree with what the organizer would consider "their" day, so slots can be mis-attributed to (or wrongly excluded from) a date override. The conversion should be done with the timezone plugin explicitly: e.g. `dayjs(date.start).tz(organizerTimeZone).format('YYYY MM DD')` compared to `slotStartTime.tz(organizerTimeZone).format('YYYY MM DD')`.

Date-override timezone offset formula is incorrect

The new formula is `offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset`, then `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + minute()`. Because `override.start` is a moment in time already represented in UTC, adding `organizerUtcOffset` (the organizer's offset) actively shifts the result away from the correct invitee-local minutes. The correct conversion is to add the invitee's offset only (`dayjs(override.start).utc().add(inviteeUtcOffset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + minute()`) or, cleaner, `dayjs(override.start).tz(timeZone).hour() * 60 + minute()`. With the current formula, an organizer with a non-UTC timezone paired with any invitee in a different timezone will produce override start/end values that are off by the organizer's UTC offset, causing slots to appear at the wrong hour for the invitee.

Unnecessary Date#toString and redundant dayjs calls

`dayjs(override.start.toString())` converts a Date to an ISO string and back to dayjs, which loses no information but is a code smell and risks platform-dependent string formatting. The same `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute')` is computed twice in the return expression; caching it into a local would halve the work and make the intent clearer. Not a correctness bug on its own but worth fixing alongside the offset formula.

The added test reuses the IST schedule for both the IST and the BDT invitee and only asserts the same UTC strings (`08:30:00.000Z` ... `11:30:00.000Z`). Since slots are always returned in UTC and the override's UTC moment does not change, both code paths (original buggy `getUTCHours()` and the new formula) happen to land on the same UTC times for this scenario. The test would not catch the offset-formula bug above (e.g., an organizer in IST with a 14:00 IST override, plus an invitee in `Asia/Dhaka`, would yield wrong slot hours). The PR claims a timezone regression; the test must use a cross-timezone schedule (e.g., organizer in `Asia/Kolkata`, override "14:00" local, invitee in `America/New_York`) and assert the resulting invitee-local slot times to actually prove the fix works.

The new code added in this PR calls `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key: ... } })` (line 96) but `prisma` is not imported in this file. The imports end at `getAppKeysFromSlug` and `parseRefreshTokenResponse`. This is an immediate runtime crash for a previously-working integration.

findFirst-then-create is not atomic; webhook can produce duplicate credentials

The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst(...)` followed by `prisma.credential.create(...)` if no row matches, with no transaction and no unique constraint to lean on. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same `(userId, appId)` will both observe no row and both insert a new credential, leaving the user with multiple rows for the same app — a state the rest of the codebase assumes does not happen (e.g. lark's callback, webex/zoom/office365 callbacks all explicitly delete pre-existing rows). The `findFirst` lookup also doesn't filter by `type`, so when the same `appId` exists with multiple legacy `type` values, an update may be applied to the wrong row. The docstring even acknowledges this with "Can't use prisma upsert as we don't know the id of the credential", but a race-free approach (e.g. `prisma.credential.deleteMany({ userId, appId })` inside a transaction, or an upsert on a composite key) would be safer.

Webhook handler accepts any HTTP method and has no body-size, replay, or method check

The handler does not check `req.method`, so any method with the correct secret header (e.g. GET, PUT) reaches the database mutation path; only the secret comparison and `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` flag gate it. There is also no body-size limit, no timestamp/nonce, and no signature scheme beyond a static shared secret. Combined with the fact that anyone in possession of `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` can create or replace credentials for any userId in the system, an attacker who learns or leaks the secret (e.g. via logs, env backups) can rewrite every user's app tokens by replaying the request. At minimum, restrict to POST and verify a recent timestamp.

The function POSTs only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` (form-urlencoded) to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` and returns the raw response unmodified. Without a clear spec, the feature is unusable in practice.

Outbound call to sync endpoint has no authentication from Cal.com side

`fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)` is sent with no headers, no signature, and no client identity. The receiving service has no way to verify that the call came from this Cal.com instance or that `appSlug`/`calcomUserId` weren't tampered with by a network attacker or a mis-routed proxy. Combined with the fact that `userId` is trusted blindly to look up tokens server-side, anyone who can intercept traffic to the configured endpoint can impersonate any user. The endpoint should require a Cal.com-issued signature (e.g. an HMAC of the body using a shared key) so the parent service can reject forged refresh requests.

The PR introduces three pieces of behavior with no test coverage: the new `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` webhook (including auth/secret checking, decryption, and the find/update/create branches), `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts` (sharing vs. non-sharing branches, including what the returned value looks like to callers), and `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts` (the broken minimum-token schema and the refresh-token overwrite). Lines 553-567 fire calendar/video deletions with `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); })` and there is no try/catch at all in this scope. Because forEach does not await the async callback, a rejection from `await getCalendar` (from the now-dynamic `appStore[...]` import) becomes an unhandled rejection. The mutation returns success while the prior calendar events on the attendee/organizer calendars may never have been deleted, leading to stale events being shown on those calendars after a reschedule.

getCachedResults awaits all getCalendar calls sequentially inside the map

In `getCachedResults`, the calendars are now loaded with `await Promise.all(calendarCredentials.map((credential) => getCalendar(credential)))`, which is correctly parallelized. However the subsequent `results = calendars.map(async (c, i) => { ... })` then immediately awaits via `Promise.all`, which is fine. The new `getCalendarCredentials` function on the other hand still loads calendars sequentially (one `flatMap` callback at a time), and the `getVideoAdapters` factory in `packages/core/videoClient.ts` was also rewritten as a serial `for` loop rather than a `Promise.all` over credentials. For tenants with several credentials the first booking/cancellation pays N×(module-fetch latency) serially; parallelizing the per-credential fetches would substantially reduce tail latency of the first request after a cold start.

No tests added for the async app-store refactor

This PR converts a large surface area of calendar/video/payment loaders from synchronous to dynamic-import-based, including `getCalendar`, `getVideoAdapters`, `getCalendarCredentials`, the reschedule handlers in `vital` and `wipemycalother`, the cancellation handlers in `handleCancelBooking`, the `requestReschedule` tRPC mutation, the `confirm` mutation's refund path, and both `handlePayment` and `deletePayment`. Despite touching every booking lifecycle path, no test files are added or modified in the diff. There is no coverage that the now-dynamic imports resolve and behave identically, that error paths (missing app, broken module) return null instead of throwing, or that the new `await` placements actually preserve execution ordering. Given the scale of the refactor, this is a significant test gap.

true_positives.golden_comment: The OptimizedCursorPaginator in organization_auditlogs.py attempts to use negative slice offsets on Django querysets, but Django querysets do not support negative slicing and will raise an AssertionError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset branch is unreachable / raises AssertionError in Django

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0, the code does `results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop])` with start_offset < 0. Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ asserts that a slice start must be non-negative (`assert (k.start is None or k.start >= 0), 'Negative indexing is not supported.'`), so this branch raises AssertionError in normal Python and produces undefined SQL offsets under python -O. Cursor.from_string happily parses a negative offset via `int(bits[1])`, so an admin who sends ?optimized_pagination=true with a crafted cursor (e.g. '0:-5:0') will crash the endpoint. The claim in the comment that 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is factually wrong; Django never supported negative slicing on querysets.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: OptimizedCursorPaginator applies negative slice offsets to a Django QuerySet, which does not support negative slicing and raises an AssertionError.

false_positives.candidate:
'Performance optimization' comments are misleading

The block comment at lines 179-181 and the docstring of OptimizedCursorPaginator (lines 822-832) claim this is a 'performance optimization', provides 'efficient bidirectional pagination without full dataset scanning', 'streamlined boundary condition handling', and 'optimized query path for large datasets'. None of these are real. Compared to BasePaginator, OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result only changes behavior when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0, and even that change is broken (see the negative-offset finding). The change to BasePaginator itself (line 182-184) only clamps a negative offset to 0 in the non-prev case; that is a defensive fix, not an optimization. The repeated blank lines at lines 819-820 also suggest the class was tacked on without review.

has_global_access on RpcOrganizationMember is not a known attribute

`organization_context.member.has_global_access` accesses a Python attribute on the RpcOrganizationMember RPC type. RpcOrganizationMember typically exposes role/flags (e.g. `flags.global_access` bit) rather than a `has_global_access` property. If the attribute does not exist, this expression raises AttributeError on every request from a non-superuser, which would 500 the entire audit log endpoint for ordinary members. The reviewer needs to confirm the actual attribute name and that it represents the intended privilege (vs. e.g. `role` or a flags bit). Also, since the entire `use_optimized and enable_advanced` branch is gated to superusers or admins, exposing it via a user-controlled `?optimized_pagination=true` query parameter does not actually grant any new capability and should be questioned.

New paginator branch has no tests

No tests were added for the new optimized_pagination code path. A maintainer should at minimum cover: (1) optimized_pagination=true with a superuser hits OptimizedCursorPaginator; (2) optimized_pagination=true with a regular member falls through to DateTimePaginator; (3) OptimizedCursorPaginator with enable_advanced_features=True and a negative-offset cursor does not raise (today it will). The whole feature is unverified.

OptimizedCursorPaginator duplicates BasePaginator.get_result

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result (lines 845-911) is an almost line-for-line copy of BasePaginator.get_result (lines 136-215); the only meaningful difference is the negative-offset branch. Subclassing only to flip one branch in one method duplicates ~70 lines of cursor/offset/extra/hits/post_query_filter logic. Any future fix to BasePaginator (including the pre-existing `order_b` typo on line 105) must be made in two places. A maintainer would prefer a single `enable_advanced_features` flag on BasePaginator, or an override of just the slicing step.

Pre-existing typo 'order_b' silently breaks ASC re-ordering

Pre-existing but in the file being changed and directly relevant to pagination correctness. Line 105 reads `queryset.query.order_b = tuple(new_order_by)` instead of `queryset.query.order_by = tuple(new_order_by)`. This means when the cursor's key is currently ordered DESC (`-%s` % self.key in order_by) and `asc` is True, the queryset's order_by is never actually flipped to ascending, so the descending-order rows are then compared with an ascending comparison operator, producing wrong results. Worth fixing while this file is being touched.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Concurrent searches for the same NamespacedResource can trigger duplicate full index builds

getOrCreateIndex reads s.search.GetIndex (which checks a non-locked-ish cache via RWMutex) and, if nil, calls s.build, which in turn invokes SearchBackend.BuildIndex. There is no per-key synchronization. Two concurrent callers for the same key therefore both see a cache miss, both run the full document builder (potentially listing and indexing millions of rows), both flush, and the second write to b.cache[key] wins. The first caller's *ResourceIndex is still valid, but the cost of building was paid twice and the second build can also starve the watcher of resources. The pre-existing TODO right above the function (`// TODO??? // We want to block while building the index and return the same index for the key`) acknowledges this. The PR's change in bleve.go (releasing cacheMu before building) is correct for different keys but does nothing for same-key races; with the move from lazy to eager init the probability of overlapping first-request races goes up. At minimum the PR should add per-key locking around the GetIndex + BuildIndex sequence (e.g., singleflight.Group, or a sync.Map of per-key *sync.Mutex).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race: narrowing cacheMu protection allows concurrent callers for the same key to perform duplicate expensive index builds before the final cache assignment. The candidate explicitly connects the race to releasing the lock before building.

false_positives.candidate:
Goroutine and resource leak when NewResourceServer init fails

After constructing the server struct (which creates a cancellable ctx/cancel pair stored on the struct), NewResourceServer now eagerly calls s.Init(ctx). If Init returns an error (e.g., search.init fails partway through, or s.initWatcher fails), the function logs the error and returns nil, err. Because s is nil and cancel was never invoked, any goroutines that Init started cannot be cleaned up: the s.initWatcher goroutine + SQL poller run on s.ctx and will keep polling the database; the search.init watch goroutine (see search.go) runs on context.Background() and is not tied to s.ctx at all, so it is orphaned regardless. There is no way for the caller of NewResourceServer to stop them. Before this PR Init was idempotently deferred to the first RPC, where they would only be retained on the returned server. The fix is to defer cancel() at the top of NewResourceServer (and ideally make search.init's watchctx derive from s.ctx), so a partial init always tears its goroutines down.

search.init's watcher uses context.Background(), preventing server.Stop from stopping it

In searchSupport.init the watch is set up with `watchctx := context.Background() // new context?` and the resulting events channel is consumed by `go func() { for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) } }()`. The author even left a question mark in the comment. Because watchctx is background, calling server.Stop (which cancels s.ctx) does not stop this goroutine or its underlying storage backend poller; it will only exit if the storage backend itself is independently stopped. The symmetric watcher created by initWatcher in server.go uses s.ctx and so is cancelled correctly. This asymmetry is also what makes the Init failure leak above worse: even calling cancel after a failed Init cannot reach this watch. search.init should accept and use the long-lived s.ctx (or a child of it) for both WatchWriteEvents and the goroutine, so a single Stop cleans up everything.

Trace propagation fix is inconsistent across the sql backend

The PR correctly changes GetResourceStats from `_, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` to `ctx, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` so the span context flows into the WithTx call below it. The same broken pattern is left in place in this same file for WriteEvent (line 158), create (174), update (236), delete (298), ReadResource (353), ListIterator (388), poller (580), listLatestRVs (619), poll (664) and resourceVersionAtomicInc (718). All of them discard the returned ctx, so the OpenTelemetry spans they start are not parents of the SQL calls made inside them. The fix in GetResourceStats was presumably driven by tracing the new eager index build; the same one-line fix should be applied to all the other methods that start a span and then perform work under that context, otherwise half the storage trace tree is broken.

Init error is logged twice

Init already logs `s.log.Error("error initializing resource server", "error", s.initErr)` inside the s.once.Do block, and the new caller in NewResourceServer then logs the same error again with the same message right before returning nil, err. Pick one site and drop the other to avoid the duplicate entry and to keep the error format consistent with the other NewResourceServer error paths (which only return).

BuildIndex still shadows the trace context with its span

Unlike search.go and sql/backend.go's GetResourceStats, bleve.go's BuildIndex uses `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, tracingPrexfixBleve+"BuildIndex")` and discards the returned ctx. The same trace-propagation bug the PR is trying to fix elsewhere therefore remains in this hot path: the call to `builder(idx)` (which runs the entire list-iterator + builder loop) does not see the BuildIndex span as its parent, and traces of the index build will be missing the bleve-level span. The same one-character fix (`ctx, span := ...`) should be applied here for consistency with the other files in the PR.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.

test_dedupe in TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue has mismatched group_keys, will fail

The test builds the expected `occurrence` and `event_data` with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`, so the occurrence's fingerprint is `[f"{handler.detector.id}:val1"]` (via `handler.build_fingerprint("val1")`). However, the test then constructs `expected_result = DetectorEvaluationResult("group_key", ...)` and passes `expected_result.group_key` (i.e. `"group_key"`) into `handler.evaluate_group_key_value(...)`. Internally that calls `self.build_occurrence_and_event_data("group_key", 10, PriorityLevel.HIGH)` -> `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "group_key", 10, ...)` producing an occurrence whose fingerprint is `[f"{handler.detector.id}:group_key"]`. In `StatefulDetectorHandler.evaluate_group_key_value`, `self.enqueue_dedupe_update(group_key, dedupe_value)` is called immediately after the dedupe check and BEFORE the `if not self.condition_group: ... return None` early return. If the condition group is later attached, those prior packets will be skipped even though no evaluation actually ran for them, causing potentially missed detections. The enqueue should be moved after the condition_group check, or only enqueued on the paths that perform real evaluation.

Kafka produce exceptions prevent state commit, causing duplicate detections

`process_detectors` calls `create_issue_occurrence_from_result` (which calls `produce_occurrence_to_kafka`) BEFORE `handler.commit_state_updates()`. If Kafka is unavailable or `produce_occurrence_to_kafka` raises, the exception propagates out of the loop and `commit_state_updates()` is never executed for that detector. The Redis dedupe value is therefore not updated, so on the next processing of the same data packet the detector will re-emit the same occurrence (and re-trigger downstream workflows). This is also exposed more by the new `build_occurrence_and_event_data` path which can now raise from subclass code and have the same effect. Either wrap the produce in a try/except or commit dedupe state after successful produces.
