Mutable default value: `queued: datetime = timezone.now()`

In a dataclass, a default value of `timezone.now()` is evaluated once at class definition time and is then shared by every instance created without an explicit `queued` argument. Every `AssignmentSource(source_name=..., integration_id=...)` constructed in a worker will therefore have the same `queued` datetime (the import time of the module), not the time the source was actually queued. The field is not yet consulted in any comparison logic in this PR, so the cycle-breaking itself still works, but the field is serialized through Celery as `to_dict` / `from_dict` and any future use of `queued` for staleness, deduplication, or analytics will be incorrect. false_positives.candidate:
commit() called with one argument but arroyo's Commit requires two

In `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`, the inner `commit_offsets` closure calls `commit(commit_data)` with a single argument, but arroyo's `Commit` type is `Callable[[Mapping[Partition, int], bool], None]`. At runtime this raises `TypeError: missing 1 required positional argument: 'force'`, which is swallowed by the broad `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop`. The result is that offsets are never committed, the offset tracker grows without bound, and on restart the consumer re-reads everything it has already processed (defeating the whole point of the commit loop and potentially causing data-integrity issues for non-idempotent result processors). The fix is `commit(commit_data, False)` (or wrap with `CommitOffsets`). The unit tests miss this because they pass a mock with a default for `force`.

test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps references undefined variables

Inside `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` only `all_commits` and `test_partition` are defined, but the final assertion reads `committed_offsets[partition] == 103`. Neither `committed_offsets` nor `partition` exists in the test scope, so the test raises `NameError` before any assertion runs and provides no coverage of the gap-fill behavior it claims to test. The assertion should use `all_commits[-1][test_partition]` (or similar) so it actually exercises the production code path.

test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps asserts wrong offset value

After filling the gap by submitting offset 101, all of offsets 100-103 are processed, so `get_committable_offsets` returns `{test_partition: 103}`. `commit_offsets` then adds +1 (it explicitly comments "the committed offset should represent the next offset to read from") and calls `commit({test_partition: 104})`. The test asserts `committed_offsets[partition] == 103`, but the actual value should be 104. This is inconsistent with the first assertion in the same test (`actual_offset == 101` for processing up to 100) which correctly accounts for the +1.

get_queue_for_group uses Python's hash(), not consistent hashing

`get_queue_for_group` is implemented as `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` and its docstring says "consistent hashing". Python's built-in `hash()` for strings is randomized across processes (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the same `group_key` can be assigned to a different queue on every restart. Within a single process lifetime ordering is preserved (which is what the consumer relies on, since in-flight items are lost on restart anyway), but the function does not provide the cross-process stability the docstring advertises, and it isn't true consistent hashing (e.g. it doesn't survive changes in `num_queues`). Use a stable hash like `hashlib.md5(group_key.encode()).digest()` or `zlib.crc32` and either drop the "consistent" wording or use a hash ring.

--mode help text does not describe thread-queue-parallel

`uptime_options` adds `"thread-queue-parallel"` to the choice list, but the `help` text still reads "The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading." with no mention of the new mode or how its parallelism differs (queue-based, per-group ordering, etc.). Operators picking the mode have no way to know what the new option does or how it differs from the existing parallel modes.

Queue depth metric is not tagged by worker/queue

`OrderedQueueWorker.run` emits `remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth` only with `tags={"identifier": self.identifier}`. With `num_queues=20` workers sharing the same identifier, all depth values are aggregated into one series and individual hot queues cannot be distinguished, defeating the purpose of the metric for diagnosing the very backlog problem the PR is meant to address. The worker_id (and ideally the queue index) should be in the tags.

`FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty` is defined but never called by the strategy or factory. It also has subtle correctness issues if ever used (it polls `qsize()` rather than tracking completion, so it can race against in-flight items). Either remove it or document and test its intended use.

false_positives.candidate:
Redirect resolution loop limit silently reduced 10000 -> 1000

The redirect resolution loop iterates from `for i = 0, 1000 do` (line 30) but the original code used `for i = 0, 10000 do` and explicitly noted in the comment that this limit governs whether deep segment trees are joined correctly: 'theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' Reducing the limit to 1000 silently breaks any trace whose redirect chain has depth between 1000 and 10000 — those spans will not be merged into the same set. No tests exercise deep trees, so this regression is not caught. Consequence: traces with deep span trees (1000+) end up split across multiple buffer sets and get flushed as incomplete segments, losing parent/child relationships downstream.

Eviction silently drops spans from oversized segments without logging

Lines 62–64 add `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`, which silently removes the oldest (lowest `end_timestamp_precise`) spans from any set exceeding 1000 entries. The previous Python-side check at `_load_segment_data` would `metrics.incr('spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded')` and log an error before discarding the entire segment; this is now gone (see `src/sentry/spans/buffer.py`). The new behavior silently loses individual spans with no metric, no log, no error — only `zpopmin` happens. Consequence: for any segment with more than 1000 spans, downstream flushing will emit truncated segments, and operators will have no signal that data was dropped. Also note that `zpopmin` breaks ties by lexicographic member order when `end_timestamp_precise` is identical (common for sibling spans in the same transaction), making the lost-span set effectively non-deterministic.

`max_segment_spans` constructor parameter is now orphaned

`SpansBuffer.__init__` (around line 150) still defines and stores `self.max_segment_spans = max_segment_spans` with default 1001, but the consumer-side enforcement in `_load_segment_data` that read `self.max_segment_spans` was deleted in this PR. The parameter is still accepted in `__reduce__` callers and tests, but never used. Consequence: configuration knob is misleading and dead; anyone increasing `max_segment_spans` expects larger segments to be allowed, but the Lua-side eviction now silently caps segments at 1000 regardless. The Python constant and constructor argument should either be removed or actually consulted (e.g., passed to the Lua script as a configurable limit).

BasePaginator silently clamps negative offsets for non-prev cursors

The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` (line 182) introduces a behavior change from the original `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` for cursors with `is_prev=False` and a negative `offset`. Django's queryset slicing natively supports negative offsets; the new code silently clamps them to 0. The comment ('Performance optimization: For high-traffic scenarios, allow negative offsets…') is misleading — the change actually restricts offset semantics in the base paginator. Consequence: any caller (in this repo or downstream) that previously relied on Django's negative slicing for forward cursors will silently get the first page of results instead of the tail, with no error. There is no test that exercises the negative-offset path, and the change is rolled out to all paginator subclasses (DateTimePaginator, Paginator, etc.) via inheritance.

OptimizedCursorPaginator is a near-verbatim copy of Paginator/BasePaginator with misleading docstring

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` (lines 821–911) duplicates `get_item_key` and `value_from_cursor` byte-for-byte from `Paginator` (lines 222–227) and reimplements `get_result` almost identically to `BasePaginator.get_result`, differing only in whether a negative offset passes through when `enable_advanced_features` is set. The docstring claims 'Negative offset support for efficient reverse pagination', 'Streamlined boundary condition handling', and 'Optimized query path for large datasets', but only the first is implemented (and Django natively), and the others describe no actual behavior. Consequence: dead code, false documentation, and a privileged code path ('control optimizations') that is exposed via a query parameter (see `organization_auditlogs.py`) for superusers, with no test coverage in the diff. A senior reviewer would want this consolidated into a flag on `BasePaginator` rather than a duplicate class.

`organization_context.member.has_global_access` may AttributeError if member is None

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` (line 71) unconditionally accesses `.member.has_global_access` whenever the requester is not a superuser. If `organization_context.member` is None for any path that reaches this endpoint (e.g., a service user or a context shape returned for non-members of the org being queried), the request will raise `AttributeError` and return a 500. The original code never touched `organization_context.member`, so this PR introduces the regression. Guard with `organization_context.member is not None and organization_context.member.has_global_access` (or equivalent), or move the check inside the `optimized_pagination` branch where it is actually consumed.

Privileged pagination feature is gated by a client-controlled query parameter

`use_optimized = request.GET.get('optimized_pagination') == 'true'` (line 70) lets any requester who is also a superuser (or has global access) flip on `enable_advanced_features=True` for that single request. Privileged behavior is typically gated by server-side configuration or user attributes, not a query parameter, because query-parameter gating leaves no audit trail and is trivially selectable. The 'feature' itself just re-enables Django's native negative-offset slicing that the BasePaginator change (line 182 in paginator.py) just removed. Either move the toggle behind a server-side feature flag/setting, or drop it — the parameter offers no functional benefit beyond Django's existing behavior.

No tests cover the new eviction-on-insert behavior

The PR adds Lua-side eviction at >1000 spans (`zpopmin`), but no test in `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py`, `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_buffer.py`, or `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_flusher.py` constructs a segment with more than 1000 spans to assert (a) the cap is enforced, (b) which spans are kept vs dropped, or (c) that a metric/log is emitted. The existing parametrized tests use 4–5 spans per case. Without a test, a future change to the score semantics (e.g., switching from `end_timestamp_precise` to something else) or to the threshold could regress silently and drop arbitrary spans in production with no detection. At minimum, add a test that pushes >1000 spans into one segment and asserts the flushed result contains exactly 1000 and that the kept spans are the latest by `end_timestamp_precise`.

No tests cover the redirect-loop limit change (10000 -> 1000) or the new OptimizedCursorPaginator path

Two important behavioral changes ship without test coverage: (1) the add-buffer.lua redirect-resolution loop limit is reduced from 10000 to 1000, and (2) the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True` (used by `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` for superusers/global-access members) is exercised in no test in this PR. The audit-logs endpoint change should at least have a test that constructs a request as a superuser with `?optimized_pagination=true` and asserts it returns a successful paginated response, and the redirect limit should be covered by a test feeding a synthetic deep tree.

`cast(SpanEvent, …)` provides no runtime validation; missing `end_timestamp_precise` will KeyError

Line 134 does `val = cast(SpanEvent, rapidjson.loads(payload.value))`, which is purely a type-hint operation at runtime — it does not validate the payload. The very next reference, `end_timestamp_precise=val['end_timestamp_precise']` (line 141), will raise `KeyError` if any incoming payload (older producers, schema drift, malformed Kafka message) omits the field, and `TypeError` if it is `None`. Consequence: a single bad message kills the batch processing and the consumer may stall. Either validate against the schema (e.g., `sentry_kafka_schemas.codecs.decode`) before constructing the `Span`, or guard with `val.get('end_timestamp_precise', default)` and skip/log the malformed message.

Comment claims int(offset) enables negative offsets but it doesn't

Lines 26–27 add `# Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios / # This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets`, but the actual code is the unchanged `self.offset = int(offset)`. `int()` is just a numeric coercion — it does not 'allow' negatives (Python ints already accept them) and does not change pagination behavior. The comment misleads readers into believing the Cursor constructor is doing something that it is not; the actual negative-offset semantics were (re)moved in `paginator.py`. Either delete the comment or move the explanatory text to the place that actually implements the feature.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker shortened 10x without justification

Ticker changed from `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 10)` to `time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)`. The PR description is solely about fixing a MySQL deadlock via query restructuring; nothing in the description or the referenced issue (grafana/grafana#64979) justifies a 10x increase in cleanup frequency. This multiplies the database load of every cleanup job by 10x, including annotation cleanup, dashboard version cleanup, short URL cleanup, query history cleanup, etc. Combined with the noisy Error logs added in xorm_store.go, this materially changes operational behavior and should either be split into its own change or justified explicitly. Note also that `cleanUpOldAnnotations` is called inside this 1-minute loop, and the new fetch+delete implementation uses two round-trips per batch instead of one, compounding the load.
true_positives.reasoning: Both flag the cleanup ticker changing from 10 minutes to 1 minute and the resulting risk of increased database load and contention. The candidate adds context but identifies the same underlying performance concern.

false_positives.candidate:
O(N^2) string building in SQLite IN-list inlining

In deleteByIDs, when SQLite is used and the configured batch size exceeds the parameter limit, IDs are concatenated into a SQL literal:
    values := fmt.Sprint(ids[0])
    for _, v := range ids[1:] {
        values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)
    }
Each iteration rebuilds the whole string from scratch, giving O(N^2) time and memory growth proportional to len(ids)^2. With AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize configured as high as 32767, this produces a string of ~300k+ characters built through tens of thousands of allocations on every cleanup batch. Should use strings.Builder (or similar) to build the IN-list in a single pass. Also, for the typical case where len(ids) is much smaller than the configured batch size (because there are simply few rows to clean), the branch condition checks `r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` instead of `len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit`, so the slower inlining path is taken even when the placeholder path would work fine.

SQLite parameter-limit branch checks config, not actual ID count

The branch `if r.db.GetDBType() == migrator.SQLite && r.cfg.AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > sqliteParameterLimit` decides whether to inline IDs into the SQL based on the configured batch size, not on `len(ids)`. The actual number of parameters needed equals `len(ids)`, which is bounded by `LIMIT AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` but usually far smaller (cleanup often finds only a handful of rows). When the operator sets a large batch size (e.g., the new test exercises 32767), the inlining path is taken on every call even if only a few rows are being deleted, building a needless literal string and skipping the (correct) parameterized path. Use `len(ids) > sqliteParameterLimit`.

Log fields include 'err' even when fetch succeeded

Each new cleanup log line passes `"err", err` as a structured field. The `err` here is the result of `fetchIDs`, which is nil on the success path. Every successful cleanup therefore emits `"err": <nil>` in its log payload, which is misleading to operators triaging errors (especially since these are emitted at Error level - see the other finding). The 'err' field should only be included when err is non-nil, or the message should be split so success and failure paths log different things.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete attaches d.Log to context instead of the enriched logger

Every other method in this file does `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, log)` using the local `log` variable that already carries name/kind/method. Delete builds that local log on line 96 but then sets `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`, so the legacy store (and any code reading the logger from the context) only sees the bare DualWriterMode3 logger with mode=3 and loses name, kind, and method. Inconsistent with Create/Get/List/Update/DeleteCollection and reduces observability of async legacy writes.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same issue: the logging context is created with d.Log instead of the enriched local log variable, so name, kind, and method are not propagated.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Kind metric label is set to the resource name

The success branch of Delete calls d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage). Every other recorder in the file uses options.Kind as the kind label, but here `name` (the resource identifier) is passed instead. This (a) makes the metric inconsistent with the rest of mode 3 and (b) blows up the metric cardinality because each deleted resource name becomes a label value. Should be options.Kind.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same inconsistency: Delete passes the resource name rather than options.Kind as the metric kind label, unlike other methods. The cardinality concern is additional context for the same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Storage failure recorded under the legacy duration metric

When d.Storage.Create returns an error the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...). The metric name (legacy vs storage) is used by dashboards/alerts to distinguish the two backends, so a storage failure ends up inflating the legacy error metric and the storage success metric is never recorded for this path. The success path on line 48 correctly uses recordStorageDuration, so the error branch should mirror it: d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). The same pattern is repeated in the Update method (line 129).

Storage Update failure recorded under the legacy duration metric

Mirrors the bug on line 45. When d.Storage.Update fails, d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) is called, attributing the storage failure to the legacy backend in the metrics. The success branch on line 132 correctly uses recordStorageDuration, so the failure branch should be d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

Update no longer wraps objInfo for the legacy call

The previous implementation precomputed `updated` from the storage copy, then passed an `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: ...}` to both Storage.Update and Legacy.Update so both backends received the exact same resolved object. The new code passes the raw objInfo to d.Legacy.Update. If Storage and Legacy disagree on the previous object (e.g. they have drifted) or if objInfo.UpdatedObject behaves differently in the two implementations, the two stores can now persist different versions of the same object, producing data drift between unified storage and legacy storage. This is a real behavioural regression, not just a refactor.

Legacy DeleteCollection duration recorded under storage metric

In the async goroutine for DeleteCollection the legacy result is timed and then d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy) is called. This is the legacy path, so it should be d.recordLegacyDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy). As written, a legacy DeleteCollection failure silently inflates the storage metric, and the legacy duration histogram never receives any samples from DeleteCollection.

Async legacy writes inherit the cancelled request context

All four async goroutines (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) derive their context with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...). `ctx` is the API server request context, which is cancelled as soon as the handler returns and the response is sent. In practice that means the legacy goroutines often start in an already-cancelled context and the 10-second safety net never has a chance to fire. Result: legacy writes are aborted shortly after the user sees a success response, and because the failure is only logged via metrics, the user has no visibility. For 'safe measure' dual writes this defeats the purpose. Detach from the request lifetime (e.g. context.WithoutCancel or context.Background preserving values) and rely solely on the timeout.

TestMode3_Create 'unified store fails' case does not set up the storage mock

The second test case sets up only the legacy mock and leaves setupStorageFn nil. Mode3 calls d.Storage.Create before d.Legacy.Create (see dualwriter_mode3.go line 42), so on the testify mock the Storage.Create invocation is unexpected and the test will panic/fail before reaching the legacy mock at all. The test does not exercise the intended path ('storage Create fails, no legacy call'). It needs a setupStorageFn returning an error and either no legacy expectation or an AssertNotCalled for legacy.

No test verifies that the async legacy write actually happens

TestMode3_Create, TestMode3_Update, TestMode3_Delete and TestMode3_DeleteCollection all set up the legacy mock with m.On(...) but never assert that it was called (no mock.AssertCalled for the legacy backend). The goroutine in dualwriter_mode3.go has no synchronization with the test, so on a fast machine the test function can return and t.Run can finish before the goroutine has dispatched, meaning a regression that simply removed the goroutine would still pass the tests. Add an explicit AssertCalled (and ideally a small synchronization point) to prove the async write really happened.

TestMode3_Get creates a local Prometheus registry instead of using the package-level `p`

All other tests in this file (and the matching Mode1 tests in dualwriter_mode1_test.go, which were just refactored away from this pattern in the same PR) use the shared `var p = prometheus.NewRegistry()` declared in dualwriter_mode1_test.go. TestMode3_Get introduces a local `p := prometheus.NewRegistry()` on line 119. It works but is inconsistent and looks like a missed cleanup. Use the shared registry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
GrafanaRuleListItem returned from .map() is missing a `key` prop

true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the missing React key prop on GrafanaRuleListItem rendered in a list and the resulting rendering or state preservation issues when the list order changes.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu item silently does nothing in the alert list view

When GrafanaRuleListItem renders a rule from Prometheus data only, RuleActionsButtons receives promRule but no rulerRule. The Silence menu item in AlertRuleMenu is gated only by `canSilence` (it does NOT check `rulerRule`), so it is rendered. Clicking it triggers `setShowSilenceDrawer(true)`, but the SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer is conditionally rendered as `{rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer && <SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer rulerRule={rule} ... />}`. When `rule` is undefined this short-circuits to false, so the drawer never renders. The user clicks Silence in the menu, the menu closes, and nothing visible happens, with no error feedback. Either the Silence menu item must also be gated on `rulerRule` (matching Delete/Pause) or SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer must be updated to accept promRule-based data.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: list-view Grafana rules pass only promRule, allowing the Silence menu action while the drawer still requires a Grafana rulerRule. Clicking the action therefore changes state but renders no drawer and has no visible effect.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete menu item is no longer reachable in the alert list view (feature regression)

The Delete menu item is rendered as `{canDelete && rulerRule && (...)}`. In the alert list view, GrafanaRuleListItem passes only `promRule` to RuleActionsButtons, so `rulerRule` is undefined and Delete never appears, even when `canDelete` is true (which is now legitimately computed from `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`). Previously, the list view loaded the ruler rule for each Grafana rule and Delete was reachable. After this PR a user can view a Grafana rule in the list and edit it but cannot delete it from the list at all. Either remove `rulerRule &&` from the gate (and rework the onClick to not pass rulerRule) or document/handle the regression explicitly.

GrafanaGroupLoader tests assert Silence menu appears but do not verify the click works in list view

The new tests in GrafanaGroupLoader.test.tsx assert that the Silence menu item is in the dropdown (`expect(ui.menuItems.silence().get()).toBeInTheDocument()`). They do not click Silence to verify a silence drawer actually opens. With the new render path, `rulerRule` is undefined so the SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer never mounts (see finding on RuleActionsButtons.V2.tsx line 104), making the assertion misleading: the menu item is present but the feature is non-functional. Add a test that clicks Silence and verifies a drawer/silence creation flow actually opens (or assert the menu item is NOT present when rulerRule is unavailable).

New useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities family has no dedicated unit tests

The newly added hooks `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, `useGrafanaPromRuleAbility`, `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, and `useIsGrafanaPromRuleEditable` (lines 287-406) are only exercised indirectly through RulesTable/AlertRuleMenu tests. Behavioral differences vs the ruler versions are subtle and untested: e.g. silence ability is `[silenceSupported, canSilenceInFolder && isAlertingRule]` (recording rules can never be silenced), `isProvisioned` uses promRule.provenance, and `MaybeSupported` is hardcoded to AlwaysSupported (no `isRulerAvailable` flag). Without dedicated tests a regression in any of these branches (particularly the recording-rule silencing guard, which differs from the previous ruler behavior) could land unnoticed.

useAllAlertRuleAbilities is now deprecated but still exported and called from new code

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` is marked `@deprecated` in favor of `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`. The new AlertRuleMenu still computes abilities using both `useRulerRuleAbilities` AND `useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities` (an OR), and the new RuleActionsButtons.V2 follows the same pattern. There is no public hook that combines rule + groupIdentifier into a single OR of (ruler-based, prom-based) abilities for a CombinedRule. As written, every consumer has to manually call both hooks and OR the results, which is duplicated several times already (AlertRuleMenu does it 5 times). Consider exposing a combined `useAllAlertRuleAbilitiesFor(rule: CombinedRule | GrafanaPromRuleDTO, ...)` helper so the OR logic lives in one place and isn't re-implemented (and possibly desynchronized) at every callsite.

userEvent instance is shared across all tests instead of being recreated per test

`const user = userEvent.setup();` is created at module scope and shared by every test in the file. userEvent accumulates internal queues/state across tests; reusing the same instance across tests can lead to flakiness or interleaved events when tests run in parallel or share state. Standard practice is to call `userEvent.setup()` (or `render` returned `user`) inside each test or in `beforeEach` for a fresh setup.

$__range check ineffective after interpolation breaks splitting logic for range queries

The change interpolates queries upfront via `applyTemplateVariables` (line 299), but the `querySupportsSplitting` check at line 282 is still applied to the interpolated queries via `partition` at line 300. The check `!isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr)` is intended to prevent splitting queries that contain `$__range`, but after `applyTemplateVariables` replaces `$__range` with a literal duration (e.g., `3d` or `259200000ms`), the check always returns true. As a result, queries like `count_over_time({a="b"}[$__range])` will now be split into sub-requests, but the `$__range` literal value baked into the query is the FULL range (since interpolation uses `request.range`), not the split range. This produces semantically incorrect results: each sub-request queries `[3d]` worth of data but only returns a window of 1d. The accompanying comment at lines 285-286 explicitly states that `$__range` queries should NOT be split. The `isQueryWithRangeVariable` check needs to be applied before interpolation (e.g., on the original `request.targets`), or `$__range` needs to be left uninterpolated and re-applied per sub-request.

No test covers $__range behavior after interpolation change

The new test 'Interpolates queries before execution' (line 75) only verifies `$__auto` and `$step` interpolation. There is no test for `$__range` queries after this change. A regression test should verify that queries containing `$__range` are still routed to the non-splitting path (i.e., they should not be split because the interpolated `$__range` value would be incorrect for split sub-requests). Without such a test, the `$__range` regression described in the primary finding could go undetected.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TOCTOU race allows exceeding device limit

In CreateOrUpdateDevice, the device count is read in one DB session (s.CountDevices) and the subsequent INSERT/UPDATE runs in a separate session. Under concurrent load, multiple requests can all observe count < limit and all proceed to INSERT, allowing the actual device count to exceed the configured limit by the number of in-flight requests. The check-then-act must be wrapped in a transaction with appropriate locking, or the limit enforced by a DB-level mechanism, to guarantee the cap.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same check-then-act race: concurrent requests can pass the device count check and create devices beyond the limit. Both recommend transactions or locking to enforce the cap.

true_positives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Auth-flow behavior change for ErrDeviceLimitReached has no test

Anonymous.Authenticate now propagates anonstore.ErrDeviceLimitReached up so authentication fails when the limit is hit. The new integration test (TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit) only covers the store-level CreateOrUpdateDevice path; there is no test that exercises Anonymous.Authenticate to confirm (1) ErrDeviceLimitReached causes Authenticate to return an error rather than a successful identity, and (2) other errors from TagDevice are still swallowed with a warning. This is a behavior change that warrants a dedicated test, including asserting what HTTP status / message a real request would receive.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies the same behavior change: Anonymous.Authenticate propagates ErrDeviceLimitReached from TagDevice, causing authentication to fail when the device limit is reached. Although framed as missing test coverage, it describes the same underlying authentication regression.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateDevice query does not handle new vs expired-device distinction

When count >= deviceLimit the code routes to updateDevice, whose WHERE clause requires updated_at BETWEEN device.UpdatedAt-30d AND device.UpdatedAt+1m. A row that exists but whose updated_at is older than 30 days (still within the 61-day cleanup window) will be reported as 'no rows affected' and surface ErrDeviceLimitReached, indistinguishable from a genuinely new device. The caller cannot tell whether to retry later (e.g. after cleanup) or give up. Either the WHERE should also match such rows so they get refreshed, or the error should distinguish 'limit reached' from 'device expired/not found'.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that updateDevice incorrectly maps zero affected rows to ErrDeviceLimitReached, even though the row may be missing or excluded by the timestamp window. The candidate highlights expired rows as a specific instance of the same error-semantics bug.

false_positives.candidate:
TagDevice moved to synchronous request context

The previous implementation called TagDevice in a goroutine with an independent 2-minute context (context.Background() + WithTimeout). The new code calls TagDevice synchronously using the request context. Consequences: (a) every anonymous auth now pays the full DB latency (count + insert/update) on the hot path; (b) if the client cancels the request, the request context is cancelled and the device is never tagged, which both skews the usage stat 'stats.anonymous.device.ui.count' and lets a device avoid being counted against the limit. The async design should be retained for non-limit errors and only the limit-exceeded path needs to surface synchronously.

Extra COUNT(*) on every anonymous auth when limit is set

CreateOrUpdateDevice now issues a SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE updated_at BETWEEN ... AND ... on every call when deviceLimit > 0. There is no caching of the count and the check runs unconditionally on the auth hot path, adding a full table scan (or index scan) to every anonymous request even when the limit is nowhere near being reached.

New device_limit setting has no user-facing documentation

The PR adds cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit read from [auth.anonymous] device_limit with default 0 (treated as unlimited), but no documentation file (e.g. docs/sources/setup-grafana/configure-grafana/_index.md or similar) is updated. Operators have no way to learn about the new key, its semantics (0 = unlimited, what happens at the limit, interaction with the 30-day cleanup window), or its env-var override name (expected GF_AUTH_ANONYMOUS_DEVICE_LIMIT). The default sentinel of 0 and the rejection semantics (new devices rejected, existing devices continue to update) also need to be called out.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.

true_positives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
@loaded_locales ||= [] in ensure_loaded! is racy

`ensure_loaded!` does `@loaded_locales ||= []` outside of `LOAD_MUTEX`. Under MRI this is benign because of the GIL, but the assignment is not atomic and the subsequent `@loaded_locales.include?(locale)` is also unsynchronized. The actual file loading is protected by `load_locale`'s mutex, so correctness is preserved, but the pre-check is misleading: two threads can both fall through to `load_locale` and serialize on the mutex for no reason, and a `reload!` interleaved between the `||=` and the include? check could change the meaning of the check. Move the include? and load inside the mutex, or accept the duplication explicitly with a comment.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same unsynchronized lazy initialization and concurrent access to @loaded_locales, specifically the ||= assignment and include? check outside LOAD_MUTEX. Its qualifications about impact do not change the underlying issue identified.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Mixed string/symbol in fallback list causes duplicate locale file loads

`FallbackLocaleList#[]` builds `[locale, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact`. `SiteSetting.default_locale` is a String (from the model) and `:en` is a Symbol, so the array mixes types. `Array#uniq` compares with `eql?`/`hash`, and `:en.eql?("en")` is `false`, so `["en", :en, :en].uniq` returns `["en", :en]` instead of one element. The result is then iterated by `ensure_loaded!`, calling `I18n.ensure_loaded!` for both `"en"` and `:en`. Each call ends up in `translate_accelerator.rb#load_locale`, where `Regexp.new("\\.#{locale}\\.yml$")` matches the same `*.en.yml` file for both the String and the Symbol, so the file is loaded and parsed twice on the first request from an English (or default-English) user. Fix by coercing consistently, e.g. `[locale.to_sym, SiteSetting.default_locale.to_sym, :en].uniq.compact`, and storing/comparing `@loaded_locales` as Symbols in `translate_accelerator.rb`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify inconsistent String/Symbol locale handling as causing duplicate loading of the same locale files and recommend normalizing locales for checks and loading. The candidate adds detail about the fallback list and loaded-locale tracking but addresses the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
FallbackLocaleList subclasses Hash but never uses Hash storage

`class FallbackLocaleList < Hash` only overrides `[]` and `ensure_loaded!`; no value is ever written to the underlying hash. This will silently drop any assignments made by `I18n::Backend::Fallbacks` or callers that expect a real map (for example, an `I18n.fallbacks[locale] = [...]` override in a plugin or future Rails internal). Either drop the `Hash` superclass and just respond to `[]`, or actually populate the hash so callers can read the configured chain (e.g. for diagnostics or plugin overrides).

No test covers the new ensure_loaded! call in set_locale

The added `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` introduces a custom fallback chain (user locale → site default → English) and triggers translation loading on every request, but no controller or initializer test is included. In particular there is no coverage for: (a) anonymous users falling back to `SiteSetting.default_locale`, (b) a logged-in user whose `effective_locale` differs from the site default, (c) the dedup behaviour between `SiteSetting.default_locale` and `:en`. The PR description ("Test 9") does not point at any spec either.

PR description "Test 9" does not describe the change

The PR body is just "Test 9" and there are no specs in the diff, so reviewers and future archeology cannot tell what behaviour was intended to be exercised. At minimum the description should enumerate which fallback chains and which anonymous/logged-in locale combinations are being validated, and link to the relevant spec files.

Test function name not renamed to match the middleware

The test function is still named `TestInstrumentationMiddleware` even though the file and the middleware it tests were renamed to `MetricsMiddleware`. The diff only updates the internal call to `newMetricsMiddleware`, leaving the outer test name stale, which makes the test hard to find, breaks grep-based filtering (`-run TestMetricsMiddleware`), and signals that the rename was applied incompletely.

New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no test coverage

The new `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` (and its `instrumentContext` helper, which builds the `endpoint`/`pluginId`/`dsName`/`dsUID`/`uname` attribute slice) is added with 69 lines of behavior but no accompanying `_test.go` file. The previous `instrumentContext` lived inside `instrumentation_middleware.go` and was likewise uncovered, but the move to a dedicated middleware is the right moment to add at least a basic test that verifies the contextual attributes are correctly populated (including the nil checks for `DataSourceInstanceSettings` and `User`) and are present on the downstream context.

LoggerMiddleware silently loses contextual fields if ContextualLoggerMiddleware is removed from the chain

The previous `logRequest` explicitly added `pluginId`, `endpoint`, `uname`, `dsName`, `dsUID`, and `traceID` as explicit log parameters. The new implementation strips all of those from `logParams` and relies on `m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...)` to pick them up from the request context. That only works if `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` (which calls `log.WithContextualAttributes`) sits between `MetricsMiddleware` and `LoggerMiddleware` in the chain. Today this is true (see `pluginsintegration.go` lines 158-161), but the dependency is now implicit: any future refactor that reorders, conditionally registers, or removes the contextual-logger middleware will cause `Plugin Request Completed` log lines to silently lose identifying fields (plugin id, datasource uid, user, endpoint, trace id) with no compile-time or test-time signal. Either keep an explicit fallback that logs those fields if they are missing from context, or add a test that asserts the chain ordering.

FromContext falls back to a context-less logger when the type assertion fails

`grafanaInfraLogWrapper.FromContext` does `d.l.FromContext(ctx).(*log.ConcreteLogger)`. If the type assertion ever fails (e.g. a future change in `pkg/infra/log` returns a different concrete type, or a test fakes the infra logger), the code falls back to `d.New()`, silently discarding every contextual attribute that `ContextualLoggerMiddleware` placed on the context. Since `LoggerMiddleware` now depends on this method to surface `pluginId`/`endpoint`/`uname` in production logs, a silent attribute drop here directly degrades log quality. Returning the asserted value (or logging/returning an error) is safer than constructing a fresh logger with no context.

validate_each calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which writes to the blocked_emails table (match_count and last_match_at) on every match. The controller sets `response.headers['X-Frame-Options'] = "ALLOWALL"`. `ALLOWALL` is not one of the standardized X-Frame-Options values (DENY / SAMEORIGIN / ALLOW-FROM uri) and browsers ignore unknown values, falling back to whatever default framing policy is in effect. If the host previously sent a stricter value, or modern browsers apply a stricter default, the embed iframe will be blocked cross-origin, defeating the purpose of the embed controller. Use a `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self' https://<embeddable-host>` header (or `ALLOW-FROM` plus that host) to actually permit cross-origin framing.

In `perform_retrieve`, when `SiteSetting.feed_polling_enabled?` is on, the retriever invokes `Jobs::PollFeed.new.execute({})` inline for every embed page load. PollFeed fetches and parses the full RSS/ATOM feed and calls `TopicEmbed.import` on every item. A busy embeddable page can therefore trigger many redundant full-feed imports. The scheduled job should be allowed to run on its own cadence and the retriever should not invoke it inline; only an explicit per-URL RSS lookup should be performed here.

`self.import` first does `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` to decide whether to insert, and only then calls `TopicEmbed.create!`. The migration creates a unique index on `embed_url`, but nothing in `import` rescues the duplicate-key exception that arises if a second concurrent job (e.g. two simultaneous loads of the same embeddable URL while retrieve_topic jobs run in parallel) reaches the insertion point. The losing transaction raises, and since the `Topic.transaction` block already ran a real `PostCreator.create`, an orphan topic and first post are left behind with no `TopicEmbed` row. Either guard the insert with the unique index in a single upsert, or rescue `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique` and re-read the existing record.

`:unsubscribe` is added to the `ensure_logged_in` before_filter list (line 28), so a recipient clicking the unsubscribe link delivered in an email — who by definition is not authenticated — is bounced to the login page before reaching the action. The entire purpose of the per-topic unsubscribe link is to give the user a single, friction-free way out from their mail client; forcing a login defeats that. The action either needs to be excluded from `ensure_logged_in` and instead authorised via a signed, expiring token (the RFC 8058 one-click unsubscribe pattern), or the link should not be sent to anyone who isn't already signed in. As shipped, the new email copy added in server.en.yml (`unsubscribe_link`) and the `unsubscribe_url` interpolation in user_notifications.rb route users into a flow that will not work.

The `unsubscribe` action at lines 98-116 introduces nontrivial behaviour — slug-aware 301 redirect to `topic.unsubscribe_url`, conditional demotion of `TopicUser.notification_level` between `:regular` and `:muted`, mutation via direct `find_by` + `save!` rather than `TopicUser.change` (so it bypasses the `MessageBus` publish and `notifications_changed_at`/`notifications_reason_id` updates other code paths rely on), and rendering `show` via `perform_show_response` — yet the PR adds no controller request spec. This is a copy-paste error: the intent is clearly to compare the slot start time against `workingHour.startTime` and the slot end time against `workingHour.endTime` (i.e., `end` should be `slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()`). Because both sides compare the same point, a slot starting 5 minutes before the working-hour end but lasting well past it (e.g., 60-minute event ending at 6:05 PM with hours ending 6:00 PM) is wrongly considered available.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: the end time is calculated using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime, causing slots that extend beyond working hours to be accepted.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')` compares dayjs instances with `===`. Dayjs objects should be compared with `.isSame()`. The strict equality only works for the same instance reference; two separately constructed dayjs objects representing the same moment are not `===`. false_positives.candidate:
Working hours day check uses UTC, not organizer timezone

`slotStartTime.day()` is computed from `time.utc()` and returns the UTC day-of-week, while `workingHour.days` are in the organizer's timezone (the schedule TZ). For a slot at e.g. 18:30 UTC on Tuesday, the organizer (IST, UTC+5:30) is already at 00:00 Wednesday; `workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())` will fail to match a Wednesday working-hour entry. Slots near the day boundary in the organizer's TZ will be incorrectly marked unavailable. Consequence: false double-bookings prevented, or more commonly, valid slots hidden.

Working hours time check uses UTC, not organizer timezone

`slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` is UTC minutes-since-midnight, but `workingHour.startTime` / `workingHour.endTime` are minutes-since-midnight in the organizer's timezone (per the WorkingHours type comment). Comparing UTC minutes against organizer minutes produces incorrect results for any organizer not in UTC. Even though `checkIfIsAvailable` receives `organizerTimeZone`, it never uses it for the day/time comparison, making the parameter useless for its main job.

Selected-slot availability check skips date overrides and working hours

In the selected-slots branch (lines 581-588), `checkIfIsAvailable` is called with only `time`, `busy`, `...availabilityCheckProps`, and `organizerTimeZone`. It does NOT spread `...userSchedule` (which contains `dateOverrides` and `workingHours`). Because `dateOverrides` and `workingHours` are defaulted to `[]` in the function signature, the date-override and working-hours checks are completely skipped for slots held by users with `selectedSlots`. A user that is on a date-override that closes their availability can still block / be blocked through `selectedSlots`, leading to bookings that violate the organizer's date override.

Date override day comparison mixes timezones

The override day is computed via the server's local timezone (`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format(...)`) which is fragile and depends on the server's TZ. The slot's day is in UTC (`slotStartTime.format(...)`). For slots near midnight in either timezone, the comparison may disagree with what the organizer would consider "their" day, so slots can be mis-attributed to (or wrongly excluded from) a date override. The conversion should be done with the timezone plugin explicitly: e.g. `dayjs(date.start).tz(organizerTimeZone).format('YYYY MM DD')` compared to `slotStartTime.tz(organizerTimeZone).format('YYYY MM DD')`.

Date-override timezone offset formula is incorrect

The new formula is `offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset`, then `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + minute()`. Because `override.start` is a moment in time already represented in UTC, adding `organizerUtcOffset` (the organizer's offset) actively shifts the result away from the correct invitee-local minutes. The correct conversion is to add the invitee's offset only (`dayjs(override.start).utc().add(inviteeUtcOffset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + minute()`) or, cleaner, `dayjs(override.start).tz(timeZone).hour() * 60 + minute()`. With the current formula, an organizer with a non-UTC timezone paired with any invitee in a different timezone will produce override start/end values that are off by the organizer's UTC offset, causing slots to appear at the wrong hour for the invitee.

Unnecessary Date#toString and redundant dayjs calls

`dayjs(override.start.toString())` converts a Date to an ISO string and back to dayjs, which loses no information but is a code smell and risks platform-dependent string formatting. The same `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute')` is computed twice in the return expression; caching it into a local would halve the work and make the intent clearer. Not a correctness bug on its own but worth fixing alongside the offset formula.

New test does not actually verify the timezone fix

The added test reuses the IST schedule for both the IST and the BDT invitee and only asserts the same UTC strings (`08:30:00.000Z` ... `11:30:00.000Z`). Since slots are always returned in UTC and the override's UTC moment does not change, both code paths (original buggy `getUTCHours()` and the new formula) happen to land on the same UTC times for this scenario. The test would not catch the offset-formula bug above (e.g., an organizer in IST with a 14:00 IST override, plus an invitee in `Asia/Dhaka`, would yield wrong slot hours). The PR claims a timezone regression; the test must use a cross-timezone schedule (e.g., organizer in `Asia/Kolkata`, override "14:00" local, invitee in `America/New_York`) and assert the resulting invitee-local slot times to actually prove the fix works.

false_positives.candidate:
Missing `prisma` import causes runtime ReferenceError

The new code added in this PR calls `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key: ... } })` (line 96) but `prisma` is not imported in this file. The imports end at `getAppKeysFromSlug` and `parseRefreshTokenResponse`. Hitting the salesforce CalendarService code path (which happens on every salesforce CalendarService instantiation that goes through `getClient`) will throw `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined`, breaking salesforce bookings entirely for everyone — including self-hosters that never opt into credential sharing. This is an immediate runtime crash for a previously-working integration.

findFirst-then-create is not atomic; webhook can produce duplicate credentials

The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst(...)` followed by `prisma.credential.create(...)` if no row matches, with no transaction and no unique constraint to lean on. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same `(userId, appId)` will both observe no row and both insert a new credential, leaving the user with multiple rows for the same app — a state the rest of the codebase assumes does not happen (e.g. lark's callback, webex/zoom/office365 callbacks all explicitly delete pre-existing rows). The `findFirst` lookup also doesn't filter by `type`, so when the same `appId` exists with multiple legacy `type` values, an update may be applied to the wrong row. The docstring even acknowledges this with "Can't use prisma upsert as we don't know the id of the credential", but a race-free approach (e.g. `prisma.credential.deleteMany({ userId, appId })` inside a transaction, or an upsert on a composite key) would be safer.

Webhook handler accepts any HTTP method and has no body-size, replay, or method check

The handler does not check `req.method`, so any method with the correct secret header (e.g. GET, PUT) reaches the database mutation path; only the secret comparison and `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` flag gate it. There is also no body-size limit, no timestamp/nonce, and no signature scheme beyond a static shared secret. Combined with the fact that anyone in possession of `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` can create or replace credentials for any userId in the system, an attacker who learns or leaks the secret (e.g. via logs, env backups) can rewrite every user's app tokens by replaying the request. At minimum, restrict to POST and verify a recent timestamp.

Credential sync endpoint contract is undefined and inconsistent across integrations

The function POSTs only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` (form-urlencoded) to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` and returns the raw response unmodified. But each integration expects the response to have a different exact shape: google expects `{access_token, expiry_date}`, office365 expects `{access_token, expires_in, refresh_token?}`, hubspot expects a full `HubspotToken`, lark expects `{data:{access_token, refresh_token, expires_in, refresh_expires_in}}`, etc. Self-hosters implementing the parent endpoint have no documentation describing these required shapes (or the URL/return value must instead be customized per app — which contradicts the function being shared). Without a clear spec, the feature is unusable in practice.

Outbound call to sync endpoint has no authentication from Cal.com side

`fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)` is sent with no headers, no signature, and no client identity. The receiving service has no way to verify that the call came from this Cal.com instance or that `appSlug`/`calcomUserId` weren't tampered with by a network attacker or a mis-routed proxy. Combined with the fact that `userId` is trusted blindly to look up tokens server-side, anyone who can intercept traffic to the configured endpoint can impersonate any user. The endpoint should require a Cal.com-issued signature (e.g. an HMAC of the body using a shared key) so the parent service can reject forged refresh requests.

The PR introduces three pieces of behavior with no test coverage: the new `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` webhook (including auth/secret checking, decryption, and the find/update/create branches), `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts` (sharing vs. non-sharing branches, including what the returned value looks like to callers), and `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts` (the broken minimum-token schema and the refresh-token overwrite). The PR description explicitly states no tests were added and existing tests were not run. Given the multiple integration-affecting bugs above, merging without tests risks regressing every OAuth integration.

`crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")` always emits lowercase, but the lookup uses `credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", "")` with no `.toLowerCase()` and no `.trim()`. A user who pastes or types a code with caps, surrounding whitespace, or different separators (space, period) will get `IncorrectBackupCode` even though they have a valid code, which is especially painful here because the input is a long hex string with no character-class hint. true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TOCTOU race allows a single backup code to be used to log in more than once

The backup-code branch decrypts `user.backupCodes`, calls `indexOf`, sets `backupCodes[index] = null`, then re-encrypts and `prisma.user.update`s — but this is done as separate read/transform/write with no `WHERE backupCodes = ...` predicate or transaction. Two concurrent login attempts using the same code both find it at the same index before either write lands, both set the slot to null, and both succeed. Backup codes are explicitly documented as single-use, so reuse defeats the feature. Either wrap the read+write in a transaction with a predicate that matches the current `backupCodes` value (optimistic concurrency) or, better, persist codes as rows so consumption can be a single atomic UPDATE/DELETE on the matching row.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same race condition: concurrent login requests can read and validate the same backup code before either persists its consumption, allowing a supposedly single-use code to authenticate more than once.

true_positives.golden_comment: Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

The booking is marked cancelled in the DB while the actual calendar event remains. Access token `jti` now encodes grant type, session type and lightweight flag visible to clients

`initToken` now sets `token.id(encoder.encodeTokenId(tokenCtx))`, which prepends a 6-character prefix (e.g. `onrtac:`) to the UUID used as the JWT `jti` and as `Details.TOKEN_ID`. false_positives.candidate:
Goroutine and resource leak when NewResourceServer init fails

After constructing the server struct (which creates a cancellable ctx/cancel pair stored on the struct), NewResourceServer now eagerly calls s.Init(ctx). If Init returns an error (e.g., search.init fails partway through, or s.initWatcher fails), the function logs the error and returns nil, err. Because s is nil and cancel was never invoked, any goroutines that Init started cannot be cleaned up: the s.initWatcher goroutine + SQL poller run on s.ctx and will keep polling the database; the search.init watch goroutine (see search.go) runs on context.Background() and is not tied to s.ctx at all, so it is orphaned regardless. There is no way for the caller of NewResourceServer to stop them. Before this PR Init was idempotently deferred to the first RPC, where they would only be retained on the returned server. The fix is to defer cancel() at the top of NewResourceServer (and ideally make search.init's watchctx derive from s.ctx), so a partial init always tears its goroutines down.

search.init's watcher uses context.Background(), preventing server.Stop from stopping it

In searchSupport.init the watch is set up with `watchctx := context.Background() // new context?` and the resulting events channel is consumed by `go func() { for { v := <-events; s.handleEvent(watchctx, v) } }()`. The author even left a question mark in the comment. Because watchctx is background, calling server.Stop (which cancels s.ctx) does not stop this goroutine or its underlying storage backend poller; it will only exit if the storage backend itself is independently stopped. The symmetric watcher created by initWatcher in server.go uses s.ctx and so is cancelled correctly. This asymmetry is also what makes the Init failure leak above worse: even calling cancel after a failed Init cannot reach this watch. search.init should accept and use the long-lived s.ctx (or a child of it) for both WatchWriteEvents and the goroutine, so a single Stop cleans up everything.

The PR correctly changes GetResourceStats from `_, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` to `ctx, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` so the span context flows into the WithTx call below it. The same broken pattern is left in place in this same file for WriteEvent (line 158), create (174), update (236), delete (298), ReadResource (353), ListIterator (388), poller (580), listLatestRVs (619), poll (664) and resourceVersionAtomicInc (718). All of them discard the returned ctx, so the OpenTelemetry spans they start are not parents of the SQL calls made inside them. The fix in GetResourceStats was presumably driven by tracing the new eager index build; the same one-line fix should be applied to all the other methods that start a span and then perform work under that context, otherwise half the storage trace tree is broken.

Init error is logged twice

Init already logs `s.log.Error("error initializing resource server", "error", s.initErr)` inside the s.once.Do block, and the new caller in NewResourceServer then logs the same error again with the same message right before returning nil, err. Pick one site and drop the other to avoid the duplicate entry and to keep the error format consistent with the other NewResourceServer error paths (which only return).

Unlike search.go and sql/backend.go's GetResourceStats, bleve.go's BuildIndex uses `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, tracingPrexfixBleve+"BuildIndex")` and discards the returned ctx. The same trace-propagation bug the PR is trying to fix elsewhere therefore remains in this hot path: the call to `builder(idx)` (which runs the entire list-iterator + builder loop) does not see the BuildIndex span as its parent, and traces of the index build will be missing the bleve-level span. The same one-character fix (`ctx, span := ...`) should be applied here for consistency with the other files in the PR.

The test builds the expected `occurrence` and `event_data` with `build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH)`, so the occurrence's fingerprint is `[f"{handler.detector.id}:val1"]` (via `handler.build_fingerprint("val1")`). false_positives.candidate:
commit() called with one argument but arroyo's Commit requires two

In `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker`, the inner `commit_offsets` closure calls `commit(commit_data)` with a single argument, but arroyo's `Commit` type is `Callable[[Mapping[Partition, int], bool], None]`. At runtime this raises `TypeError: missing 1 required positional argument: 'force'`, which is swallowed by the broad `except Exception` in `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy._commit_loop`. The result is that offsets are never committed, the offset tracker grows without bound, and on restart the consumer re-reads everything it has already processed (defeating the whole point of the commit loop and potentially causing data-integrity issues for non-idempotent result processors). The fix is `commit(commit_data, False)` (or wrap with `CommitOffsets`). The unit tests miss this because they pass a mock with a default for `force`.

test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps references undefined variables

Inside `test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps` only `all_commits` and `test_partition` are defined, but the final assertion reads `committed_offsets[partition] == 103`. Neither `committed_offsets` nor `partition` exists in the test scope, so the test raises `NameError` before any assertion runs and provides no coverage of the gap-fill behavior it claims to test. The assertion should use `all_commits[-1][test_partition]` (or similar) so it actually exercises the production code path.

test_thread_queue_parallel_offset_gaps asserts wrong offset value

After filling the gap by submitting offset 101, all of offsets 100-103 are processed, so `get_committable_offsets` returns `{test_partition: 103}`. `commit_offsets` then adds +1 (it explicitly comments "the committed offset should represent the next offset to read from") and calls `commit({test_partition: 104})`. The test asserts `committed_offsets[partition] == 103`, but the actual value should be 104. This is inconsistent with the first assertion in the same test (`actual_offset == 101` for processing up to 100) which correctly accounts for the +1.

get_queue_for_group uses Python's hash(), not consistent hashing

`get_queue_for_group` is implemented as `hash(group_key) % self.num_queues` and its docstring says "consistent hashing". Python's built-in `hash()` for strings is randomized across processes (PYTHONHASHSEED), so the same `group_key` can be assigned to a different queue on every restart. Within a single process lifetime ordering is preserved (which is what the consumer relies on, since in-flight items are lost on restart anyway), but the function does not provide the cross-process stability the docstring advertises, and it isn't true consistent hashing (e.g. it doesn't survive changes in `num_queues`). Use a stable hash like `hashlib.md5(group_key.encode()).digest()` or `zlib.crc32` and either drop the "consistent" wording or use a hash ring.

--mode help text does not describe thread-queue-parallel

`uptime_options` adds `"thread-queue-parallel"` to the choice list, but the `help` text still reads "The mode to process results in. Parallel uses multithreading." with no mention of the new mode or how its parallelism differs (queue-based, per-group ordering, etc.). Operators picking the mode have no way to know what the new option does or how it differs from the existing parallel modes.

`OrderedQueueWorker.run` emits `remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth` only with `tags={"identifier": self.identifier}`. With `num_queues=20` workers sharing the same identifier, all depth values are aggregated into one series and individual hot queues cannot be distinguished, defeating the purpose of the metric for diagnosing the very backlog problem the PR is meant to address. The worker_id (and ideally the queue index) should be in the tags.

wait_until_empty is dead code

`FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty` is defined but never called by the strategy or factory. It also has subtle correctness issues if ever used (it polls `qsize()` rather than tracking completion, so it can race against in-flight items). Either remove it or document and test its intended use.

The redirect resolution loop iterates from `for i = 0, 1000 do` (line 30) but the original code used `for i = 0, 10000 do` and explicitly noted in the comment that this limit governs whether deep segment trees are joined correctly: 'theoretically this limit means that segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly.' Reducing the limit to 1000 silently breaks any trace whose redirect chain has depth between 1000 and 10000 — those spans will not be merged into the same set. No tests exercise deep trees, so this regression is not caught. Consequence: traces with deep span trees (1000+) end up split across multiple buffer sets and get flushed as incomplete segments, losing parent/child relationships downstream.

Eviction silently drops spans from oversized segments without logging

Lines 62–64 add `if span_count > 1000 then redis.call('zpopmin', set_key, span_count - 1000) end`, which silently removes the oldest (lowest `end_timestamp_precise`) spans from any set exceeding 1000 entries. The previous Python-side check at `_load_segment_data` would `metrics.incr('spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded')` and log an error before discarding the entire segment; this is now gone (see `src/sentry/spans/buffer.py`). The new behavior silently loses individual spans with no metric, no log, no error — only `zpopmin` happens. Consequence: for any segment with more than 1000 spans, downstream flushing will emit truncated segments, and operators will have no signal that data was dropped. Also note that `zpopmin` breaks ties by lexicographic member order when `end_timestamp_precise` is identical (common for sibling spans in the same transaction), making the lost-span set effectively non-deterministic.

`max_segment_spans` constructor parameter is now orphaned

`SpansBuffer.__init__` (around line 150) still defines and stores `self.max_segment_spans = max_segment_spans` with default 1001, but the consumer-side enforcement in `_load_segment_data` that read `self.max_segment_spans` was deleted in this PR. The parameter is still accepted in `__reduce__` callers and tests, but never used. Consequence: configuration knob is misleading and dead; anyone increasing `max_segment_spans` expects larger segments to be allowed, but the Lua-side eviction now silently caps segments at 1000 regardless. The Python constant and constructor argument should either be removed or actually consulted (e.g., passed to the Lua script as a configurable limit).

The change `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` (line 182) introduces a behavior change from the original `results = list(queryset[offset:stop])` for cursors with `is_prev=False` and a negative `offset`. Django's queryset slicing natively supports negative offsets; the new code silently clamps them to 0. The comment ('Performance optimization: For high-traffic scenarios, allow negative offsets…') is misleading — the change actually restricts offset semantics in the base paginator. Consequence: any caller (in this repo or downstream) that previously relied on Django's negative slicing for forward cursors will silently get the first page of results instead of the tail, with no error. There is no test that exercises the negative-offset path, and the change is rolled out to all paginator subclasses (DateTimePaginator, Paginator, etc.) via inheritance.

OptimizedCursorPaginator is a near-verbatim copy of Paginator/BasePaginator with misleading docstring

`OptimizedCursorPaginator` (lines 821–911) duplicates `get_item_key` and `value_from_cursor` byte-for-byte from `Paginator` (lines 222–227) and reimplements `get_result` almost identically to `BasePaginator.get_result`, differing only in whether a negative offset passes through when `enable_advanced_features` is set. The docstring claims 'Negative offset support for efficient reverse pagination', 'Streamlined boundary condition handling', and 'Optimized query path for large datasets', but only the first is implemented (and Django natively), and the others describe no actual behavior. Consequence: dead code, false documentation, and a privileged code path ('control optimizations') that is exposed via a query parameter (see `organization_auditlogs.py`) for superusers, with no test coverage in the diff. A senior reviewer would want this consolidated into a flag on `BasePaginator` rather than a duplicate class.

Privileged pagination feature is gated by a client-controlled query parameter

`use_optimized = request.GET.get('optimized_pagination') == 'true'` (line 70) lets any requester who is also a superuser (or has global access) flip on `enable_advanced_features=True` for that single request. Privileged behavior is typically gated by server-side configuration or user attributes, not a query parameter, because query-parameter gating leaves no audit trail and is trivially selectable. The 'feature' itself just re-enables Django's native negative-offset slicing that the BasePaginator change (line 182 in paginator.py) just removed. Either move the toggle behind a server-side feature flag/setting, or drop it — the parameter offers no functional benefit beyond Django's existing behavior.

No tests cover the new eviction-on-insert behavior

The PR adds Lua-side eviction at >1000 spans (`zpopmin`), but no test in `tests/sentry/spans/test_buffer.py`, `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_buffer.py`, or `tests/sentry/spans/consumers/process/test_flusher.py` constructs a segment with more than 1000 spans to assert (a) the cap is enforced, (b) which spans are kept vs dropped, or (c) that a metric/log is emitted. The existing parametrized tests use 4–5 spans per case. Without a test, a future change to the score semantics (e.g., switching from `end_timestamp_precise` to something else) or to the threshold could regress silently and drop arbitrary spans in production with no detection. At minimum, add a test that pushes >1000 spans into one segment and asserts the flushed result contains exactly 1000 and that the kept spans are the latest by `end_timestamp_precise`.

Two important behavioral changes ship without test coverage: (1) the add-buffer.lua redirect-resolution loop limit is reduced from 10000 to 1000, and (2) the new `OptimizedCursorPaginator` with `enable_advanced_features=True` (used by `OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint` for superusers/global-access members) is exercised in no test in this PR. The audit-logs endpoint change should at least have a test that constructs a request as a superuser with `?optimized_pagination=true` and asserts it returns a successful paginated response, and the redirect limit should be covered by a test feeding a synthetic deep tree.

`cast(SpanEvent, …)` provides no runtime validation; missing `end_timestamp_precise` will KeyError

Line 134 does `val = cast(SpanEvent, rapidjson.loads(payload.value))`, which is purely a type-hint operation at runtime — it does not validate the payload. The very next reference, `end_timestamp_precise=val['end_timestamp_precise']` (line 141), will raise `KeyError` if any incoming payload (older producers, schema drift, malformed Kafka message) omits the field, and `TypeError` if it is `None`. Consequence: a single bad message kills the batch processing and the consumer may stall. Either validate against the schema (e.g., `sentry_kafka_schemas.codecs.decode`) before constructing the `Span`, or guard with `val.get('end_timestamp_precise', default)` and skip/log the malformed message.

Comment claims int(offset) enables negative offsets but it doesn't

Lines 26–27 add `# Performance optimization: Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios / # This enables efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets`, but the actual code is the unchanged `self.offset = int(offset)`. `int()` is just a numeric coercion — it does not 'allow' negatives (Python ints already accept them) and does not change pagination behavior. The comment misleads readers into believing the Cursor constructor is doing something that it is not; the actual negative-offset semantics were (re)moved in `paginator.py`. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. Adding a re-check of `entryPointAssetsCache` after the Lock() (classic double-checked locking) would eliminate the redundant I/O on the cold-start path. The success path on line 48 correctly uses recordStorageDuration, so the error branch should mirror it: d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage). The same pattern is repeated in the Update method (line 129).

Mirrors the bug on line 45. When d.Storage.Update fails, d.recordLegacyDuration(true, ...) is called, attributing the storage failure to the legacy backend in the metrics. The success branch on line 132 correctly uses recordStorageDuration, so the failure branch should be d.recordStorageDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage).

The previous implementation precomputed `updated` from the storage copy, then passed an `updateWrapper{upstream: objInfo, updated: ...}` to both Storage.Update and Legacy.Update so both backends received the exact same resolved object.
