If Storage and Legacy disagree on the previous object (e.g. they have drifted) or if objInfo.UpdatedObject behaves differently in the two implementations, the two stores can now persist different versions of the same object, producing data drift between unified storage and legacy storage. All four async goroutines (Create line 51, Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) derive their context with context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...). `ctx` is the API server request context, which is cancelled as soon as the handler returns and the response is sent. false_positives.candidate:
ensure_logged_in before_filter breaks the email one-click unsubscribe flow

`:unsubscribe` is added to the `ensure_logged_in` before_filter list (line 28), so a recipient clicking the unsubscribe link delivered in an email — who by definition is not authenticated — is bounced to the login page before reaching the action. The entire purpose of the per-topic unsubscribe link is to give the user a single, friction-free way out from their mail client; forcing a login defeats that. The action either needs to be excluded from `ensure_logged_in` and instead authorised via a signed, expiring token (the RFC 8058 one-click unsubscribe pattern), or the link should not be sent to anyone who isn't already signed in. As shipped, the new email copy added in server.en.yml (`unsubscribe_link`) and the `unsubscribe_url` interpolation in user_notifications.rb route users into a flow that will not work.

Per-topic unsubscribe is a GET with side effects, no CSRF token, and no per-user signature Both unsubscribe routes are defined as `get` and the controller action mutates `TopicUser#notification_level`. There is no signed token in `topic.unsubscribe_url` (it is just `#{Discourse.base_url}/t/#{slug}/#{id}/unsubscribe`, which is guessable from the topic id alone) and Rails' request forgery protection only applies to non-GET verbs. Consequence is twofold: (1) any third-party page can CSRF a logged-in Discourse user into being silently demoted from a topic via `` or a similar tag; (2) combined with the `ensure_logged_in` issue above, the action also doesn't authorise the email recipient — once the recipient logs in, whoever's session that is has their preference for that topic changed, which is the wrong user. This should be either a POST endpoint protected by CSRF token, or a GET that requires a server-signed token tied to (user, topic) — the same pattern already used by `EmailUnsubscribeKey` in Discourse.

A regression where the new `%{unsubscribe_url}` placeholder is silently dropped (e.g. a missing I18n interpolation variable, or a typo in the gsub) would not be caught. Add an assertion such as `expect(message_with_unsubscribe.body).to match("/t/1234/unsubscribe")` and one for `html_part` too.

New TopicsController#unsubscribe action has no controller spec

The `unsubscribe` action at lines 98-116 introduces nontrivial behaviour — slug-aware 301 redirect to `topic.unsubscribe_url`, conditional demotion of `TopicUser.notification_level` between `:regular` and `:muted`, mutation via direct `find_by` + `save!` rather than `TopicUser.change` (so it bypasses the `MessageBus` publish and `notifications_changed_at`/`notifications_reason_id` updates other code paths rely on), and rendering `show` via `perform_show_response` — yet the PR adds no controller request spec. This is a copy-paste error: the intent is clearly to compare the slot start time against `workingHour.startTime` and the slot end time against `workingHour.endTime` (i.e., `end` should be `slotEndTime.hour() * 60 + slotEndTime.minute()`). Because both sides compare the same point, a slot starting 5 minutes before the working-hour end but lasting well past it (e.g., 60-minute event ending at 6:05 PM with hours ending 6:00 PM) is wrongly considered available.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same bug: the end time is computed from slotStartTime when it should use slotEndTime.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Identity comparison of two dayjs objects

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')` compares dayjs instances with `===`. Dayjs objects should be compared with `.isSame()`. The strict equality only works for the same instance reference; two separately constructed dayjs objects representing the same moment are not `===`. This branch is intended to detect zero-length (start == end) overrides, and will not trigger when it should.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same bug: comparing two dayjs objects with === checks reference identity, not value, so it never matches. Both recommend using .isSame() instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Working hours day check uses UTC, not organizer timezone

`slotStartTime.day()` is computed from `time.utc()` and returns the UTC day-of-week, while `workingHour.days` are in the organizer's timezone (the schedule TZ). For a slot at e.g. 18:30 UTC on Tuesday, the organizer (IST, UTC+5:30) is already at 00:00 Wednesday; `workingHour.days.includes(slotStartTime.day())` will fail to match a Wednesday working-hour entry. Slots near the day boundary in the organizer's TZ will be incorrectly marked unavailable. Consequence: false double-bookings prevented, or more commonly, valid slots hidden.

Working hours time check uses UTC, not organizer timezone

`slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute()` is UTC minutes-since-midnight, but `workingHour.startTime` / `workingHour.endTime` are minutes-since-midnight in the organizer's timezone (per the WorkingHours type comment). Comparing UTC minutes against organizer minutes produces incorrect results for any organizer not in UTC. Even though `checkIfIsAvailable` receives `organizerTimeZone`, it never uses it for the day/time comparison, making the parameter useless for its main job.

Selected-slot availability check skips date overrides and working hours

In the selected-slots branch (lines 581-588), `checkIfIsAvailable` is called with only `time`, `busy`, `...availabilityCheckProps`, and `organizerTimeZone`. It does NOT spread `...userSchedule` (which contains `dateOverrides` and `workingHours`). Because `dateOverrides` and `workingHours` are defaulted to `[]` in the function signature, the date-override and working-hours checks are completely skipped for slots held by users with `selectedSlots`. A user that is on a date-override that closes their availability can still block / be blocked through `selectedSlots`, leading to bookings that violate the organizer's date override.

Date override day comparison mixes timezones

The override day is computed via the server's local timezone (`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format(...)`) which is fragile and depends on the server's TZ. The slot's day is in UTC (`slotStartTime.format(...)`). For slots near midnight in either timezone, the comparison may disagree with what the organizer would consider "their" day, so slots can be mis-attributed to (or wrongly excluded from) a date override. The conversion should be done with the timezone plugin explicitly: e.g. `dayjs(date.start).tz(organizerTimeZone).format('YYYY MM DD')` compared to `slotStartTime.tz(organizerTimeZone).format('YYYY MM DD')`.

Date-override timezone offset formula is incorrect

The new formula is `offset = inviteeUtcOffset - organizerUtcOffset`, then `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + minute()`. Because `override.start` is a moment in time already represented in UTC, adding `organizerUtcOffset` (the organizer's offset) actively shifts the result away from the correct invitee-local minutes. The correct conversion is to add the invitee's offset only (`dayjs(override.start).utc().add(inviteeUtcOffset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + minute()`) or, cleaner, `dayjs(override.start).tz(timeZone).hour() * 60 + minute()`. With the current formula, an organizer with a non-UTC timezone paired with any invitee in a different timezone will produce override start/end values that are off by the organizer's UTC offset, causing slots to appear at the wrong hour for the invitee.

Unnecessary Date#toString and redundant dayjs calls

`dayjs(override.start.toString())` converts a Date to an ISO string and back to dayjs, which loses no information but is a code smell and risks platform-dependent string formatting. The same `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute')` is computed twice in the return expression; caching it into a local would halve the work and make the intent clearer. Not a correctness bug on its own but worth fixing alongside the offset formula.

New test does not actually verify the timezone fix

The added test reuses the IST schedule for both the IST and the BDT invitee and only asserts the same UTC strings (`08:30:00.000Z` ... `11:30:00.000Z`). Since slots are always returned in UTC and the override's UTC moment does not change, both code paths (original buggy `getUTCHours()` and the new formula) happen to land on the same UTC times for this scenario. The test would not catch the offset-formula bug above (e.g., an organizer in IST with a 14:00 IST override, plus an invitee in `Asia/Dhaka`, would yield wrong slot hours). The PR claims a timezone regression; the test must use a cross-timezone schedule (e.g., organizer in `Asia/Kolkata`, override "14:00" local, invitee in `America/New_York`) and assert the resulting invitee-local slot times to actually prove the fix works.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount update is non-atomic; parallel runs double-count

The handler reads `reminder.retryCount` from the findMany result and writes `reminder.retryCount + 1` in a separate update. If two cron invocations (or this handler and any other process touching the same row) overlap, both will read the same `retryCount` value and both will write `value + 1`, undercounting retries by 1. This matters here because the deletion threshold (`gt: 1`) is tight — a single lost increment means a perpetually-failing reminder is retried indefinitely instead of being deleted after 2 attempts. The update should use a conditional increment (`{ retryCount: { increment: 1 } }`) or be guarded by a `where: { id, retryCount: reminder.retryCount }` clause so concurrent writers can't clobber each other.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same problem. The update writes a stale read of retryCount + 1, so concurrent runs can lose increments. Both suggest Prisma's atomic increment as the fix. The candidate's title says 'double-count', which is inconsistent with its own body, but the body correctly describes undercounting caused by lost increments.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount delete branch is not scoped to SMS method

In the new OR clause of the deleteMany, the `retryCount > 1` branch has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, while the sibling branch is filtered to SMS. The original deleteMany only ever deleted SMS reminders. retryCount is currently only ever incremented in this SMS handler, so today no non-SMS row can reach retryCount > 1, but the schema places `retryCount` on the shared `WorkflowReminder` model (used by EMAIL/SMS/WHATSAPP). If a future change (or manual DB edit) sets retryCount > 1 on an EMAIL or WHATSAPP reminder, this cron will silently delete it. The OR branch should be wrapped under the same `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` predicate as the other branch, e.g. `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, scheduledDate: { lte: now }` OR `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS, retryCount: { gt: 1 }`, or expressed as `method: SMS AND (scheduledDate <= now OR retryCount > 1)`.

false_positives.candidate:
Stale comment above deleteMany

The comment `//delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date` no longer describes the deleteMany. The query now also deletes reminders with `retryCount > 1`, and after the OR rewrite it deletes any reminder (regardless of method) that matches either branch. The comment should be updated to reflect the new semantics, otherwise future readers will misunderstand the cleanup behavior.

No tests cover the new retry/delete behavior

The PR introduces a meaningful behavior change in a cron-handler that mutates the database on every run (increment of retryCount on Twilio failure and on throw, plus deletion of reminders with retryCount > 1). There are no tests in the diff covering: (a) retryCount increments on a falsy return from twilio.scheduleSMS, (b) retryCount increments inside the catch block, (c) deleteMany removing reminders with retryCount > 1, (d) a reminder that fails twice being deleted on the subsequent run. Without tests, regressions in retry semantics (e.g. off-by-one in the threshold, double-increment under retry, or accidentally deleting scheduled rows) would go unnoticed.

Retries continue past scheduledDate once retryCount is < 2

The findMany filter is `scheduledDate: { lte: dayjs().add(7, 'day').toISOString() }`, which still includes reminders whose scheduledDate is in the past. Combined with the new retry logic, a reminder that fails twice will sit in the DB with retryCount=2 and scheduledDate in the past, then be deleted on the next cron run by the `retryCount > 1` branch. However, on the second cron run, after the first failure (retryCount=1) the reminder with a past-dated scheduledDate is not deleted by either branch (date <= now but method=SMS only matches the first OR branch, which it does — actually the date-past branch matches, so this is fine). The real concern is that between the first and second failure, the reminder whose date has passed continues to be passed to twilio.scheduleSMS in subsequent cron runs even though Twilio will obviously reject a send in the past, only to fail again and waste the second retry budget. The findMany should either skip past-dated unscheduled rows or the deleteMany should also delete past-dated + retryCount > 0 rows so a wasted retry isn't spent on an already-elapsed reminder.

Three tests assert expect(conditions).toEqual(Prisma.sql`...`) against SQL returned by the service. The service builds SQL using a reduce over a Prisma.Sql[] array (insightsBooking.ts lines 119-122, 171-174, 204-207), wrapping each inner Sql with `(${acc}) OR (${condition})` or `(${acc}) AND (${condition})`. Each wrap adds new entries to the inner strings array (one per interpolation point introduced by the wrapper). The expected SQL in the tests is written as a single tagged template literal, producing a Sql whose strings array only has entries at the original placeholders. Prisma's Sql class does not override equality, so Vitest's toEqual does structural comparison of strings and values. For example, the team scope test (line 295) expects strings of length 3, while the service produces strings of length 7 after the OR-reduce wraps the two inner Sql fragments with parens. The same mismatch affects the org scope test at line 332 (3 vs 7) and the combined filter test at line 429 (4 vs 7). The simpler tests pass (NOTHING_CONDITION, user scope, single filter eventTypeId, single filter memberUserId) because they use a single template literal in the service that matches the test literal exactly. Suggested fix: compare conditions.toString() against the expected SQL string, build the expected Sql with the same nested reduce pattern, or assert against actual database query results rather than Sql structure. The PR description already flags that tests were not run due to runner configuration issues, but the structural mismatch will cause these specific tests to fail regardless.

The PR description focuses on test updates and does not document this breaking change or describe how existing consumers should migrate to the new pattern of calling getBaseConditions() and passing the resulting Prisma.Sql into prisma.$queryRaw. true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Refresh token is overwritten with the literal string "refresh_token"

After a successful parse, the function unconditionally does `if (!refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token) { refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"; }`. Whenever the parsed payload lacks `refresh_token` (which is true for every credential-sharing response, since the broken schema above never retains one), the real refresh token is replaced in-memory with the placeholder literal `"refresh_token"`. The integrations then write this garbage value into the database (`prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } })`). Future refresh attempts will send the literal string `"refresh_token"` to the OAuth provider and fail with `invalid_grant`, permanently invalidating the credential. false_positives.candidate:
Missing `prisma` import causes runtime ReferenceError

The new code added in this PR calls `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, data: { key: ... } })` (line 96) but `prisma` is not imported in this file. The imports end at `getAppKeysFromSlug` and `parseRefreshTokenResponse`. Hitting the salesforce CalendarService code path (which happens on every salesforce CalendarService instantiation that goes through `getClient`) will throw `ReferenceError: prisma is not defined`, breaking salesforce bookings entirely for everyone — including self-hosters that never opt into credential sharing. This is an immediate runtime crash for a previously-working integration.

findFirst-then-create is not atomic; webhook can produce duplicate credentials

The handler does `prisma.credential.findFirst(...)` followed by `prisma.credential.create(...)` if no row matches, with no transaction and no unique constraint to lean on. Two concurrent webhook deliveries for the same `(userId, appId)` will both observe no row and both insert a new credential, leaving the user with multiple rows for the same app — a state the rest of the codebase assumes does not happen (e.g. lark's callback, webex/zoom/office365 callbacks all explicitly delete pre-existing rows). The `findFirst` lookup also doesn't filter by `type`, so when the same `appId` exists with multiple legacy `type` values, an update may be applied to the wrong row. The docstring even acknowledges this with "Can't use prisma upsert as we don't know the id of the credential", but a race-free approach (e.g. `prisma.credential.deleteMany({ userId, appId })` inside a transaction, or an upsert on a composite key) would be safer.

Webhook handler accepts any HTTP method and has no body-size, replay, or method check

The handler does not check `req.method`, so any method with the correct secret header (e.g. GET, PUT) reaches the database mutation path; only the secret comparison and `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED` flag gate it. There is also no body-size limit, no timestamp/nonce, and no signature scheme beyond a static shared secret. Combined with the fact that anyone in possession of `CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET` can create or replace credentials for any userId in the system, an attacker who learns or leaks the secret (e.g. via logs, env backups) can rewrite every user's app tokens by replaying the request. At minimum, restrict to POST and verify a recent timestamp.

Credential sync endpoint contract is undefined and inconsistent across integrations

The function POSTs only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` (form-urlencoded) to `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` and returns the raw response unmodified. But each integration expects the response to have a different exact shape: google expects `{access_token, expiry_date}`, office365 expects `{access_token, expires_in, refresh_token?}`, hubspot expects a full `HubspotToken`, lark expects `{data:{access_token, refresh_token, expires_in, refresh_expires_in}}`, etc. Self-hosters implementing the parent endpoint have no documentation describing these required shapes (or the URL/return value must instead be customized per app — which contradicts the function being shared). Without a clear spec, the feature is unusable in practice.

Outbound call to sync endpoint has no authentication from Cal.com side

`fetch(process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT, ...)` is sent with no headers, no signature, and no client identity. The receiving service has no way to verify that the call came from this Cal.com instance or that `appSlug`/`calcomUserId` weren't tampered with by a network attacker or a mis-routed proxy. Combined with the fact that `userId` is trusted blindly to look up tokens server-side, anyone who can intercept traffic to the configured endpoint can impersonate any user. The endpoint should require a Cal.com-issued signature (e.g. an HMAC of the body using a shared key) so the parent service can reject forged refresh requests.

The PR introduces three pieces of behavior with no test coverage: the new `apps/web/pages/api/webhook/app-credential.ts` webhook (including auth/secret checking, decryption, and the find/update/create branches), `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/refreshOAuthTokens.ts` (sharing vs. non-sharing branches, including what the returned value looks like to callers), and `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts` (the broken minimum-token schema and the refresh-token overwrite). The PR description explicitly states no tests were added and existing tests were not run. Given the multiple integration-affecting bugs above, merging without tests risks regressing every OAuth integration.

Wrap the decrypt+parse in try/catch and return `ErrorCode.InternalServerError` (or a clearer code) so the response is well-formed and the failure is logged with the user id, instead of an unhandled exception surfacing through NextAuth.

Same issue as in `next-auth-options.ts`: `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(user.backupCodes, process.env.CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY))` is not wrapped in try/catch. If the encrypted payload is unreadable (corruption, schema drift after key rotation, partial DB write), the handler throws an uncaught error and the user is unable to disable 2FA via a backup code — which is the very path designed for 'lost access'. The handler should catch the failure, log it, and return a clear error (e.g. `ErrorCode.MissingBackupCodes` or `InternalServerError`) rather than letting it bubble to a 500.

The PR adds the new backup-code login branch in `next-auth-options.ts`, the new `backupCode` field in the login form, and a new disable-via-backup-code branch in `disable.ts` and `DisableTwoFactorModal.tsx`. The e2e file only exercises the post-enable display dialog (download/copy/close buttons) and does not cover the security-critical paths: logging in with a backup code, exercising the 'Lost access' toggle on the login page, or disabling 2FA via a backup code (the exact flow the feature was built for, and which is gated by `twoFactorLostAccess` and `backupCode` in `DisableTwoFactorModal`). The author explicitly flagged this as a TODO at line 12. Given that backup-code handling involves the TOCTOU race and decrypt-and-parse logic reviewed in the other findings, an e2e that signs in with a valid code and a second time with the same code (expecting rejection) is necessary before merging.

Line 15 awaits the dynamic import directly: `const calendarApp = await appStore[calendarType.split("_").join("") as keyof typeof appStore];`. After the PR, `appStore` values are dynamic-import Promises that can reject if the underlying module fails to evaluate (bad syntax, missing dependency, server-side import error, etc.). true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach(async ...) swallows errors from getCalendar in recurring cancellation path

Lines 457-470 use `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... })`. `Array.prototype.forEach` does not await async callbacks, and there is no try/catch around the dynamic import. If `await getCalendar(credential)` rejects (for example because one of the calendar app modules fails to load), the rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection rather than being routed to the existing `logger.error`/cancellation logic, and the corresponding calendar entries are never deleted. The booking is marked cancelled in the DB while the actual calendar event remains. The surrounding `try/catch` at lines 135-139 (in the reschedule files) gives the false impression that errors are caught — they are not, because async callback errors from forEach escape. The same pattern exists in other files modified by this PR.

false_positives.candidate:
getCalendarCredentials returns Promise values from a synchronous function

After the async refactor, `getCalendar(credential)` now returns `Promise<Calendar | null>`, but `getCalendarCredentials` is still declared as a synchronous function and pushes that Promise into the returned objects as `calendar`. This silently changes the public contract of the exported function: callers that previously received a `Calendar | null` now receive an unawaited Promise, and any new caller (and any existing caller that does not already do `await item.calendar`) will silently treat the Promise as truthy and call methods on it, causing runtime TypeErrors. `getCalendarCredentials` should be made `async` (or the calendar should be awaited inside the flatMap) so the returned `calendar` field is always `Calendar | null`.

forEach(async ...) in vital reschedule swallows getCalendar failures

Line 125 wraps the reference-cancellation loop in `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` inside a `try { ... } catch` block. forEach does not await async callbacks, so a rejection from the dynamic import (`getCalendar` → `appStore[calendarType]` → `import("./...")`) propagates as an unhandled promise rejection rather than being caught by the surrounding try/catch (which only sees sync throws and the resolved values of the inner promises). The reschedule returns success even when calendar delete calls never executed, leaving stale calendar events on the user's calendars.

forEach(async ...) in wipemycalother reschedule swallows getCalendar failures

Same pattern as in `packages/app-store/vital/lib/reschedule.ts`: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { ... await getCalendar(...) ... })` inside a try/catch. forEach does not await async callbacks, so any rejection from `await getCalendar` (caused by a broken app module or a missing dependency) is not routed to the existing `logger.error` branch and becomes an unhandled rejection. Calendar/video deletions can silently fail.

forEach(async ...) in requestReschedule swallows getCalendar failures

Lines 553-567 fire calendar/video deletions with `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); })` and there is no try/catch at all in this scope. Because forEach does not await the async callback, a rejection from `await getCalendar` (from the now-dynamic `appStore[...]` import) becomes an unhandled rejection. The mutation returns success while the prior calendar events on the attendee/organizer calendars may never have been deleted, leading to stale events being shown on those calendars after a reschedule.

getCachedResults awaits all getCalendar calls sequentially inside the map

In `getCachedResults`, the calendars are now loaded with `await Promise.all(calendarCredentials.map((credential) => getCalendar(credential)))`, which is correctly parallelized. However the subsequent `results = calendars.map(async (c, i) => { ... })` then immediately awaits via `Promise.all`, which is fine. The new `getCalendarCredentials` function on the other hand still loads calendars sequentially (one `flatMap` callback at a time), and the `getVideoAdapters` factory in `packages/core/videoClient.ts` was also rewritten as a serial `for` loop rather than a `Promise.all` over credentials. For tenants with several credentials the first booking/cancellation pays N×(module-fetch latency) serially; parallelizing the per-credential fetches would substantially reduce tail latency of the first request after a cold start.

No tests added for the async app-store refactor

This PR converts a large surface area of calendar/video/payment loaders from synchronous to dynamic-import-based, including `getCalendar`, `getVideoAdapters`, `getCalendarCredentials`, the reschedule handlers in `vital` and `wipemycalother`, the cancellation handlers in `handleCancelBooking`, the `requestReschedule` tRPC mutation, the `confirm` mutation's refund path, and both `handlePayment` and `deletePayment`. Despite touching every booking lifecycle path, no test files are added or modified in the diff. There is no coverage that the now-dynamic imports resolve and behave identically, that error paths (missing app, broken module) return null instead of throwing, or that the new `await` placements actually preserve execution ordering. Given the scale of the refactor, this is a significant test gap.
